**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 34 (Saba'), verse 1:**

Surat Saba' is Meccan, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. In al-Tahrir it is said to be Meccan by the consensus of the scholars. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is Meccan except for the verse, ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6]. al-Tirmidhi narrated from Farwah ibn Musayk al-Muradi, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I not fight those among my people who turn their backs?'" [the hadith continues]. In it: "And something was revealed concerning Saba' that was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is Saba'?" [the hadith continues]. Ibn al-Hassar said: this indicates that this story is Medinan, because Farwah's migration came after the conversion of Thaqif in the ninth year. It is possible, however, that his words "and it was revealed" are a report of what was revealed before his migration, so this does not preclude the surah being Meccan.

Its verses number fifty-five according to the Syrian reckoning, and fifty-four according to the others. What is said about forty-five is an error of the copyist's pen. The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that the attributes ascribed to Allah Most High at its beginning are suited to the wisdoms mentioned at the end of the previous surah, in His saying: ﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73], and so on.

Also, it was mentioned earlier that the disbelievers asked about the Hour in a mocking manner, whereas here their denial of it is stated explicitly, and those who affirm the Return are attacked in the most complete manner. Here is also mentioned what relates to that which was not mentioned there. In al-Bahr it is said that the occasion of its revelation was that

[Page 103]

Abu Sufyan said to the disbelievers of Mecca, when they heard ﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women﴾: "It is as if Muhammad threatens us with punishment after we die, and frightens us with the Resurrection. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the Hour will never come to us, and we will never be raised." Allah Most High said: "Say, O Muhammad: 'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be raised.'" This was related by Muqatil. The rest of the surah is a warning and intimidation for them. From this the connection between this surah and the one before it becomes clear. End of quotation.

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. That is: to Him, Mighty and Majestic, belong the creation, dominion, and disposal, by bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death, of everything that exists in them, whether it is intrinsic to their reality or external to them and established within them. It is as if it were said: this world belongs to Him in its entirety. The description of Him, Exalted, with this, according to what Abu al-Su'ud said, serves to establish what the attachment of praise, defined by the definite article of the genus (al-hamd), implies according to the scholars of verification: that all individual created beings are exclusively His, by clarifying His unique and independent possession of what necessitates this. Every other existent besides Him, Glorified be He, including man, is under His dominion, Exalted be He. In its own essence it has no entitlement to existence, let alone to its other attributes. Rather, all of that is bounty overflowing upon it from Him, Mighty and Majestic. Whatever is of this nature is far from deserving praise, which is founded on beauty proceeding from one who is capable and acts by choice. Thus the exclusivity of all its individuals to Him, Exalted be He, becomes clear. In describing Him with what has been mentioned there is also an indication that He, Exalted be He, is the one praised for the blessings of this world, since He follows the praise with what comprises all worldly blessings. The statement is thus like your saying: "Praise your brother who carried you and clothed you," for you mean by it: praise him for his carrying you and clothing you.

As for the conjunction of His saying, Exalted be He, ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ with the relative clause, as is apparent, it indicates that He, Glorified be He, is the one praised for the blessings of the Hereafter, so that the statement is harmonious. In restricting the praise there to the Hereafter as its place, there is an indication that the place of the first praise is this world, and so the two clauses together convey that He, Mighty and Majestic, is praised in this world for its blessings, and that He, Blessed and Exalted, is praised in it for the blessings of the Hereafter. It is also permissible that the statement contains the rhetorical device of al-ihtibak (the figure in which something is omitted from each of two parts and each part is supplied with what is omitted from the other). Its underlying form would be: "All praise is due to Allah..." in this world, and "to Him belongs what is in the Hereafter, and praise in it." Thus what was omitted from each is affirmed in the other. Abu al-Su'ud said: the second clause is for the exclusivity of the praise of the Hereafter to Him, Exalted be He, following the explanation of the exclusivity of the worldly praise to Him, Glorified be He. Here "in the Hereafter" is attached either to the praise itself or to what is attached to "to Him" of the notion of being established. Its being left unqualified by mention of what indicates the one praised for it is not for the sake of being satisfied with mentioning that it is in the Hereafter, without specifying, as it was satisfied earlier with mentioning that the one praised for it is in this world, without mentioning that the praise is also in it. Rather, it is so that it encompasses the blessings of the Hereafter, as in His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land, to settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74], and His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative. He who has settled us in the home of permanence, by His bounty﴾ [Fatir: 34–35], and what serves as a means to attaining them of worldly blessings, as in His saying, Exalted be He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. That is: to that for which the reward is this bliss, namely faith and righteous deeds.

You know that what comes first to the mind is what was established first. The difference between the two praises, given that the blessings of this world and the blessings of the Hereafter are both by way of bounty, is that the first is in the manner of worship, and the second is in the manner of delight and gladness. It has been reported in a khabar (report) that the people of Paradise are inspired to glorify Allah just as they are inspired to breathe. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that the first is obligatory because it is for a bounty bestowed as grace, while the second is not obligatory because it is for a bounty that must be delivered to its deserving recipient, this is based on the opinion of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that Allah is bound to do what is best for His servants). This is so on the understanding that the phrase "for a bounty that must be delivered" is not to be taken unqualifiedly according to them, because what Allah Most High gives His servants in the Hereafter is not restricted, according to them, to recompense. Rather, some of it is grace and some of it is wages.

The predicate is placed before the subject in the second clause to strengthen the restriction derived from the lam, as is common, out of concern for the matter of the blessings of the Hereafter. It has been said: it is for exclusivity, because worldly blessings may come through the agency of one who deserves praise for them, whereas the blessings of the Hereafter are not like this. It seems he meant to strengthen the exclusivity, or he based the matter on the idea that the exclusivity derived from the lam is by the meaning of complete connection (mulabasah), not restriction, as the eminent Yemeni scholar explained in detail. As for his saying that it is for the exclusivity of exclusivity, then, as you see, it is not so. And his statement, "whereas the blessings of the Hereafter are not like this," is refuted by His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. So reflect.

﴿And He is the Wise﴾, who has perfected the affairs of both abodes and arranged them as wisdom requires, ﴿the All-Aware﴾, who knows the hidden aspects of things and their inner contents. It necessarily follows from this that His knowledge extends to other than these. Some have generalized it from the very beginning of the matter. What has been mentioned is based on what some lexicographers said: that khibrah (expertise) is specific to inner realities, since it derives from "khabara al-ard," meaning when he split the earth. In this concluding phrase there is an indication that just as He, Exalted be He, deserves praise because He is a benefactor who merits it, He also deserves it because He, Glorified be He, is described with perfection by choice. The completion of the meaning of His being a benefactor is that it is also in the manner of wisdom and rightness, and with knowledge of the place of entitlement and merit, unlike one who is called a benefactor only metaphorically.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what enters the earth﴾, etc., is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that elaborates on what precedes it) detailing some of the matters that His knowledge encompasses, matters on which their religious and worldly interests depend. It is also permissible that it be an explanation of *Khabir* (the All-Aware), and that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun of Him, Exalted is He, in ﴿to Him belongs what is in the heavens﴾. In that case, (to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter) would be a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*) inserted between the circumstantial clause and its subject. The meaning is: with His knowledge, glory be to Him, of what enters the earth, namely the rain, ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, namely the plants. This was stated by al-Suddi. Al-Kalbi said: what enters it of the dead, and what comes out of it of the substances of minerals. The better view is to generalise both relative clauses, so that they include everything that enters the earth, even by being placed in it, and everything that comes out of it, up to and including animals, since all of them are created from dust.

﴿And what descends from the sky and what ascends into it﴾: that is, of the angels, as stated by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. The better view is generalisation, so that ﴿what descends﴾ includes rain, snow, hail, lightning, decrees and the like. ﴿What ascends﴾ includes vapours, smoke, the deeds of servants, their supplications and the like. By "the sky" is meant the direction of height in general. Perhaps the ordering of the coordinated items, as you have heard, indicates an ascent in praise. The verb *ya'ruju* (ascend) has been taken to include the meaning of motion (*sair*) or settling (*istiqrar*), according to what has been said; therefore it is followed by *fi* rather than *ila*. It has also been said that there is no need to posit this implicit meaning (*tadmin*). By "what ascends into it" is meant what ascends within the thickness of the sky. Knowledge of this entails knowledge of what ascends toward it, a fortiori. So reflect.

Ali, may God honour his face, and al-Sulami read *yunazzilu* with a *ḍamma* on the *ya'* and a *fatḥa* on the *nun* and a *shadda* on the *zay*, meaning that God is the subject. This is what is mentioned in al-Bahr. In al-Kashshaf it is reported from Ali, may God honour his face, that he read *nunazzilu* with the *shadda* and the *nun* of majesty.

﴿And He is the Merciful, the Forgiving﴾, despite the abundance of His blessings and the completeness of His grace, toward those who fall short in fulfilling the duties of thanking them. This closing remark (*tadhyil*), while confirming His awareness, elaborates what was stated in summary in His saying, Glory be to Him: ﴿To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾. From it one learns how all of it is a blessing, and it serves as a kind of insight into the general types of blessings. Each of these is from Him, and of the preceding closing remark, in its proper place, is what follows. So do not imagine that the reverse arrangement is more fitting.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 3:**

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾ By the first-person pronoun they meant the whole of mankind, not themselves alone or only their contemporaries. By negating its coming they meant the complete negation of its existence, not merely the absence of its presence while it is established in reality. They expressed it this way because they were being threatened with its coming. It has also been said that the existence of future temporal events, especially the parts of time, can only be through coming and presence. It has further been said that this is a request for the promised coming to be hastened, in a mocking and derisive manner, like their saying: ﴿When will this promise be fulfilled?﴾ [al-Mulk: 25]
Page 105
The first view is preferable. It has been said that the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, as the coordination of one narrative with another. Making it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) is not evident.

﴿Say: "Yes indeed."﴾ This is a rejection of their statement and an affirmation of what they denied, meaning: the matter is nothing but its coming. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By my Lord, it will certainly come upon you﴾ is an emphasis of this in the most complete and perfect manner. The oath by the Lord came to indicate that its coming is among the affairs of lordship. It was mentioned with the Lord attributed to his pronoun ﷺ, to show the intensity of the oath. Hārūn related, as Ibn Jinnī said, from Ṭalīq, who said: "I heard our shaykhs reading ‘la-ya'tiyannakum’ (it will certainly come upon you) with the yā' of the third person." It is explained that the subject is the pronoun referring to resurrection, because their intended meaning in denying the coming of the Hour was that they would not be resurrected. It has also been said that the subject is the pronoun referring to the Hour, interpreted as the Day or the Time. Abū Ḥayyān criticized this, saying it is far-fetched, since such a construction occurs only in poetry, as in the line:

*"Nor a land whose greenery sprouts as quickly as its sprouting."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Knower of the Unseen﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the one sworn by, according to the view of al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqā', and it was permitted that it be an explicative appositive (ʿaṭf bayān). Abū al-Baqā' permitted that it be an adjective of Him.

It was objected that it is an adjective in the form of the attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah), and that, as Sībawayh stated in the *Kitāb*, such an adjective does not become definite through being attributed to a definite noun. The majority, however, hold that it does become definite through it, and for this reason a group of the eminent scholars held that it is an adjective. He, glorified be He, was described with the comprehensiveness of knowledge, to add support to the emphasis and to intensify it after an intensification. The greatness of the state of the one sworn by indicates the strength of the state of what is sworn about and the firmness and steadfastness of it, for this is like calling a witness to a matter; and whenever the one called as witness is higher in standing, more distinguished in merit and loftier in rank, the testimony is stronger and more binding, and what is testified to is more established and firmer. This attribute was singled out for mention from among the attributes, although every attribute that implies greatness would achieve this, because it has a particular connection to what is sworn about, for it is the most evident of the individual items of the unseen in its hiddenness. Thus, along with preserving the emphasis, there is in it the elegance of an oath in the manner of the line: *"And your front teeth, indeed they are sparkling white."* It is as though it was said: "By my Lord, the Knower of the time of its establishment, it will certainly come upon you." In it there is also an implicit inclusion (idmāj) that there is no discussion about its occurrence.

The author of *al-Farā'id* said: The attribute mentioned was brought because their denial of resurrection was based on the consideration that the scattered, dispersed parts cannot be reassembled as they were. This is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ [Qāf: 4], and so forth. Therefore, describing Him with these attributes is a refutation of their claim of impossibility, namely that one whose knowledge is of this degree cannot be prevented from doing that. End of quote. Al-Ṭībī approved this. In *al-Baḥr* it is said: The oath was followed by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Knower of the Unseen﴾ and what follows it, so that it is known that its coming is from the Unseen, which He, mighty and majestic, alone possesses. What was mentioned earlier is more remote in its implication. The purpose of commanding this degree of oath is that no excuse at all remains for the obstinate ones, for they knew his trustworthiness and integrity (ﷺ), far removed from the stain of falsehood, let alone a false oath. They did not believe him (ﷺ) only out of arrogance. The author of *al-Farā'id* overlooked this point and said: The situation required an oath, because whoever denies what has been said to him, then what is obligatory after that, if the statement is to be repeated to him, is that it be accompanied by an oath; otherwise it would be an error from the standpoint of the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿānī), although correct from the standpoint of Arabic grammar and syntax. Even the clever may be heedless.

Nāfi', Ibn ʿĀmir, Ruways, Salām, al-Jaḥdarī and Qa'nab read *ʿālimu* with a *ḍamma* (nominative), on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the Knower." al-Ḥawfī permitted that it be the subject, whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "The Knower of the Unseen is He." He and Abū al-Baqā' permitted that it be the subject, with the following clause as its predicate.

Ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *ʿallāmi* in the intensive form (ṣīghat al-mubālaghah) and in the genitive. It was also read *ʿālimu* in the nominative, which would be without intensiveness, and *al-ghuyūb* (the unseens) in the plural.

﴿Nothing is hidden from Him﴾ means: nothing is far from Him. From this is the phrase *rawḍun ʿazīb*, meaning a meadow far from people. al-Kisā'ī read it with a *kasrah* on the *zāy*.

﴿Not even the weight of an atom﴾: the measure of the smallest ant ﴿in the heavens or in the earth﴾: meaning existing in them; ﴿nor anything smaller than that﴾: meaning than the weight of an atom; ﴿nor greater﴾: meaning than it. The expression is in the pattern of ﴿It leaves nothing small or great﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) according to the majority. [The phrase] "ʿnor anything smaller … nor greater" is read in the nominative by way of inception and predicate.

The sentence is an emphasis of the negation of being far (ʿuzūb). al-Aʿmash, Qatādah, Abū ʿAmr and Nāfi', in one narration from them, read *wa-lā aṣghara wa-lā akbara* in the accusative, on the basis that *lā* is for the negation of the genus, functioning like *inna*, and its noun is in the accusative with it, because it resembles a prefixed noun (muḍāf), and it is not given tanwīn due to its being an attribute and fitting the pattern of a verb. This is not like *lā māniʿa li-mā aʿṭayta*. The predicate is the same predicate in the reading of the majority. Abū Ḥayyān said: *lā* is for the negation of the genus, and it together with what follows it is a subject according to the view of Sībawayh, and the predicate is ﴿except in a Book﴾. What we have mentioned in explaining the two readings is what many of the eminent scholars held. It has been said that in the nominative reading it is coordinated with ﴿the weight﴾, and in the other reading with ﴿atom﴾, and the fatḥah in it is a substitute for the kasrah because of the attribute and the pattern. This is the view of Abū al-Baqā'. It has been objected that, on this, the meaning becomes, if the exception is connected as is the original, "there is not hidden from His knowledge the weight of an atom in the earth nor in the heaven, nor anything smaller than that, nor greater, except that in a clear Book it is hidden from Him," and its corruption is evident. Al-Sirāj al-Bulqīnī, on the assumption of the mentioned coordination, took the exception to be from an omitted noun, and the estimate being: "nor anything, except that it is in a clear Book." Then he said: there is no harm in omitting what is estimated when the context indicates it. From all of this there results the affirmation that God, exalted is He, has knowledge of every known thing, and that everything is written in the Book. It has also been said that the coordination is with what was mentioned, and the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), and the meaning is: nothing of that is hidden from Him, exalted is He, but it is in a Book. It has been said that the coordination is with that, and the speech is in the style of the line:

*"They have no fault, except that their swords are notched from the clash of battalions."*

So the meaning is: if anything is hidden from Him, it is that which is in a clear Book; but what is in the Book is not hidden from Him, so nothing is hidden from Him. In this there is what there is of remoteness. It has been said: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿is far﴾ and so on is that He is knowing of it. The intended meaning of His saying, glorified be He, ﴿except in a Book﴾ is similar to that, because the Book is the knowledge of God, exalted is He. The meaning is: nothing of the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heaven is hidden from Him except that He knows it; nor anything smaller than that nor greater except that it is in His knowledge. This is like His saying: ﴿Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry, but it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-Anʿām: 59]. In this there is that it is more remote than what precedes it. It has been said: *yaʿzub* means "to appear" and "to go away," and the coordination is with what you have heard, and the meaning is: nothing appeared from God, exalted is He, after His creating it, except that it is written in the Preserved Tablet. Its summary: every created thing is written. In this there is that this meaning of *yaʿzub* is not known; what is known is what was mentioned earlier. Yes, al-Ṣaghānī said in *al-ʿUbāb*: Abū Saʿīd al-Ḍarīr said: it is said, "So-and-so has no wife who makes him *ʿazabah*," i.e., removes his bachelorhood through marriage, like your saying "she nurses him," i.e., she stands by him in his sickness. Then al-Ṣaghānī said: the root indicates distance and withdrawal, so interpreting it as "appearing" is remote, and even if we grant its nearness, then for what reason are "appearing" and "going away" combined? It has also been said that *illā* is in the sense of *wa* (and), and it is implied in the speech, and the speech is complete at ﴿greater﴾, as if it was said: "nothing of that is hidden from Him, and it is in a Book." The use of *illā* in the sense of *wa* was held by al-Akhfash from the Basrans and al-Farrā' from the Kufans.

Some scholars used this to explain: ﴿who avoid the major sins and the abominations, except the minor faults﴾ [al-Najm: 32], and ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hūd: 107]. Makkī mentioned this view regarding the analogous verse, then said: "It is a good view, were it not that all the Basrans only recognize *illā* in the sense of *wa*," as if he had not come across the view of al-Akhfash, who is one of the leading grammarians of Basra, or did not take it into account, which is why he said "all the Basrans." The discussion of this aspect has been extensive, and al-Sirāj al-Bulqīnī approved it, but I do not find it satisfactory, even if a thousand lamps were lit for it.

It has also been said that the coordination is with what you have heard, and the pronoun in ʿ*ʿanhu* (from Him) refers to the Unseen. Then there is no difficulty, for the meaning then is: nothing is far from His Unseen except what is in the Preserved Tablet, because it emerges from the Unseen into the visible and is observed by the Highest Assembly. This was objected to on the grounds that the meaning does not support it, for when an unseen matter emerges into the visible, it is not far from Him; rather it remains in the Unseen as it was, even as it emerges. Its meaning is that its being in the Preserved Tablet is a metaphor for its being among His known things, exalted is He, and these are either hidden or manifest; and everything hidden will become manifest, otherwise it would be non-existent rather than hidden. Its manifestation at the time of its manifestation does not remove its being hidden, so this is not a connected exception. Do you not see that if you said, "the knowledge of the Hour is hidden from people, except their knowledge of it when it arises and they witness it," this exception would not be connected? Thus it has been said, so reflect and do not be heedless. You know that this aspect, even supposing what was objected to is not raised against it, is weak, because the apparent meaning required by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And nothing is far from your Lord of an atom's weight in the earth or in the heaven﴾, and so on, is that the pronoun returns to God, mighty and majestic is He. What Abū Ḥayyān held is that the Book is not the Tablet, and that the speech is merely a metaphor for the control of a thing and its safeguarding.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with both of them, read ﴿nor anything smaller than that, nor greater﴾ with a *kasrah* on the two *rā'*s. It is explained as intending a suffixed pronoun (muḍāf ilayhi), the estimate being "nor smaller than it, nor greater than it." And ﴿than that﴾ is not connected to the elative (afʿal) but is an explanation (tabyīn); since the suffixed noun was omitted, it became vague in form, so it was clarified by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿than that﴾, meaning: "I mean, than that." It is not hidden that this is a grammatical aberration.

The clause ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is related to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿it will certainly come to you﴾, as its cause (ʿillah) and an explanation of what its coming requires. It is therefore part of what is sworn to. The sense of the statement is that wisdom requires its establishment, the all-encompassing and complete knowledge of the Unseen and of all particulars, the manifest and the hidden, is present, and the power required to create the world and what is in it and to make it a blessing, as has passed, is present. The requirement is thus fulfilled and the obstacle removed. There is therefore no sufficiency in the verse in refuting them by oaths alone. Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr) favoured its being related to ﴿and not escapes Him﴾.

Abu al-Baqa' (al-ʿUkbari) held that it is related to this, but this was criticised on the grounds that God's knowledge is not for the sake of the reward. It was also said that it is related to what is related to ﴿in a Book﴾, and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") with respect to its being qualified by what is in its relative clause (al-silah, the clause following the relative pronoun). The distance implied in it is to signal the great distance of their rank in excellence and nobility. That is, ﴿those﴾ who are described as believing and doing righteous deeds, ﴿for them﴾ by virtue of that, ﴿is forgiveness﴾ for what has proceeded from them of certain lapses, which humans rarely are free from, ﴿and a noble provision﴾, good, with no toil in it and no reproach attached to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 5:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by discrediting them and turning people away from believing in them, ﴿seeking to frustrate [them]﴾ (*mu'ajizin*), meaning competing, thinking that they can escape Us. This is the view of Qatadah. Ikrimah said: "defying" (*muraghimin*). Ibn Zayd said: "striving to nullify them" (*mujahidin fi ibtaliha*).

A group read «*mu'jizin*» (with *mukhaffafan*, a light pronunciation of the 'ayn, i.e., without shaddah), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Jahdari and Abu al-Sammal read it *muthaqqalan* (with the shaddah, i.e., *mu'ajjizin*/*mu'ajjizin* in the intensive form). Ibn al-Zubayr said: meaning those who dissuade from faith whoever wishes it, causing weakness in his determination. It was also said: meaning those who make the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, appear weak in their assumption.

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by what has been mentioned, and in this there is an indication of how far their rank is in evil. ﴿For them﴾, because of that, ﴿is a punishment of a painful kind (*rijz*)﴾ — meaning, of the worst and most severe punishment; *min* here is *lil-bayan* (explicative, specifying the kind). ﴿Painful﴾ (*alim*), with *raf'* (nominative), is an adjective of "punishment" (*'adhab*). Most of the seven readers read it with *jarr* (genitive), as an emphatic adjective (*sifa mu'akkidah*) of *rijz*, based on what you have heard of its meaning. Some made it an establishing adjective (*sifa mu'assisah*) for it, on the basis that *rijz*, as related from Qatadah, means punishment in general. It was also permitted to make it an adjective of "punishment" as well, with the *jarr* by proximity (*lil-mujawarah*). The apparent reading is that the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*, i.e., "those who") is the subject, and the predicate is the clause ﴿those, for them is a punishment﴾. It was also permitted that it be in the accusative position as a conjunction with the relative pronoun before it, i.e., "and He recompenses those who strove," and the clause ﴿those, for them﴾ and what follows it is a new sentence, while the one before it is an intervening clause. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), it is possible, on the assumption of conjunction with the relative pronoun, that the two clauses introduced by "those" are themselves the reward and the punishment, and it is possible that they are both new sentences, with the reward and punishment being other than what they contain, such as the eternal pleasure of Allah, Exalted, with the believer and His eternal wrath upon the disbeliever. In this there is an objection: how can it be that this is taken to mean Allah's pleasure and its opposite, when He has explicitly mentioned first forgiveness and generous provision, and, in contrast to it, the painful punishment, and made the first one the recompense?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 6:**

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾, that is, the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those of his community who follow in their footsteps, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, or those among the scholars of the People of the Book who believed, as narrated from Qatadah, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, Ka'b, and their like, may God be pleased with them all.

﴿That which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿is the truth﴾, with the accusative (al-haqqa) being read as the second object of *yara* (see), and the first object being the relative pronoun *al-ladhi*, while *huwa* is the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl).

Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the nominative (al-haqqu), making the pronoun the subject (mubtada') and *al-haqq* its predicate (khabar), so the clause occupies the position of the second object of *yara*. This is the dialect of the Tamim, who treat what is a separating pronoun in other dialects as a subject.

God's words *wa-yara* and what follows begin a new statement, not conjoined to what precedes it, and are intended to cite the people of knowledge against the ignorant who strive against the verses. In al-Kashshaf, it is said to be conjoined to God's words ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come upon us"﴾, meaning: "And the ignorant said: there is no Hour; and those of knowledge know that it is the truth which the one sent down to you has spoken, the truth." This has been criticized as a far-fetched strained interpretation, since the sense of the noble composition only indicates concern for the matter of the Qur'an and nothing more. It has been replied to this: you know well that what precedes it, God's words ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "Will we direct you to a man who will inform you"﴾ etc., concerns the Hour and those who deny the Resurrection, so how could what was mentioned be far-fetched, with the soundness of al-Amir? He mentioned the truth of the Qur'an by way of digression, while the primary purpose is the truth of what was spoken about the matter of the Hour.

Al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi said: *yara* is in the accusative by an implied fatha, conjoined to *yajziya* (that He may recompense), meaning: and that those of knowledge may know, at the coming of the Hour, by direct observation, that it is the truth, as they knew it before by proof, and may argue with it against the deniers. On this view, God's words ﴿And those who strove﴾ are conjoined to the first relative clause, or form a new subject with the sentence being parenthetical, so the separation does not harm, as was supposed.

It is also permitted that by "those of knowledge" is meant those among the rabbis who did not believe, meaning: that they will know on that day that it is the truth, so they will increase in regret and grief.

It has been objected to this that describing them as "those of knowledge" contradicts it, since it is a commendatory description; perhaps the one who permits it does not accept this. Yes, that this is far-fetched cannot be denied, especially since the apparent contrast with God's words

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 7:**

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ requires that it be taken as referring to the believers. ﴿And He guides to the path of the Mighty﴾ who overpowers and is not overpowered, ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾ who is praised in all His affairs, exalted and majestic is He. By "His path" is meant tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and taqwa (God-consciousness). The subject of "yahdi" (guides) is either the pronoun referring to ﴿who was sent down﴾, or the pronoun referring to God, the Exalted; in the latter case there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person) in ﴿the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾. According to the first possibility, the clause is either a new independent sentence, or it is in the position of a hal (circumstantial clause) relating to "alladhi" (who), with an implied mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), meaning "and he guides," as in the line:

*I escaped, and I left Malik to them as a pledge.*

Or it is coordinated with "al-Haqq" (the Truth), with the sense of "and indeed He guides." It is also permissible for "yahdi" to be coordinated with "al-Haqq" as the coordination of a verb with a noun, because it is in the sense of a noun, as in God's words: ﴿in ranks, and folding [their wings]﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "in ranks and folding." The reverse also occurs, in his words:

*I found him one day destroying his enemy, and a sea of giving deserving of the crossers.*

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said, speaking to one another with astonishment and mockery: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). Referring to him (peace and blessings be upon him) in this way is a rhetorical feigning of ignorance, as if they knew of him (ﷺ) only that he was a man, although he (peace and blessings be upon him) was, in their eyes, more evident than the sun:

*Your saying this will not harm him; the Arabs and the non-Arabs know whom you deny.*

﴿Will inform you﴾: will tell you of a matter that is strange and wondrous. Zayd ibn Ali (may God be pleased with both of them) read "yunabbikum" with the hamza replaced by a pure ya', and it is reported from him "yunbi'ukum" with the hamza, from anba'a. ﴿When you are completely torn apart, indeed you will be in a new creation﴾. "Idha" is conditional, and its answer is omitted, since what follows indicates it, meaning "you will be resurrected" or "you will be gathered." According to the view of the majority, it is this omitted answer that governs "idha." The entire conditional clause is an object governed by "yunabbi'ukum," because it has the meaning of "says to you: when you are torn apart completely, you will be resurrected." Then this was emphasized by His words: ﴿indeed you will be in a new creation﴾. It is also permitted that ﴿indeed you will be in a new creation﴾ is the object of "yunabbi'ukum," and it is then suspended (ta'liq). Were it not for the lam in the predicate of inna, it would have been fatha-vowelled, and the clause would take the place of the two objects. On this view the conditional clause is parenthetical (i'tiraḍ). Some people have prohibited ta'liq in the case of a'lamu (to know), but the correct view is that it is permissible, and his words support it:

*Beware, for you have been informed that you are one who will be repaid for what you strive, so you will be happy or wretched.*

It is also permitted that "idha" be purely temporal, in which case its governing element is what the following indicates, presumed to be placed earlier, meaning: "you will be resurrected or gathered when you are torn apart." It is not permissible for the governing element to be ﴿we direct you﴾ or ﴿will inform you﴾, because of the lack of concurrence (in time); nor ﴿you are torn apart﴾, because "idha" is in the genitive position of an annexed noun, and the annexed-to noun does not govern the noun it is annexed to; nor ﴿creation﴾ nor ﴿new﴾, because inna has the initial position, so what follows it does not govern what precedes it.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Idha" is in the accusative position with "muzziqtum" (you are torn apart), and it is like "man" in the conditional sense, governed by the element immediately following it. Al-Sajawandi said: the governing element is omitted, and what follows "idha" governs it only when it is jussive with it, and this is restricted to poetic necessity, as in:

*And when poverty befalls you, then show dignity.*

Therefore the Qur'an is not to be interpreted this way. When it is not jussive, it is annexed to what follows it, and the annexed-to noun does not govern the annexed noun.

Abu Hayyan said: the correct view is that its governing element is the conditional verb, like the other conditional particles. The full discussion of this is in the books of grammar. ﴿Muzzaq﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) that came in the pattern of the passive participle, like *musarrah* in his words:

*Do you not know that my verses are let loose, with no incapacity in them nor forcing?*

Tamzeeq (tearing) of a thing is ripping it and making it into pieces, and from it is his words:

*If you are to be eaten, be the best eater; otherwise overtake me before I am torn apart.*

The intended meaning is: when you die and your bodies are scattered in every possible scattering, such that you become dust and earth.

The accusative of ﴿kulla﴾ (every) is as a verbal noun (masdar). It is permissible that it be a noun of place, in which case the accusative of ﴿kulla﴾ is adverbial (zarf), because it has the rule of what it is annexed to, meaning: when your bodies are scattered in every place, in the graves, in the bellies of birds and beasts, in whatever the torrents have carried off in every direction, and whatever the winds have blown and cast in every place.

﴿Jadid﴾ is an adjective of the form fa'il in the sense of fa'il according to the Basrans, from *jadda al-shay'* (the thing became new), and in the sense of maf'ul according to the Kufans, from *jaddahu* (he cut it), and then it became common for anything new, even if it was not cut, as with a building. The reason for the disagreement is that they observed the Arabs do not make it feminine, and they say *milhafa jadid* (a new sheet), not *jadida*. So the Kufans held that it means maf'ul, while the Basrans held the opposite, and they said the omission of the feminine marker is due to interpreting it as "a new thing," or to treating it as fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Thus it is said.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 8:**

﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah,﴾ concerning what is attributed to Him about the Resurrection, ﴿or is there madness in him?﴾ That is, is there insanity that makes him imagine this and puts it on his tongue? Abu Amr al-Jahiz (d. 255 AH) used this verse as evidence for his view that the truthfulness of a report (sidq, *sadq*) is its correspondence to reality together with belief in it, and its falsehood (kadhib) is the absence of that correspondence together with belief. Anything else is neither true nor false. His argument runs as follows. The disbelievers were intelligent people, native speakers of Arabic who knew the language well, and they restricted the reports of the Prophet ﷺ about the Resurrection to fabrication (iftira'), while the reports concerning Paradise were stated as a restriction on absence of emptiness (*man' al-khuluw*) in the more general sense. There is no doubt that what is meant by the second category is not falsehood, because it is the counterpart (qasim) of falsehood, and not truth, because they believed it lacked truth. Furthermore, their statement ﴿or is there madness in him?﴾ does not indicate the meaning "or is there truth in any way at all." Therefore some of the report must be neither true nor false, so that it may be considered from their perspective to be that, even if in fact it is true. The clarification of this is that the apparent meaning of their words indicates a request to specify one of the two states of the Prophet ﷺ that are equal in the mind of the speaker at the time of reporting the Resurrection. This requires specifying one of the two states of the report. The interrogative here is for affirmation (*taqrir*), and so it establishes that one of the two states belongs to the report. There is no doubt that establishing one of them does not establish an intermediate state (*wasita*), unless their mutual exclusion is taken into account. Likewise, their mutual exclusion in combination does not establish it either; rather, there must be mutual exclusion in negation. That is, his report ﷺ about the Resurrection is not free of one of two mutually exclusive matters. So what is meant by the second is what is contrary to and a counterpart of the first, and it is known that it is not truth. Therefore truth is not merely the correspondence to reality, and falsehood is not merely the lack of such correspondence, as the majority (*al-jumhur*) say. Nor is truth the correspondence to belief and falsehood its non-correspondence, as al-Nazzam says. Rather, the two are expressions of their correspondence and non-correspondence, and an intermediate state is established.

It has been answered that the meaning of ﴿or is there madness in him?﴾ is: "or he did not fabricate." So non-fabrication is expressed by madness, because the madman necessarily has no fabrication, as the reports of the scholars (*al-a'imma*) indicate. Also, the Arabs use the word "lie" (kadhib) for what is done deliberately, and the madman has no deliberate intent. So the second category is not the counterpart of lying but of what is more specific than it, namely fabrication (iftira'). Thus this constitutes a restriction of the report that they considered false to its two types: lying deliberately and lying without deliberate intent. Even if it is granted that fabrication means lying in the absolute sense, the meaning would be: "He intended fabrication, i.e., lying, or he did not intend it, but lied without intent because of the madness in him."

It has also been said that the meaning is: "He fabricated, or he did not fabricate, but rather there is madness in him, and the speech of a madman is not a report, because he has no intention that is taken into account and no awareness." So their intent is to restrict it to being either a false report or not a report at all. Thus a report that is neither true nor false is not established. This was discussed, as is not hidden from anyone who consults the books of the sciences of meaning (*ilm al-ma'ani*).

A question remains here: al-Tibi (d. 743 AH) pointed out that the basis of the argument is that *am* (or) is connective (*muttasila*), and he objected to this, saying that the apparent reading is that it is disconnected (*munqati'a*), either verbally, because the object of the interrogative hamza (*al-hamza*) and of *am* differ, or in meaning. The meaning is that when the stubborn disbelievers presented their statement "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you..." as a matter of conjecture and mockery, pretending ignorance of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his words about the raising and gathering (of the dead), and followed it with their statement ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah?﴾, they turned away from it to something more forceful, ascending gradually from the lighter to the more severe, from attributing madness to him, far be it from him ﷺ. So it is as though they said: "Leave the talk of fabrication, for here there is something more pleasing than it, since how could a sensible person speak of creating a new creation after bones have crumbled and become dust?" Since the reliance was on what comes after the turning away, namely affirming madness, the second turn was placed in the speech of the Exalted as a refutation of their claim, a negation of madness from him, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and an affirmation of it in them, and so on to the end of what he said. The author of al-Kashf (al-Tibi's companion) did not accept this. He said, regarding the words of al-Zamakhshari's Kashshaf, that it is an indication that *am* is connective: "The benefit of shifting from the verb in *junna* (he became mad) is to indicate that what is established is that one of the two parts, as though it were said: 'Is this strange lie from fabrication, or from madness?' The contrast is because the madman has no fabrication. So the argument for disconnection through the difference between the two equal alternatives falls." As for the progression from the connective, it is also as he hinted, in a more subtle manner. End of quote.

You know that the apparent argument requires connection. But al-Khafaji said: "That the argument is based on connection is not accepted, so consider this." The apparent reading is that ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ is the speech of some of them to others. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr (d. 745 AH) said it is possible that it is the speech of a listener who answers one who said "Shall we direct you...", expressing hesitation between two things without deciding on either, because each of them is shocking.

﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ This is a refutation from Him, exalted is He, of what they said in both its alternatives, and an affirmation of what is even more severe and terrible for them. For this reason He placed ﴿those who do not believe﴾ in the position of the pronoun, as a rebuke to them and an indication of the cause of the judgment that follows, as though it were said: "The matter is not as they claimed. Rather, they are in complete derangement of intellect and extreme error regarding understanding and perception, which is madness in reality. And they are in what this leads to of punishment, since they denied the wisdom of Allah, exalted is He, in creating the world, and they denied Him, Mighty and Majestic, regarding His promise and threat, and they exposed themselves to His wrath, glory be to Him." The mention of the punishment before what necessitates and entails it is for hastening to clarify what distresses them and weakens their resolve, and to indicate the extreme speed with which it follows, as though it were racing ahead and it overtakes it. The description of the error as far-off, which is a description of the one who errs, is for emphasis, because if their error is far-off in itself, then how about them and their own selves?

[Page 111]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or drop upon them pieces from the sky.﴾ It has been said: this is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse), brought to remind them of what they see with their own eyes, which indicates the perfection of His power, glory be to Him, and to alert them to the great matters that may occur, to remove their denial of resurrection, to the point that they said what they said about the one who informed them of it, and as a threat for what they dared to do. The meaning is: they were blind, so they did not look at what surrounds them on all sides, of heaven and earth, and did not reflect that they are stronger in creation or it is. And [it means]: if We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them as We swallowed it with Qarun, or drop upon them pieces (*kisaf*, i.e. fragments) from the sky, as We dropped it upon the People of the Thicket, because they denied the signs after the clear proofs had appeared. This is an interpretation suitable to the context, except that linking His saying ﴿If We will﴾ and so on to what precedes it in the way mentioned is remote.

In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*), it is said that He, exalted is He, made them stand, in this matter, before His overwhelming power, and warned them of the encompassing of them by heaven and earth. It is as if there is an omitted circumstantial clause (*hal mahdhufa*), meaning: "Do they not look at what encompasses them of heaven and earth, subdued under Our power, which We dispose of as We wish? If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them," etc. Or: "Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them, encompassing them while they are subdued in what it contains? If We will…" etc. And this does not escape some difficulty.

Al-ʿAllama Abu al-Suʿud said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not looked﴾ and so on, is a resumptive sentence brought to magnify what they dared to do of denying the signs of God, exalted is He, and to emphasize the magnitude of what they said regarding Him, upon him be prayer and peace, and that it is among the great matters that necessitate the descent of the severest punishment and the arrival of the most dreadful torment without delay or postponement. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If We will﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what the mention of their encompassing by the two indicates of the dreaded harm expected from them. In it is an alert that there remains of the causes of its occurrence only the attachment of the Will to it. That is: they did what they did of the enormous evil that entails punishment; so they did not look at what encompasses them from all their sides, such that there is no escape for them from it nor any refuge, ﴿If We will﴾, in accordance with what their crimes necessitate, ﴿We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾, and so on. It is not hidden that in this there is remoteness and weakness of connection relative to what you heard first, together with the fact that what follows does not have much suitability with what precedes it.

It occurs to me that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not looked﴾, is brought to remind them of the most manifest thing to them, such that they witness it wherever they turn, and it does not disappear from their sight wherever they go, which indicates the perfection of His power, glory be to Him, as a removal of what prompted them to that mockery and disparagement of the Master of the Prophets, upon him and upon them be prayer and peace, from their assumption of the deficiency of His power, exalted is He, regarding resurrection and revival, since whoever is able to create those great bodies is not incapable of restoring bodies which are, relative to those bodies, nothing. As He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 81]. In this is an alert to the greater ignorance of theirs indicated by the far error, and what it contains.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e. in what has been mentioned of what is before them and behind them of heaven and earth, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, i.e. a clear indication of the perfection of the power of God, glory and majesty be to Him, and that resurrection after death and the dispersal of the parts encompassed by the two is not beyond Him, ﴿for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾, i.e. one who returns to his Lord, exalted is He, obedient to Him, exalted is His majesty. Because the one who turns in repentance does not fail to look at the signs of God, glory and majesty be to Him, and to reflect upon them, [this is] as an explanation for what His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Have they not looked﴾ and so on indicates of the urging to derive proof from that for what removes their denial of resurrection. In it is an allusion that they turn away from their Lord, glory be to Him, not obedient to Him, exalted is His majesty and exalted is He. And it leads on to mentioning those who turn in repentance to Him, exalted is He, according to one opinion.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If We will﴾ is like a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtiraḍ*), brought to emphasize their shortcoming and to alert that they have reached in it a level by which they deserve in this world, let alone the next, the descent of the severest punishment and the arrival of the most dreadful torment; and that there remains of the causes of that only the attachment of the Will to it, except that it has not been attached for a wisdom. My own view is that this is good, and the verse may bear other than this, and God, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book. It has also been said: that (*dhalika*) is a reference to the verbal noun of ﴿yarawā﴾, which is the seeing (*al-ruʾya*), and it is mentioned because it is interpreted as looking (*al-nazar*), and what is meant by it is reflection (*al-fikr*). And it has been said it is a reference to what follows of the revelation which speaks of what has been mentioned.

Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Ibn Thabbat, ʿIsa, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Musharrif read ﴿yashaʾ﴾, ﴿yakhsif﴾, and ﴿yuskit﴾ with the *yāʾ* in all of them. Al-Kisaʾi assimilated the *fāʾ* into the *bāʾ* in ﴿yakhsif bihim﴾. Abu ʿAli said: this is not permissible, because the *bāʾ* is weaker in sound than the *fāʾ*, so the *fāʾ* is not assimilated into it; and although the *bāʾ* is assimilated into the *fāʾ*, as in *idrib fulānan* (strike so-and-so), and this is like the *bāʾ* being assimilated into the *mīm* as in *idrib mālikan* (strike Malik), the *mīm* is not assimilated into the *bāʾ*, as in *uḍmum bika* (gather yourself with you), because the *bāʾ* is lower than the *mīm* by the loss of the nasalization (*ghunna*) that is in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Kisaʾi read «yakhsif bihim» with assimilation, and it is not strong; and you know that recitation is a followed tradition (*sunna muttabaʿa*), and there exists in it the eloquent and the more eloquent, and that is from God's facilitation of the Qur'an for remembrance. Al-Kisaʾi assimilated only on the basis of transmission (*samaʿ*), so there is no regard for the words of Abu ʿAli nor of al-Zamakhshari.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 10:**

﴿And We certainly gave David grace from Us,﴾ meaning: We gave it to him for the goodness of his turning back (inabah) and the soundness of his repentance. ﴿grace﴾ means blessing and kindness. It has also been said: grace and increase over the other prophets who came before him, or over the prophets of the Children of Israel, or over all who are other than our Prophet (ﷺ). This is because there is no virtue found in any of the prophets (peace be upon them) except that the Prophet (ﷺ) was given its like in actuality, or was able to attain it but chose not to display it. Or it means over the prophets in general. It may be that the less excellent has something that others do not have. The Prophet (peace be upon him) was alone in what is mentioned here. It has also been said: or over all people, so that prophethood, the Book, kingship and a beautiful voice are included in it.

It has been objected that if what is meant is that each of these is a grace not found in other people, then the lack of a kingship like his and a voice like his is open to doubt. If what is meant is the whole collectively, insofar as it is a negation, then it is not found among the prophets either, and there is no basis for restricting it to this sense. I think that ﴿grace﴾ (fadl) is an explanation of "grace" as "kindness," and its indefiniteness is for magnification.

﴿From Us﴾ means without intermediary, to emphasise his intrinsic magnificence by his relational magnificence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We taught him knowledge from Us﴾. Placing it before the direct object is for the sake of attention to what is placed first and the arousing of desire for what comes after, so that it settles in the soul upon its arrival with the greatest settling. Mentioning the affairs of David and Solomon (peace be upon them both) here is for the connection to the mention of the one who turns back (munib) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns back (munib)﴾, as we have pointed out.

Abu Hayyan said: the connection of the two stories, peace be upon them both, to what precedes them is that those disbelievers denied resurrection on the claim that it is impossible. So they were informed of the occurrence of what is, by custom, impossible, which they cannot deny, since their reports and poetry overflowed with some of it. It has also been said: He, glorified is He, mentioned His blessing upon them both as an argument for what He granted our Prophet (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: do not regard this as unlikely, for We have already bestowed favours upon Our servants of old, with such and such. Then, when the illustration concerning him (ﷺ) was complete, the illustration for them returned to Sheba and what their destruction was for their disbelief and insolence.

﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾, meaning: glorify with him. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jarir related it from Abu Maysarah, except that he said: its meaning is that in the language of Abyssinia. The apparent sense is that it is Arabic, from ta'wib, and the intended meaning is: repeat the glorification with him and echo it back.

Ibn Atiyyah said: the root of its past tense is aba, and it was intensified for emphasis. Abu Hayyan criticised this in al-Bahr, saying: it appears that the doubling is for transitivity, because aba meaning "return" is intransitive and takes the preposition lam, so it was made transitive by doubling, since they explained it as "echo back with him the glorification."

It is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) glorified, the mountains glorified like his glorification, with a sound heard from them. God, mighty and majestic, is not incapable of making them glorify with an audible sound. The pebbles glorified in the palm of our Prophet (ﷺ), and his glorification was heard, and likewise in the palm of Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him). Based on this, it is not far-fetched to say that God, exalted is He, first created understanding in them, then addressed them as one addresses those who understand, and commanded them. Some said: God, glorified is He, placed the mountains in the position of rational beings, who, when commanded, obey and submit, and when called, hear and respond. This indicates that there is no animal or inanimate thing except that it is subject to His will, exalted is He, and not resistant to His desire, glorified is He, and as an evidence of the might of Lordship and the greatness of Divinity, in that He called the mountains and commanded them. It has also been said: the meaning of their echoing is that they are moved by it to glorify when they contemplate what is in them. But this, besides being contrary to what is transmitted, is refuted by the word ﴿with him﴾ (ma'ahu). Moreover, he (peace be upon him) has no exclusive claim to the echoing of the mountains in this sense, so that he would be distinguished by it or it would be a miracle for him. It has also been said: he (peace be upon him) used to lament over his sin with a melodious and mournful tone, and the mountains would help him with their echoes.

In this there is an objection: the echo is not in reality the voice of the mountains, but is rather a trace of the voice of the speaker, as established by proof. God, exalted is He, called the mountains and commanded them to echo with him. Moreover, what exclusivity does he (peace be upon him) have in this, when every person's voice has an echo at the mountains?

From al-Hasan: the meaning of ﴿echo with him﴾ is: travel with him wherever he travels. Ta'wib is the travel of the day, as if a person travels by night and then returns the travel by day, that is, repeats it. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

*We joined a tribe who travelled the journey repeatedly, after we had pushed back the rays of the sun, while the glance inclines.*

And the saying of another:

*Two days: a day of halts and gatherings, and a day of travel toward the enemies, returning (ta'wib).*

It was objected to this that the mountains are the pegs of the earth, and their movement was not transmitted along with David (peace be upon him) or others. It has also been said: the meaning is: turn about with him as he turns about, so that when he glorified, they glorified; when he wailed, they wailed; and when he recited the Psalms, they recited.

It was objected that the meaning of ta'wib as "turning about" is not known in the language of the Arabs. It has also been said: the meaning is: return to his purpose in what he intends, such as digging, drawing out springs, extracting ore, and laying out a road. The clause is governed by an implied verb, that is, our saying: O mountains, either as a substitute for ﴿grace﴾ (fadl), a substitute of whole for whole (badal kull min kull) or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), or we say: O mountains, as a substitute for ﴿We gave﴾ (atayna). It was permitted for it to be a substitute for ﴿grace﴾ on the basis that it is permissible to substitute a clause for a singular noun. Abu Hayyan permitted it to be a new independent statement (isti'naf), but this is not the right view.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿Awwibi﴾ with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the waw, as an imperative from al-awb, which means "return." Al-Raghib distinguished between the two: awb is only said of a living being that has volition, whereas return (ruju') is said of it and of other things.

According to the majority, the meaning on this reading is: return with him in glorification. The command to the mountains is like the command to a single feminine entity, because the plural of non-rational things permits this. From it is the saying: O horses of God, mount (irkabi). Likewise ﴿other uses﴾ (Ta-Ha: 18). This has also come in the plural of feminine rational beings, as the poet said:

*We left the horses and the cherished camels, and we said to the women: stay with them.*

But this is rare.

﴿And the birds﴾ is in the accusative case. According to Abu Amr ibn al-Ala, it is by implying a verb, its estimate being: and We subjugated the birds for him. Abu Ubaydah related from him that it is by coordination with ﴿grace﴾, and there is no need for an implied verb, because His giving them to him (peace be upon him) is His subjugating them for him. Al-Tibi mentioned that this is like the saying: I fed it straw and cold water. Al-Kisai said: also by coordination, except that he estimated a noun in the genitive, that is, and glorification for birds, and this is not needed. Sibawayh said: al-tayr is coordinated with the grammatical position (mahall) of ﴿mountains﴾, like the saying: O Zayd and al-Dahhak, go! with al-Dahhak in the accusative. Some grammarians prohibited this, because of the necessary presence of ya with a definite vocative marked with al-.

The one who permits it says: many a thing is permissible as a follower but not permissible independently. Al-Zajjaj said: it is accusative as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ah). Abu Hayyan objected that this is not permitted, because before it is ma'ahu, and an object of accompaniment does not admit two of its kind except by apposition or coordination. Just as one cannot say "Zayd came with Amr with Zaynab" except by coordination, so it is here. Al-Khafaji said: ma'ahu does not prevent this, whether it is attached to awwibi as an adverbial complement (zarf laghw) or is made a circumstantial phrase (hal), because the two are different governed elements: the adverbial complement or circumstantial phrase is not the object of accompaniment, and each is a category of its own. What misleads people is only the word of accompaniment. So what Abu Hayyan raised is not valid, even if it is thought to be. Worse than the fault is the excuse given, which was answered by saying that the conjunction waw may have been omitted from His saying ﴿and the birds﴾ because of the heaviness of two waws together, or that the second's dependence is considered after the first's dependence.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Hurmuz, Abu Yahya, Abu Nawfal, Ya'qub, Ibn Abi Ablah, a group from the people of Medina and Asim in one transmission read ﴿wal-tayru﴾ with a nominative. It was explained as coordinated with ﴿mountains﴾ according to its form and vowel, because the vowel that has arisen resembles the case-ending, and what is tolerated in a follower is not tolerated in the one followed. It has been said that it is coordinated with the concealed pronoun in ﴿awwibi﴾, and the intervening adverbial complement justifies this. It has also been said that it is by an implied ﴿let the birds echo﴾, like what was said regarding His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ (al-Baqarah: 35; al-A'raf: 19).

It has also been said that it is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the predicate omitted, meaning: and the birds echo.

﴿And We softened for him the iron﴾, and We made it in his hand like wax and dough: he shapes it as he wills, without fire or striking with a hammer. This was said by al-Suddi and others. It has been said: We made it soft relative to his strength, which We gave him, as hearing is soft relative to the powers of the rest of mankind.

[Page 115]

﴿Make full coats of mail﴾. "An" is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle here, and the preposition has been omitted: the sense is "We made the iron soft for him for the making of full coats of mail," or "We commanded him to make full coats of mail." The first is preferable. Al-Hawfi and others allowed that it is an explanatory (mufassirah) "an." Since the condition for an explanatory "an" is that it be preceded by the sense of speech without its letters, and ﴿and We made soft﴾ does not contain that, some scholars held that a verb with the sense of speech is implied before it, to make it valid as an explanatory "an." The meaning would be: "and We commanded him that make," that is, "make." It has been objected to this that omitting the explained element is not attested.

Al-sabighat means coats of mail. Its origin is an adjective from subugh, which means completeness and perfection, and the term came to be predominantly applied to coats of mail, as with al-abtah. The poet said:

"Neither full coats of mail nor a stout, bold shield
Protect against death when the appointed terms are fulfilled."

It is also said sawabigh, as in his saying:

"Upon them are black, fierce warriors, their coats of mail
Full and white, which arrows cannot pierce."

Thus there is no need to supply a noun modified, meaning "coats of mail that are full." This does not count as a defect in the reasoning, despite the claim that an adjective which is not specific to its noun may not have its noun omitted, as with "menstruating" (ḥā'iḍ), whose noun is not omitted. It has been read as ṣābighāt, replacing the sīn with ṣād because of the ghayn.

﴿and be measured in the joining of the links﴾. Al-sard is, originally, weaving, as al-Raghib said: stringing together what is rough and thick. Al-Shammakh said:

"Our horses swiftly appeared in your homes,
As the reins' braided thongs follow one another."

It was borrowed for the stringing together of iron. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is the following of one thing by another of its kind. A coat of mail is called masrūdah because the rings are joined to one another in it. The poet said:

"And upon the two of them are masrūdah coats of mail, which Dawud decreed,
Or the work of the full coats of mail, a Tubba' [king] of Yemen."

For its maker, there are sarrād and zarrād, with the sīn replaced by a zāy. Many interpreters explained it here as weaving, and said the meaning is: be moderate in weaving the coats of mail so that their rings are proportionate. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted from him by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim through several chains, explained it as the rings, that is, make their rings of proportionate sizes. Ibn Zayd said: do not make them small, so that they are weak and the coat of mail cannot defend, nor large, so that its wearer is harmed through its gaps. Another narration from Ibn 'Abbas explained it as the rivets, and this was also transmitted from Qatadah and Mujahid. That is, measure its rivets: do not make them thin, nor thick, but make them of a fixed measure, in thinness and in size, suited to the hole prepared for them in the ring. If they are thin, they will move loosely in it and not hold its two ends; if they are thick, they will split the edge of the ring in which they are placed and so will not hold either. What makes this unlikely is that the softening of iron for him, peace be upon him, was such that it was like wax and dough, which makes riveting unnecessary. For after gathering the rings and inserting some into others, the separation of the two ends of each ring is removed by blending the two ends, as the two ends of a ring of wax or dough are blended. The securing by this is more complete than securing by riveting; indeed, with it there remains no need for riveting at all. So if it is authentic, it is based on the premise that he, peace be upon him, made the rings without blending the two ends of each, and then riveted them to secure them after inserting some into others. This appears on the second interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We made the iron soft for him﴾, since the utmost of strength is cutting iron as one wishes without a tool, without joining one part to another. This does not conflict with what is reported from al-Biqa'i, who said: "Some who saw what is attributed to Dawud, peace be upon him, of coats of mail told us that they had no rivets." For this is transmitted from an unknown person, and such a report is not to be relied upon.

It has also been said that the meaning of "and be measured in the joining of the links" is: do not spend all your time on it, but only the amount by which you obtain sustenance; and devote the rest to worship. It is said this is the more suitable reading in light of the command that follows. It is related that he, peace be upon him, was the first to make coats of mail of rings, when previously they had been plates. This is related from Qatadah.

It is also reported from Muqatil that when he, peace be upon him, was made king over the Children of Israel, he would go out in disguise and ask the people about their condition. An angel appeared to him in the form of a man, and he asked him, and the man said: "What an excellent servant, were it not for a flaw in him." He said: "And what is it?" The man said: "He is given sustenance from the public treasury, and if he ate from the work of his hands, his virtues would be complete." So he called upon Allah, Exalted, to teach him a craft and make it easy for him, and He taught him the craft of coats of mail and softened the iron for him, and he prospered
[Page 116]
and spent a third of his wealth on the interests of the Muslims. He would finish a coat of mail in part of a day or part of a night, and its price was a thousand dirhams.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in (Nawadir al-Usul), and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn Shawdhab, who said: "Dawud, peace be upon him, would produce one coat of mail each day and sell it for six thousand dirhams: two thousand for himself and his family, and four thousand with which he fed the Children of Israel white bread." It is also said that he would sell the coat of mail for four thousand, spending from it on himself and his dependents and giving charity to the poor. In (Majma' al-Bayan), it is related from al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he made three hundred and sixty coats of mail, sold them for three hundred and sixty thousand dirhams, and thus became independent of the public treasury.

﴿And work righteousness﴾. This is addressed to Dawud and his family, peace be upon them. Although no mention of them has preceded, they are understood by implication from his mention, as al-Khafaji said. It has also been permitted that it is addressed to him, peace be upon him, alone, as an honour. In either case, the apparent meaning is a command to righteous deeds in general, and it is not, on the second interpretation, a command to make coats of mail free of defect.

﴿Indeed I am Seeing of what you do﴾: so I will reward you for it. This is the reason given for the command, or for the obligation to comply with it, by way of encouragement and warning.

﴿And for Solomon, the wind﴾: that is, We subjected the wind to him. It was also said that ﴿for Solomon﴾ is coordinated with "to him" in "We made iron soft for him," and that "the wind" is coordinated with "the iron." The softening of the wind is an expression for its subjection.

Abu Bakr read "ar-rīḥu" (the wind) in the nominative, taking it as a subject (mubtada') with ﴿for Solomon﴾ as its predicate (khabar). The sentence then implies an omitted genitive construction (muḍāf), meaning: "and for Solomon is the subjection of the wind." Many scholars held that it is a subject, and that the phrase governed by the preposition is a specific complete predicate (kawn khāṣṣ), with no omitted genitive construction, meaning: "and for Solomon, the wind is subjected." In my view, on both readings the sentence is coordinated with His saying, ﴿And We had certainly given David a bounty from Us﴾, etc., as the coordination of one narrative with another narrative. Ibn al-Shaykh said: the coordination on the first reading is with "We made iron soft for him," and both sentences are verbal. On the second reading, the coordination is with a nominal sentence that is implied, which that verbal sentence indicates, not with the verbal sentence itself, because of the difference between them. It is as if it were said: "What We have mentioned for David and for Solomon: the wind, for it was for him like a slave specially belonging to its owner, who directs it as he wishes and travels on it wherever he wills." He then said: the verse does not say "and with Solomon the wind," because its movement is not the movement of Solomon. Rather, it moves by itself, and the movement of Solomon and his troops is by its movement, and it carries them wherever he wills. This is unlike the mountains' echoing of praise (ta'wīb), which followed David's echoing, peace be upon him, which is why the word "with him" (ma'ahu) is used there.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ḥaywa and Khālid ibn Ilyās read "ar-riyāḥu" (the winds) in the nominative, in the plural. ﴿Its morning journey is a month and its evening journey is a month﴾: that is, its travel in the morning covered the distance of a month, and its travel in the evening was likewise. The sentence is either a new independent sentence or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the wind." A genitive construction must be supplied in the predicate, because morning and evening travel are not themselves the month but occur within it. There is no need to supply one in the subject, as Makki did when he said: "that is, the journey of its morning is the distance of a month, and the journey of its evening is likewise," for this is obvious. Ibn al-Ḥājib said in his Amālī: the benefit of repeating the word "month" is to inform the reader of the duration of the morning and the duration of the evening. Expressions that mark quantities do not admit pronominalization. Do you not see that you say "the weight of this is a mithqāl and the weight of this is a mithqāl," and pronominalization is not appropriate here, just as it is not appropriate in a specification (tamyīz)? Furthermore, if it were pronominalized, the pronoun would refer to what preceded it only by virtue of its specific identity, and when it lacks that identity, it is necessary to revert to the explicit noun. Do you not see that if you honored a man and clothed that very man, the expression would be "I honored a man and clothed him," but if you honored a man and clothed another man, the expression would be "I honored a man and clothed a man." Thus it is clear that it is not the placing of an explicit noun in the position of a pronoun. So said al-Ṭībī in his marginal notes, may God have mercy on him. It is not hidden that what he mentioned is based on what is most common. Otherwise, God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Neither is a long-lived man granted extended life, nor is anything reduced from his lifespan﴾ [Fāṭir: 11]. He did not limit the information to the duration of the morning so that the duration of the evening could be inferred from it, because the wind often becomes still or its movement weakens in the evening. So the explicit statement of the duration of the evening journey removed the suspicion of a difference between the two periods. Qatāda said: the wind would carry him in the morning until midday a distance of a month, and in the evening from after midday until sunset a distance of a month.

Aḥmad, in his al-Zuhd, related from al-Ḥasan that he said concerning the verse: Solomon, peace be upon him, would set out in the morning from Jerusalem and take his midday rest at Iṣṭakhr, then set out from Iṣṭakhr in the evening and take his midday rest at the fortress of Khurāsān.
