The story of this wind has been mentioned in some ancient poetry. Wahb said, and al-Bahr transmitted it from him: "I found verses engraved on a rock in the land of Kaskar, by one of the companions of Solomon, peace be upon him, and they are:

We, and there is no power save the power of our Lord, set out from the lands, from the land of Tadmur.

When we set out, our time of return was a journey of a month, and our morning departure was for the last [part of the day].

People who sold their souls to God willingly, for the victory of the son of David, the pure prophet.

For them is a bounty and an elevation in the lofty matters of religion, and if they are ever ascribed to a lineage, they are from the best of folk.

Whenever they mount the obedient wind, it hastens, eager, not falling short of its month.

Birds in ranks shade them, and whenever they flutter above them, they do not startle them."

He also mentioned, may God be pleased with him, that he, peace be upon him, had his residence at Tadmur, and that the jinn had built it for him with flat stones, pillars, white marble and red marble. He said: and about this al-Nābigha says:

Except Solomon, when God said to him: "Arise in the wilderness, and turn it back from the desert,

and the host of jinn: I have indeed permitted them to build Tadmur with flat stones and pillars."

End of quotation. What he mentioned about Tadmur is the well-known view among the common people, and al-Tha'ālibī mentioned it in his tafsir together with the verses cited, but in al-Qāmūs, "Tadmur," on the pattern of "Tanṣur," is the daughter of Ḥassān ibn Udhayna, and the city was named after her. This clearly contradicts the other account. Perhaps reliance is placed on what is in the Qāmūs if reconciliation is not possible. And God, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "ghadwatuhā" and "rawḥatuhā" on the pattern of "fa'lah," which denotes a single occurrence of going in the morning (ghadā) and going in the evening (rāḥa).

﴿And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him﴾: that is, of melted copper, from the verb qaṭara, yaqṭuru, qaṭran and qaṭarān, with the ṭā' either vocalized with sukūn or with fatḥa. It was said that the metals are copper, iron and others. The first view is that of the majority of linguists, and by "the spring of copper" is meant the copper mine. But God, glorified is He, caused it to flow just as He softened the iron for David, so that it gushed forth as water gushes from a spring. For this reason it was named "the spring of copper" after what it became. Al-Jalabī mentioned that the attribution of flowing to the spring is metaphorical, as in "the flowing of the river."

Al-Khafājī said: if "spring" here means flowing water, and the idafa (construction) is like "lujayn al-mā'" (silver of the water), then the attribution is not permissible, and it is merely a metonymy of the first kind, on the basis that the spring is the source of water. But there is no need for this. Then reflect.

Some said: "qiṭr" is copper, and "ʿayn" means "essence" (dhāt). The meaning of "asalnā" is "we melted." The meaning then is: We melted copper for him, in the manner in which iron used to become soft for David, peace be upon him, so that works could be fashioned from it while it was cold and without fire. Nothing had become soft or melted for anyone before him.

The apparent meaning, supported by reports, is that God placed it in its mine as a spring flowing like springs of water.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿIkrima that he said concerning the verse: God caused copper to flow for him for three days, flowing like water. It was asked: "To where?" He said: "I do not know." Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from al-Suddī that he said: a spring of copper flowed for him for three days. In al-Baḥr it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī and Mujāhid that they said: it was made to flow for him, peace be upon him, for three days and their nights, and it was in the land of Yemen. In another report from Mujāhid, the copper flowed from Ṣanʿā'. It was also said: it used to flow for three days in the month.

﴿And of the jinn were those who worked before him by the leave of his Lord﴾: the prepositional phrase may be connected to an omitted element that is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), with "man" (those who) in the position of a subject (mubtada') in the nominative case. It may also be connected to an omitted element that functions as a fronted circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddam) from "man," which is in the accusative case, coordinated with "the wind." It is also permissible that "of the jinn" be coordinated with "the wind," with "min" being partitive, and "man ya'mal" (those who work) being a substitute for it, but this is a forced reading. The verb "ya'mal" is either treated as intransitive, or its object is omitted and explained by what will follow, God willing, so that it is a detailed explanation after a general statement, which is more effective for the soul. ﴿By the leave of his Lord﴾: by His command, mighty and majestic.

﴿And whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾: that is, whoever of them turns away from what We commanded him, namely obedience to Solomon, peace be upon him. It was read as "yuzigh," with a ḍamma on the yā', from "azāgha," in the active voice, with its object omitted, meaning: whoever inclines and turns himself or others away. It was also said to be in the passive voice, so that no object needs to be supplied. ﴿We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾: that is, the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter, as most exegetes said, and this was related from Ibn ʿAbbās. Some said the intended meaning is his punishment in this world.

It was related from al-Suddī that he, peace be upon him, had with him an angel holding a whip of fire, and whenever a jinn disobeyed him, he would strike him from a place the jinn could not see. In some reports, he would burn whoever opposed him. The burning of a jinn, even though he was created from fire, is not impossible, for according to us he is not pure fire; rather, fire is the predominant element in him.

[Page 117]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 34, Verse 13:**

﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries﴾. *Mahārīb* is the plural of *miḥrāb*. As ʿAṭiyyah said, it means a palace (*qaṣr*). It was named after its owner because he fights (*yuḥārib*) others in defending it. In origin, *miḥrāb* is an intensive form (*ṣīghat al-mubālaghah*) meaning someone who engages in much fighting. It is not transferred from the name of an instrument, although some scholars permitted that view. Ibn Ḥayyūs said:

*He combined bravery and humility before his Lord; how fine is the sanctuary within his sanctuary.*

It is also applied to the known place where the imam stands in front of the congregation (*ṭāq*). This was among the things introduced into mosques and did not exist in the first generation, as al-Suyūṭī said, and he wrote a treatise on this matter. For this reason, the jurists disliked standing inside it.

Ibn Zayd said: the *maḥārīb* are dwellings. It was also said that they are places reached by stairs, like upper chambers (*ghuraf*). Mujāhid said: they are mosques, named after some of them by way of metonymy (*tajawwuz*), as was said. This is based on the view that *miḥrāb* is the name of a chamber in the mosque in which God Most High is worshipped, or of the imam's standing place.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Qatādah that it is to be explained as both palaces and mosques together.

The clause ﴿They made for him whatever he willed﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*) detailing what they did. It has been permitted that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), but as you see, that is far-fetched.

﴿And statues﴾. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: they were images of animals. Al-Zamakhsharī said: images of angels, prophets and righteous people were made in the mosques, of copper, brass, glass and marble, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. The making of images was permissible in that law, as the verse says: Solomon (ʿalayhi al-salām) made statues of copper, and he said: "O Lord, breathe spirit into them, for they are more capable of service." God Most High then breathed spirit into them, and they served him.

And Isfandiyār was among their remnants. This is one of the most wondrous marvels, and it is not appropriate to believe in its authenticity; it is nothing but a fable (*ḥadīth khurāfah*).

As for what is narrated, that they made for him (ʿalayhi al-salām) two lions at the bottom of his throne and two eagles above it, so that when he wished to ascend, the two lions spread their forelegs for him, and when he sat down, the two eagles shaded him with their wings, this is a matter not far-fetched, for such a thing could be done with mechanisms that move at ascent and at sitting, moving the forelegs and wings. Human craftsmanship has reached something similar in strangeness.

It was also said: the statues were talismans (*ṭalsamāt*). One makes a statue of a crocodile, a fly or a mosquito, and the thing represented does not go beyond that place as long as the statue remains there. The making of such things is well known from the philosophers, and it cannot be accomplished, in their view, except through certain celestial configurations. On the gate known as the Gate of the Talisman (*Bāb al-Ṭalsam*), one of the gates of Baghdad, there is a statue of a snake, which they claim is to prevent snakes from harming people within Baghdad. We have witnessed many times people who were bitten by snakes: some were not harmed, and some were slightly harmed. We have never witnessed anyone die from that. Yet those bitten outside Baghdad rarely escape. But we do not believe that the statue has any role in what was mentioned. We suppose that this is due to the weakness of the kind of snakes found in Baghdad and the little harm they naturally cause.

It was also said that the statues were images of trees or animals with their heads removed, which was permitted in our law. There is no need to commit to that if it is authentically transmitted. For the truth is that the prohibition of depicting a complete living creature was not in that law; it is in our law. And we make no distinction between an image that has a shadow and one that does not, such as the image of a horse drawn on paper or a wall, for example.

Makkī related in *al-Hidāyah* that a people permitted depiction, and al-Naḥḥās also related it, as did Ibn al-Faras, and they argued from this verse. You know that in our law there is a severe threat against image-makers, which has been reported, so this view is not to be heeded, and it is not valid to argue from the verse. It seems that statues were prohibited only because, with the passage of time, the ignorant took them as objects of worship and thought that placing them in temples was for that purpose, so the worship of idols spread. Or it was a closing of the door to any resemblance to idol-worshippers altogether.

﴿And basins﴾: the plural of *jafnah*, which is what food is placed in, in general, as many have mentioned. Some lexicographers said: the *jafnah* is the largest of bowls, followed by the *qaṣʿah*, which feeds ten; then the *ṣaḥfah*, which feeds five; then the *miʾkalah*, which feeds two or three; then the *ṣaḥīfah*, which feeds one. Accordingly, the meaning here is general, due to the apparent sense of His saying ﴿like cisterns﴾, that is, like great reservoirs, the plural of *jābiyah*, from *jibāyah*, meaning gathering, because it is where things are gathered. It is originally a metaphor in the sense of a place or a relation, since things are gathered into it, and not a *jābiyah* itself. Then it came to be used specifically for that vessel by the dominance of usage, as the word *dābbah* came to be used for quadrupeds.

The comparison of the *jafnah* to the *jābiyah* occurs in their speech. Among it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*A basin of the family of al-Muḥallaq removed blame, like a cistern of Iraqi flowing water overflowing.*

And the saying of al-Afwah al-Awdī:

*And cauldrons like hills fixed firmly, and basins like full cisterns.*

It is mentioned concerning the size of Solomon's basins (ʿalayhi al-salām) that upon each one of them a thousand men could sit.

It was read as *kāljawābī* with a *yāʾ*, which is the original form. Its omission is by suffice of the kasra, and treating the *al-* as having the role of the tanwin: just as it is omitted with tanwin, so it is omitted with what replaces it.

﴿And cauldrons﴾: the plural of *qidr*, which is what food is cooked in, made of earthenware or other material, in a particular shape. ﴿Fixed firmly﴾: immovable upon their stands (*athāfī*), not moving from them because of their size. This is said by Qatādah. It was also said: they were enormous like mountains.

The mihrabs were mentioned before the statues because the images are placed in the mihrabs or carved on their walls. The basins were mentioned before the cauldrons, although the cauldrons are the instrument of cooking and the basins are the instrument of eating, and cooking comes before eating. This is because, when the royal buildings were mentioned, it was fitting to indicate the magnificence of the banquet spread within them. So the basins were mentioned first, because they are present there, unlike the cauldrons, which are not present there. This is indicated by His saying ﴿fixed firmly﴾, according to what you heard earlier. It seems that when the state of the basins was explained, the mind longed to know the state of the cauldrons, so they were mentioned for the sake of connection.

﴿Work, O family of Dāwūd, in gratitude﴾. By supposing a verb of saying (*taqdīr al-qawl*), it is either a resumptive sentence or a circumstantial clause from the implied subject of (*sakhkharnā*, "We subjected"). *Āl* is a vocative noun from which the vocative particle has been omitted. *Shukran* is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*). In this there is an indication that work should be for gratitude, not for hope or fear. Or it is in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) of *iʿmalū*, since gratitude is a type of work, so it is like "I sat the crouching sitting." It was said: it is for the implied *ushkurū* (give thanks). It was said: it is for the implied *ushkurū*, or it is a circumstantial clause in the sense of an active participle, meaning "work while giving thanks," because gratitude encompasses the heart and the limbs. Or it is an attribute of an implied verbal noun, meaning "work a work of gratitude." Or it is an object of *iʿmalū* in the sense of a direct object, so the sentence is like your saying "I performed the obedience." It was also said that *iʿmalū* was used in place of *ushkurū* by way of verbal correspondence (*mushākalah*) to His saying, Glorified is He, (*yaʿmalūn*, "they work").

Ibn al-Ḥājib said: it was made a direct object by way of metonymy (*tajawwuz*). Whatever the case, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā and al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* narrated from Ibn Masʿūd who said: when it was said to them, "Work, O family of Dāwūd, in gratitude," there did not pass an hour upon the people without someone among them standing in prayer. In another narration: the prayer place of the family of Dāwūd was never empty of someone standing in prayer by night and by day, and they took turns at it. Solomon (ʿalayhi al-salām) used to eat barley bread and feed his family the coarse bran, and the poor the finest wheat flour, and he never ate his fill. It was said to him concerning this, and he said: "I fear that when I am full I will forget the hungry."

Some eminent scholars permitted the inclusion of Dāwūd (ʿalayhi al-salām) within "family" here, because the family of a man may include him.

This is supported by what Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* narrated from al-Mughīrah ibn ʿUtaybah who said: Dāwūd (ʿalayhi al-salām) said: "O Lord, has anyone of Your creation spent a night with a longer remembrance of Me than I?" God Most High revealed to him the frog. And God, Glorified is He, sent down to him (ʿalayhi al-salām): ﴿Work, O family of Dāwūd, in gratitude﴾. Dāwūd (ʿalayhi al-salām) said: "How can I bear Your gratitude, when it is You who bestow favor upon me, and then You grant me gratitude for the favor? The favor is from You and the gratitude is from You, so how can I bear Your gratitude?" He, exalted is He, said: "O Dāwūd, now you have known Me with the true knowledge of Me."

And it came in a narration of Ibn Abī Ḥātim from al-Fuḍayl that he (ʿalayhi al-salām) said: "O Lord, how can I thank You when gratitude is itself a favor from You?" He, Glorified is He, said: "Now you have thanked Me, when you knew that the favors are from Me." Likewise, what al-Firyābī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid who said: Dāwūd said to Solomon (ʿalayhimā al-salām): "God Most High has mentioned gratitude, so relieve me of standing at night, and I will relieve you [of standing in the night]." He said: "I cannot." He said: "Then relieve me of the prayer of the day," and he relieved him of it.

﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the one who gives thanks for all his states. In *al-Kashshāf*: it is the one who devotes himself to rendering gratitude, spending his utmost effort in it, having occupied his heart, tongue and limbs with it, by acknowledgment, conviction, striving, and most of his times. Al-Suddī said: it is the one who gives thanks for gratitude itself. It was also said: it is the one who sees his inability to give thanks, because his being guided to gratitude is a favor that calls for another gratitude, without end. Some have versified this:

*If my gratitude for God's favor is itself a favor upon me, for which gratitude is due in turn, then how can gratitude be attained except by His bounty, even if the days are long and life is extended?*

*If it touches me with blessings, its joy spreads; and if it touches me with hardship, the reward follows it.*

I have already heard what was narrated from Dāwūd (ʿalayhi al-salām). This sentence may be included in the address to the family of Dāwūd, which is the apparent meaning, or it may be an independent sentence brought as information for our Prophet (ﷺ), and in it is an admonition and an encouragement toward gratitude.

Ḥamzah read *ʿibādī* with a sukūn on the *yāʾ*, and the rest read it with a fatḥah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 14 (part 1 of 2):

﴿فَلَمّا قَضَيْنا عَلَيْهِ المَوْتَ﴾ ("Then when We decreed death for him"). It is said: the meaning is that We brought death upon Sulayman, judging him to die. In Majma' al-Bayan (*Majma' al-Bayan*, a tafsir by al-Tabarsi), the meaning is that We ruled on him with death. It is also said: We made it obligatory for him. In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, a tafsir by Abu Hayyan), the meaning is that We carried out upon him what We had decreed for him from eternity, namely death, and brought it into the realm of existence. This has some strain. In any case, the intended sense of *qada'* ("decree," a term for divine determination) here is not the same as *qadar* ("predestination"). So reflect. *Lamma* ("when") is a conditional particle, whose condition and response is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿ما دَلَّهم عَلى مَوْتِهِ إلا دابَّةُ الأرْضِ﴾ ("Nothing showed them his death except a creature of the earth"). It has been cited as evidence that *lamma* is a particle (*harf*), but this is open to question. The pronoun in ﴿دَلَّهُمْ﴾ ("showed them") refers to the jinn who used to work for him, peace be upon him. It is also said that it refers to the family of Sulayman, but the outward sense rejects this, given the words of Allah, the Exalted, after it: ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ﴾ ("the jinn saw clearly").

The intended "creature of the earth" is the *arada* (termite), with a fatha on the *alif* and the *ra'* [i.e., *arada*, plural *arad*]. It is a small creature that eats wood and similar things, and it is called *surfah* (a type of termite), with a damma on the *sin* and a sukun on the unpointed *ra'*, and with a *fa'*. In *Hayat al-Hayawan* (*Hayat al-Hayawan*, a zoological work by al-Damiri), on the authority of Ibn al-Sikkit, it is a creature with a black head and the rest of its body red. It makes for itself a square house from fine sticks, joining them together with its saliva, then enters it and dies. There is a proverb: "More skilled than a *surfah*." In al-Bahr it is called *susat al-khashab* (woodworm). As for *al-ard* (earth), according to Abu Hatim and a group, it is the verbal noun of *aradat al-dabbah al-khashab, ta'ruduhu* (the creature ate the wood), from the pattern *darab, yadribu*. So the construction *dabbat* ("creature") with *al-ard* is an *idafah* (genitive construction) of a thing to its action. This is supported by the recitation of Ibn Abbas and al-Abbas ibn al-Fadl, *al-aradi* (with a fatha on the *ra'*), since it is a verbal noun of *arida* (to be eaten), from the pattern *'alima*, the intransitive counterpart of *arada* from the pattern *darab*. One says *aradat al-dabbah al-khashab* (the creature ate the wood) with a fatha, then *ufida* with a kasra, just as one says *akalat al-qawadih al-asnan akla* (the decayed teeth ate the teeth, a consuming), then *ukilat akla*. So *al-ard* with a sukun is the act of eating, and *al-arad* with a fatha is the being affected by that act. The first may be interpreted as the being-affected that results from the verbal noun, so that the two recitations agree. It is also said that *al-arad* with a fatha is the plural of *aradah*, and the *idafah* of *dabbah* to it is an *idafah* of the general to the specific. It is also said that *al-ard* with a sukun has its well-known meaning, and the *idafah* of *dabbah* to it is because its action is mostly within it. It is also said that it is because it affects wood and similar things just as the earth affects them when they are buried in it. Other explanations have been given. The first interpretation is the better one, even though *al-ard* does not carry this meaning elsewhere in the Qur'an.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿تَأْكُلُ مِنسَأتَهُ﴾ ("eating his staff") are in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject) relating to *dabbah*, meaning: eating his staff. The *minsa'ah* is the staff, from *nasa'at al-ba'ir* (she drove the camel), when she drove it, because it is driven with it. Or it is from *nasa'atuhu* (she delayed it), when she delayed it, and from this comes *al-nasi'* (the intercalation of months). It appears from this that it is the large staff carried by the shepherd and his kind.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir and a group recited ﴿مِنساتَهُ﴾ ("his staff," with an *alif*). Its original form is *minsa'atahu*, so the hamza was changed to an *alif*, an irregular substitution. Abu 'Amr said: "I do not hamzate it, because I do not know its derivation. If it is one of the words that is not hamzated, then I have been careful; and if it is one of the words that is hamzated, then it may be permissible for me to omit the hamza in what is hamzated." Perhaps this explains the reason for choosing the recitation without a hamza. With the hamza it comes in the verse of the poet:

*I struck with a staff his face, so he became by that humiliated and abased.*

And without it in his words:

*When you walk upon the staff from old age, the play and the flirting have gone far from you.*

Ibn Dhakwan, Bakkar, al-Walid ibn Abi 'Utbah, Ibn Muslim and others recited ﴿مِنسَأْتَهُ﴾ ("his staff," with a sukun on the hamza). This is from making the vowelled letter quiescent for ease, and it is not a regular pattern. The grammarians considered this recitation weak, because it requires that the letter before the feminine *ta'* be quiescent, not an *alif*. It is also said that its regular form is to ease it *bayna bayn* (between the hamza and its vowel), and the transmitter did not record it correctly. Harun ibn Musa al-Akhfash al-Dimashqi recited as evidence for the sukun in this recitation the words of the rajaz poet:

*A man struck by wine rose from his drunkenness, like the rising of the old man to his staff.*

It was also recited with a fatha on the *mim* and an eased hamza, by changing and deleting it. Also ﴿مِنساءَتَهُ﴾ ("his staff," with a long vowel) on the pattern *mif'alah*, as one says *miid'ah* (a vessel for ablution), which is the vessel for ablution; it is also applied to its place, *miid'ah*. It was recited ﴿مِنسِيتَهُ﴾ with the hamza replaced by a *ya'*. A group, among them Amr ibn Thabit, reported from Ibn Jubayr, recited ﴿مِن﴾ as a separate preposition ("from") and ﴿ساتِهِ﴾ with a kasra on the *ta'*, meaning the tip of the staff. Its origin is what bends from the two ends of a bow. It is also called *siyah* (the end of a bow), and it was borrowed for what was mentioned, either as a technical borrowing, because it was green and bent from leaning on it, as you will hear, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the narrative, or as a linguistic usage, using the restricted term for the general. From what has been mentioned, the rejection of what al-Batalyawsi said is known, after he had quoted this recitation from the readers: that it is pretentious, not permissible to be used in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and there is no transmission or report of it. Moreover, it does not agree with the story of Sulayman, peace be upon him, because he was not leaning on a bow; he was leaning on a staff.

It was also recited ﴿أكَلَتْ مِنسَأتَهُ﴾ ("ate his staff") in the past tense. The sentence is then either also a *hal*, with *qad* implied or not implied, or a resumptive explanatory sentence (*isti'naf bayani*).

﴿فَلَمّا خَرَّ﴾ ("Then when he fell"), meaning he fell down. ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ﴾ ("the jinn saw clearly"), meaning they came to know, after the matter of Sulayman's life and death had been obscured to them. ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الغَيْبَ ما لَبِثُوا في العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ ("that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment"). That is, had they known the unseen as they claimed, they would have known his death at the time it occurred, and they would not have remained after him for a year in the hard labour until he fell. By "the jinn" who knew this is meant the weaker jinn, and by those from whom knowledge of the unseen was negated are meant their leaders and great ones, as is narrated from Qatadah. It is also permitted that the intended matter obscured to them is the matter of knowledge of the unseen. Or "the jinn" means the species as a whole, so that what applies to some is ascribed to all. Or the intended ones are their great ones who claimed knowledge of the unseen, meaning: those among them who claimed knowledge of the unseen came to know their own incapacity and that they do not know the unseen. Although they had known their own state before this, the purpose is mockery of them, as you say to a falsifier when you have refuted his argument: "Have you now seen clearly that you are a falsifier?", while you know that he has always been thus, clearly.

It is also permitted that *tabayyana* means *bana wa zahara* (became evident and appeared). Then it is intransitive, without an object, as in the first interpretation, for its object there is ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا﴾ etc. In this interpretation, it is a *badal* (substitution) for "the jinn," a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), like "Zayd's ignorance became clear to him." The appearing is really attributed to it, meaning: when he fell, it became evident to people and the jinn that, had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in punishment. According to what has been established, there is no need to posit an implied possessive noun which is the real subject of *tabayyana*, except that after its omission the second term of the possessive is put in its place and the verb is ascribed to it; then ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا﴾ etc. is made a *badal* from it, a *badal kull min kull* (total substitution). The original would be: "the matter of the jinn became clear, that had they known..." Some have treated the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ etc. as a qiyas (syllogism) whose major premise is omitted, so it is as if it was said: "Had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment; but they remained in the humiliating punishment; so they do not know the unseen." The use of *tabayyana* meaning *bana wa zahara* as intransitive, and meaning *adraka wa 'alima* as transitive, is found in the speech of the Arabs. The poet said:

*It has become clear to me that shortness is humiliation, and that the tall of men are the best.*

Another said:

*O Fatimah, I am dying, so make it clear to yourself, and do not grieve; every creature dies.*

In al-Bahr, quoting Ibn 'Atiyyah, he said: Sibawayh held that *an* has no grammatical position (*mawdi' min al-i'rab*), but it is treated as an oath with a verb meaning certainty and conviction, because these verbs, such as "become certain," "become convinced," "know," and similar, take the place of an oath, and *fa-ma labathu* ("then they did not remain") is the response of the oath, not the response of *law* (if). So reflect on it, for I can hardly conceive it as a view worth considering.

In *Amali al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam* (*Amali*, a work of dictations by al-'Izz ibn 'Abd al-Salam), it is stated that *al-jinn* is not the subject of *tabayyanat* but is a *mubtada'* (topic), and ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is its predicate, the sentence explaining the pronoun of the matter in ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ﴾. Otherwise the meaning of the speech would be: when Sulayman died and fell, it became evident to them that they did not know the unseen. Their knowledge of their not knowing the unseen does not depend on this; rather the meaning is: "the story became clear, what it is," and the story is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ أنْ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الغَيْبَ ما لَبِثُوا في العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ ("the jinn saw clearly that had they known the unseen they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment"). It is strange that such a view should come from one of his stature. What he took as a barrier to the *fa'iliyyah* (being the subject) of "the jinn" is refuted by what you have heard in the explanation of the verse, as is not hidden.

In the book of al-Nahhas (*I'rab al-Qur'an*, a grammatical work by al-Nahhas) there is an indication that it was recited ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنَّ﴾ ("the jinn," with an accusative) with the sense that *tabayyanat* means *'alimat* (knew), with the subject being the pronoun of humans and jinn, and *al-jinn* being its object. Ibn 'Abbas, as Ibn Khalawayh mentioned, and Ya'qub with a variant from him, recited ﴿تُبِيِّنَتِ﴾ in the passive. Ubayy recited ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الإنْسُ﴾ ("mankind saw clearly"), and al-Dahhak reported ﴿تَبايَنَتِ الإنْسُ﴾ ("mankind distinguished themselves"), meaning: separated and recognized one another. The pronoun in ﴿كانُوا﴾ ("they were") refers to the jinn mentioned earlier. Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الإنْسُ أنَّ الجِنَّ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الغَيْبَ﴾ ("mankind saw clearly that the jinn, had they known the unseen..."). These are recitations which differ considerably from the consonantal text of the codex.

Among the narratives of the story: it is reported that it was Sulayman's habit, peace be upon him, to seclude himself for long periods in the mosque of Jerusalem. When his term drew near, he did not wake in the morning without seeing in his prayer niche a tree growing, which Allah the Exalted had made speak. He would ask it, "For what purpose are you?" and it would say, "For such and such." This went on until one day he saw the carob tree and asked it. It said: "I am a plant for the ruin of this mosque." He said: "Allah the Exalted would not ruin it while I am alive. You are the one whose purpose is my destruction and the ruin of Jerusalem." So he uprooted it, planted it in a wall of his, and made from it a staff. He said: "O Allah, conceal my death from the jinn, until it is known that they do not know the unseen, as they pretend." He said to the Angel of Death: "When you are commanded concerning me, inform me." He said: "I have been commanded concerning you, and a single hour of your life remains." So he summoned the jinn, and they built around him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and his soul was taken while he was leaning on it. The jinn used to gather around his prayer niche wherever he prayed; no jinni would look at him in his prayer without being burned. A jinni passed by and did not hear his voice; then he came back and did not hear it; so he looked, and behold, Sulayman had fallen dead. They opened up to him, and behold, the staff had been eaten by the termite. They wished to know the time of his death, so they placed the termite on the staff, and it ate from it an amount in a day and a night. They calculated accordingly and found that he had died a year before. They had been working before him, supposing him alive. So it became evident that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in punishment for a year.

It is not hidden that this is a matter of guesswork and of confining oneself to the least likely estimate. Otherwise it is possible that the termite began eating only a long time after his death, and that it used to eat at times and leave off at other times.

[Page 122]

Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on surah 34, verse 14 (part 2 of 2)

As for the claim that its (the staff's) beginning was during his life, that is far-fetched. And the claim that it was by revelation to a prophet at that time, as has been said, is also weak, because if that were so they would not have needed to place the termite on the staff in order to learn the period. It is narrated that Dawud (peace be upon him) founded the building of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem) on the site of the tent of Musa (peace be upon him), but he died before completing it. He therefore bequeathed it to Sulayman, who ordered the jinn to complete it. When one year of his life remained, he asked that his death be concealed from them until they finished it, and so that their claim of knowing the unseen would be disproven. This, on its apparent meaning, contradicts what is narrated: that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was the one who founded Bayt al-Maqdis forty years after the Ka'bah, then it was ruined, and Dawud restored it and died before completing it. Also, Musa (peace be upon him) did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis but died in the wilderness (al-tih). In an authentic hadith (al-hadith al-sahih, a hadith whose chain and text meet the strictest criteria of authenticity) it is related that he (peace be upon him) asked his Lord at the time of his death to bring him near the Holy Land a stone's throw away. Also, it has been narrated that Sulayman had finished building the mosque, worshipped in it, and then prepared for the Hajj, in thanks to Allah Most High for that.

It has been answered regarding the first point that what is meant is the renewal of the foundation. Regarding the second, that what is meant by the tent of Musa is his inherited tent, which they used to pitch and worship in, seeking blessing, and not that it was pitched there in his own time (peace be upon him). This answer requires a transmitted report, since such a matter is not said by personal opinion. If it is so, then it is welcome. It has also been said that what is meant is the gathering place of worship according to the religion of Musa, as occurs in the hadith: "the tent of faith" (fustat iman).

Al-Qurtubi said in al-Tadhkirah: what is meant by it is a faction separated from others and gathered together, likened to a tent. What is wrong with these two (explanations) is not hidden, even if it is said that they are more apparent than the first. As for the third point, it is answered that what is meant by "finishing" is nearness to finishing, and what is near to a thing has its ruling. But this is far-fetched. It has been preferred that this is one report and that is another report, and Allah Most High knows best which of the two is sound.

It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) ordered a lofty palace (sarh) to be built for him, and they built it. He entered it alone so that for one day in his life he could be free of turbidity. A young man came in to him and he said: "How did you enter upon me without permission?" He said: "I entered with permission." He said: "And who gave you permission?" He said: "The Lord of this palace." So he knew that he was the Angel of Death who had come to seize his soul. He said: "Glory be to Allah, this is the day in which I sought tranquillity." He (the angel) said to him: "You sought what has not been created," and he steadied himself by leaning on his staff, so his soul was seized, and his death remained hidden from the jinn until it (the staff) fell.

It is narrated that Afridun came to ascend his throne, and when he drew near, two lions struck his leg and broke it, so no one after him dared to approach him. For this reason the jinn did not come near him, and the matter of his death was hidden from them. It has been criticized that Sulayman came after Musa by a long period, while Afridun was before him, because Manujahr was one of the descendants of Afridun, and Musa appeared in his time.

On all the reports indicating his death (peace be upon him), his falling occurred when the staff was broken because of its weakness from the termite eating it. The indication of the verse by it is an attribution to a distant cause.

Among the strange things is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: that he (peace be upon him) died in his place of worship, on his bed, having locked the door upon himself, and the termite ate the minsa'ah, that is, the threshold of the door. When it (the door) fell (kharra), his death became known. For in this there is the making of the pronoun in (kharra) refer to the door, and some have gone this way. But in this there is the point that the threshold is not known to be called minsa'ah, and also the required form would have been kharrat with the feminine ta', and its omission in such a case does not occur except in poetic necessity. And that the masculine form is used in the sense of "the roof" is far-fetched. So the apparent conclusion is that the report from the scholar (al-hibr, i.e., Ibn 'Abbas) is not sound, and Allah Most High knows best. Al-Baghawi related from him that the jinn thanked the termite, so they bring it water and clay inside the wood. This is something I do not say and I do not believe that this report is sound either.

His age (peace be upon him) was fifty-three years. He became king after his father when he was thirteen years old, and he began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign. Then he passed away and ended, and Glory be to Him whose dominion does not end and whose authority does not cease.

In the verse there is evidence that the unseen (al-ghayb) is not restricted to future matters, but also includes events that have occurred and are hidden from the person as well.

When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the state of those who are grateful for His blessings and turn back to Him, the Exalted, He mentioned the state of those who are ungrateful for the blessing and turn away from Him, may His majesty be exalted, as an admonition to the Quraysh and a warning to whoever disbelieves in the blessings and turns away from the Benefactor. ﴿Indeed there was for Saba'﴾. Saba' (a personal name, the name of a man) is originally the name of a man, namely Saba' ibn Yashjub, with the letters shin (pointed) and jim, like Yansur, the son of Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. In some reports: "From Farwa ibn Musayk, who said: I came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Saba', is he a man or a woman? He said: He is a man from the Arabs who had ten sons; six of them went to the right (tayammun) and four of them went to the left (tasha'um). As for those who went to the right, they are al-Azd, Kindah, Muhdhij, al-Ash'ariyyun, Anmar, and among them Bujaylah. As for those who went to the left, they are 'Amilah, Ghassan, Lakhm, and Judham."

In the commentary on the qasidah of 'Abd al-Majid ibn 'Abdun by 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Badrun al-Hadrami al-Busti, it is stated that Saba' ibn Yashjub was the first king of Yemen according to one opinion, and his name was 'Abd Shams. He was named Saba' because he was the first to take captives (sabi) from the descendants of Qahtan. His reign lasted four hundred and eighty-four years. Then the tribe was named after him. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr prevented it from taking tanwin, because it is treated as the name of a tribe, and so it has both the features of proper noun (ʿalamiyyah) and feminine gender (ta'nith). Qunbul read it with the hamzah sukun in the manner of pausing (waqf). From Ibn Kathir, his hamzah is changed to alif. Perhaps he first made it sukun with the intention of pausing, as Qunbul did, and then changed it to alif. When the hamzah is made sukun, its change into a letter of the same kind as the vowel before it is regular. It is also said: perhaps he pronounced it between (bayn bayn, an intermediate sound between hamzah and the vowel) and the narrator did not render it as it should have been. The meaning of Saba' here is either the tribe or the community, or the man you heard about. In the latter case the speech is according to an omitted noun (taqdir mudaf), meaning: "Indeed there was in the descendants of Saba'." It is also permitted that it refers to the land, as its use for the land is well known. In that case, the pronoun in His words, ﴿in their dwelling﴾, refers to its people, and the first use (Saba' as the land) is intended as the community, by way of istikhdam (a figure in which one word is used with one sense and its pronoun with another). The matter in this is clear according to what was mentioned before. Maskan (dwelling) is a noun of place, meaning the place of their habitation. It is like a house, applied to the whole dwelling even if it is a wide region, just as the world is called a house. Abu Hayyan said: it should be understood as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "in their living," because each person has a dwelling. In this reading it is given in the singular and the singular is used with the sense of the plural, as in the saying: "Eat in part of your belly so that you may be chaste," and the saying: "The hide of the water-buffalo has bitten their necks." According to Sibawayh this is restricted to poetic necessity. End of quote.

By what we have mentioned, there is no need for this, as is not hidden. The name of that place is Ma'rib, like Manzil. It is one of the lands of Yemen, and the distance between it and San'a' is three days' journey. Al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and 'Alqamah read ﴿maskinihim﴾ with a kasrah on the kaf, contrary to analogy, like masjid and matla', because the mafʿal form derived from a verb whose present-tense ʿayn is damma or fathah is, in time, place and verbal noun, always with fathah only. Abu al-Hasan said: kasr of the kaf is a widespread dialect, and it is the dialect of people today, while fathah is the dialect of the Hijaz, and it is rare today. Al-Farra' said: it is a fluent Yemeni dialect.

The majority read ﴿masakinihim﴾ in the plural, meaning in the places of their habitation. ﴿A sign﴾, meaning a clear indication, when considered together with its preceding and following sisters (the other signs in the surah), of the existence of the Creator who chooses, and that He, glorified be He, is able to do what He wills of wondrous things, and rewards the good-doer and the wrongdoer. It is the subject of kana (was). His words, ﴿two gardens﴾, are in apposition to it (badal), as al-Farra' indicated and Makki and others stated explicitly. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is two gardens." Agreement in number, gender, and the rest is not required in apposition, and likewise for the predicate when it is not a derived noun and the meaning does not prevent its being identical with the subject. Perhaps the reason for the singular here is like His words: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. There is no need to consider an omitted singular noun, which is the apposition or predicate, in reality, meaning "the story of two gardens." Ibn 'Atiyyah, after weakening the apposition view and without mentioning the direction, held that ﴿two gardens﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is His words, ﴿on the right and on the left﴾. This is not clear, because it is an indefinite noun with no justification for beginning a sentence with it, unless one assumes an omitted adjective, meaning "two gardens belonging to them," or "two great gardens." With this assumption the speech remains disconnected from what precedes it.

Ibn Abi 'Abalah read ﴿jannatayn﴾ in the accusative, as a praise. Abu Hayyan said: that ﴿ayah﴾ is the subject of kana and ﴿jannatayn﴾ is the predicate. In either case, the meaning of "the two gardens," according to what is reported from Qatadah, is two groups of orchards: one group on the right of their town and another group on its left. The use of the word "garden" for each group is because its members are close together and compact, so that they are like one garden, just as populated rural lands and their orchards are. It is also said: the intention is a garden for each man of them, on the right and left of his dwelling, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines﴾ [al-Kahf: 32]. It is said: it was not made plural, lest it follow that each man's dwelling has one garden, because of the matching of plural to plural. This was refuted: His words, ﴿on the right and on the left﴾, remove that, since it is considered in relation to each dwelling. However, if it were made plural it would give the impression that each dwelling has gardens on the right and gardens on the left. There is no harm in this, unless one claims that it contradicts reality. Then it is said that "fi" in what precedes means "ʿind" (at), because the dwellings are surrounded by the two gardens, and the two gardens are not containers for them. It is also said: there is no need for this, since what is near a thing may be described as being in it, as an exaggeration of extreme nearness, and for each direction. But you know that if by "the dwellings" or "the dwelling" is meant what can serve as a container for their town surrounded by the two gardens, or for the place of each of them surrounded by them, then there is no need for any interpretation at all, so do not be negligent.

﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him﴾: this is a new sentence with an implied "saying" (taqdir qawl), meaning: their prophet said to them, "Eat..." etc. In Majma' al-Bayan it is said: their dwellings were thirteen villages, and in each village there was a prophet calling them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, saying: "Eat of the provision of your Lord," etc. It is also said: there was no actual saying, but it was a saying by the language of the situation (lisan al-hal).

﴿A good land and a forgiving Lord﴾: that is, this land in which your provision is found is a good land, and your Lord, who provided for you and asked for your gratitude, is a Forgiving Lord who forgives the shortfalls of whoever thanks Him. This sentence is a new one to make explicit the requirement of gratitude. The meaning of "tayyibah" is pure and pleasant.

It is reported that its air was gentle and its soil good, such that no blight occurred in it and no harmful creatures existed in it, so that when a stranger entered it, if he had lice or fleas on his clothes, they died. It is also said: what is meant by its goodness is the soundness of its air, the sweetness of its water, the abundance of its pleasant scenery, and that there was no heat in it that harms in summer, nor cold that harms in winter.

Ruways read ﴿baldatan﴾ and everything after it in the accusative, as praise and as attributes. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is by the implied "dwell in a good land, and worship a forgiving Lord." Among the rare coincidences is that the phrase "baldatun tayyibah," calculated by the abjad method, counting the ta' marbutah as four hundred, as many scholars have stated, coincided with the date of the conquest of Constantinople, which was the pleasure-ground of the lands of the Romans.

﴿So they turned away﴾, meaning from gratitude, as the context requires. This includes turning away from faith, since it is the greatest of disbelief and ingratitude. Abu Hayyan said: They turned away from what their thirteen prophets brought them, when they called them to God Most High and reminded them of His blessings, glory be to Him. They denied them and said, "We know of no blessing from God."

﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim﴾. Al-'Arim means "the fierce," from ('arim al-rajul), when a man's character becomes harsh and difficult. It is pronounced with any of the three vowels on the r (ʿaram, ʿarim, ʿarum), so the form is ʿārim or ʿaram when his disposition is fierce and difficult. A narration from Ibn 'Abbas has the same meaning, interpreting it as "the severe." The attribution of "flood" to it is an attribution of a noun to its qualifier (idafat al-mawsuf ila al-sifa, a construct in which the noun is described by the second term). Grammarians who reject this construction say the sense is "the flood of the fierce matter" (sayl al-amr al-ʿarim).

It is also said: al-ʿarim is heavy rain, and the construction is literal. It is also said: it is the name of the rat that gnawed through their dam, which became the cause of the flood overpowering them. This is the blind mole called al-khuld, and the attribution of the flood to it is due to the slightest connection. Ibn Jubayr said: al-ʿarim is the dyke (musannat) in the language of Abyssinia. Al-Akhfash said: it is Arabic in this sense. Al-Mughira ibn Hakim and Abu Maysara said: in the dialect of Yemen, al-ʿarim is the plural of ʿurma, which is anything built or raised to hold back water. In the Hijazi dialect that structure is called al-musannat. The attribution works as in the previous case, but the connection here is stronger. From Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Muqatil: it is the name of the valley from which the flood came, and in which the dam was built. The attribution of the flood to it is clear. ʿAzra ibn al-Ward, as transmitted by Ibn Khalawayh, read "al-ʿarm" with a sukun on the r, for lightness, as they say al-kabd for al-kabid in the case of "the liver."

It is narrated that when Bilqis became queen, her people fought over the water of their valley. She gave up her kingship and settled in her palace. They pressed her to return, but she refused. They said, "You must return, or we will kill you." She said to them, "You have no minds, and you do not obey me." They said, "We will obey you." So she returned to their valley. Whenever it rained, the flood would reach them from a distance of three days' journey. She ordered that the gap between the two mountains be blocked with a dyke of rock and bitumen (qar). She held back the water behind the dam and made gates for it, some above others. Behind it she built a basin with twelve outlets, according to the number of their rivers, and the water flowed out to them equally. This continued until what happened between her and Solomon, peace be upon him, took place.

It is also said: the one who built the dam for them was Himyar, the ancestor of the Yemeni tribes. It is also said that Luqman the Elder, son of 'Ad, built it, and laid its stones with lead and iron. It was a farsakh by a farsakh (about six miles by six miles). They continued in the most pleasant life and the most fertile land, to the point that a woman would go out with a basket on her head, work with her hands and walk, and the basket would fill with what fell from the trees of their gardens. This continued until they turned away from gratitude and denied the prophets, peace be upon them. God Most High then sent the mole against their dam, and it burrowed into it and broke it. He, glory be to Him, sent a great flood, which carried away the dam, the gardens, and many people. It is also said that it removed the dam, so the distribution of water and its reaching their gardens was disrupted, and they withered and perished. This flood, it is said, occurred in the reign of Dhu al-Adhar ibn Hassan, in the interval (fatra) between our Prophet (ﷺ) and 'Isa, peace be upon him. There is a difficulty with this if we assume that the turning away was from the thirteen prophets they received, as you will know, God willing, shortly.

﴿And We replaced their two gardens﴾, meaning We removed their two gardens and brought in place of them ﴿two gardens bearing bitter fruit of khamt﴾, meaning fruit that is sour or bitter. From Ibn 'Abbas: al-khamt is the arak tree (Salvadora persica). It is said that the name applies to its fruit in general, or when it turns black and ripens into the berry (al-barbar). It is also said to be the ghada tree, though I do not know whether it has fruit. Abu 'Ubayda said: every bitter thorny tree is khamt. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is the fruit of a tree in the shape of the poppy, which is of no use, and that tree is said to be called "hyena's fart" (fasw al-dabu'). In the first explanation, khamt is an adjective of ukul ("produce"). The matter is clear in that case. In the last explanation, it is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) according to the Kufan school, which permits it with indefinite nouns. It is also said to be a substitute (badal). According to the views between these, the phrase involves an omitted modifier: the eating of produce of bitter fruit, and that omitted noun is a substitute for ukul or an explanatory apposition to it. When it is omitted, the modifier takes its place and receives its case-ending, as in al-Bahr. It is also said the phrase is in the sense of "produce of bitter fruit" (ukul dhi khamt). It is also said that it is a substitute in the pattern of "the moon pleases me, its orbit" (ya'jibuni al-qamar falakuhu), but you see that this is weak. Making it a qualifier without some interpretation is ruled out, because fruit is not described by the name of a tree. This is not because the description by solid nouns is not regular, though some such cases occur, as in "I passed by a patch of 'arfaj." Consider this.

Abu 'Amr read "ukul khamt" with the genitive construction, as in "a garment of silk" (thawb khazz). Ibn Kathir read "ukl" with a sukun on the k and tanwin.

﴿And tamarisk﴾ (athl) is a kind of tamarisk (tarfa'), according to Abu Hanifa al-Lughawi in his book on plants. Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it as tarfa'. Al-Tabarsi cites an opinion that it is the acacia (samur). It is a coordinate with ("ukul"). Al-Zamakhshari did not allow its coordination with ﴿khamt﴾, reasoning that the athl has no fruit. The physicians, such as Dawud al-Antaki and others, mention that it has a fruit like chickpeas, which breaks open to reveal small seeds stuck together. They explain athl as the large tamarisk, and say of tamarisk that the wild kind has no fruit, while the cultivated kind has fruit. Al-Khafaji said: one should not rely on medical books in such matters, and there is some doubt about this. We have verified that athl has fruit, and so does a species of tamarisk, though their fruit is not eaten. Perhaps the one who denied it meant a fruit that is eaten. Physicians count whatever a tree produces other than leaves and the like as fruit, whether it is eaten or not. The same applies to the coordination with that in the words of God Most High: ﴿and a few lote-trees﴾. Al-Fudayl ibn Ibrahim relates that it was read "athlan wa-shay'an" in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿two gardens﴾.

Al-sidr is the lote-tree that bears the nabq (jujube). Al-Azhari said: there are two kinds of sidr. One is useless, its leaves are not suitable for washing, and it has an astringent fruit that is not eaten; it is called al-dal. The other grows by the water, bears nabq as fruit, and its leaves are used as a cleansing agent (ghassul). It resembles the 'unnab tree. End of quotation. Scholars have differed about which is meant here. Some say it is the second. It is described as "few" in form and meaning, or in meaning only, which is the case when it qualifies the thing it is attached to. Its fruit is among the things whose eating is pleasant, so it was made few in what they were given in exchange. If it were abundant, it would be a blessing rather than a punishment. They were given it as a reminder of the vanished blessings, so that it would be a cause of grief for them. It is also said the intended meaning is the first, decisively, because it suits the context better. The commentator does not mention the point of describing it as few in that case.

It may be said that describing it in general as few is because the lote-tree has standing among the Arabs, which is why God Most High mentions its presence in Paradise. The cultivated kind's benefit is not hidden, and the wild kind provides shade for travelers, who take comfort in it, and it has other benefits. As evidence of its high standing, one may cite what Abu Dawud in his Sunan and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara report from 'Abd Allah ibn Habashi, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: whoever cuts a lote-tree, God will plunge his head into the Fire." And what al-Bayhaqi reports from Abu Ja'far, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may God honor his face, during his final illness: Go out, O 'Ali, and say: from God, not from the Messenger of God. God curses whoever cuts the lote-tree."

There are many reports with similar meaning, with many chains. In my view, all of them are to be understood as applying when the cutting is wanton, even if the tree is on one's own property. It is also said that the prohibition is specific to the lote-tree of Medina, and that it was forbidden to cut it so that it would be a comfort and shade for those who migrate there. It is also said that it applies to the lote-tree of the desert, so that travelers and animals may find shade under it. It is also said that it applies to the lote-tree of Mecca, because that is a sanctuary (haram). It is also said that it applies when it is on another's property and the cutting is unjust. All of these, as you see, are weak. In any case, the specific mention of it indicates that it has standing. When God, glory be to Him, mentioned what became of those who turned away and what they exchanged for their two gardens, He added something that conveys the insignificance of what they were given in return, namely the lote-tree, which has standing among the Arabs, and its scarcity. The indication of scarcity is clear. The indication of insignificance comes from naming a thing and deviating from saying "and a few lote-trees," though that would be shorter and better suited to what precedes it. This points to the extreme reversal of their condition: they were not given, after the loss of their two gardens, anything of that kind that has standing among the Arabs, except the lote-tree, and what they were given of this kind is insignificant and scarce. Calling the substitute "two gardens," though you have heard it is not, is for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakala) and mockery (al-tahakkum).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 17:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was mentioned of the replacement (al-tabdil), and the sense of distance in it (the demonstrative "that") is either to indicate the great remoteness of its rank in horror, or it refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿We requited them﴾, as was said regarding His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Its place (i'rab) according to the first view is the accusative, as a second object (maf'ul thani); according to the second view it is the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb. The fronting (al-taqdim) is for magnification and emphasis of the terror; and it was said that it is for restriction (al-takhsis), meaning: that replacement We requited them with, and not other than it; or: that horrible recompense We requited them with, not another recompense. ﴿For what they disbelieved﴾: because of their ingratitude for the blessing, in that We removed it from them and put in its place its opposite. It was also said: because of their disbelief in the thirteen messengers who were sent to them.

This has been raised as an objection together with the view that the Sayl al-Arim occurred during the period of interruption (al-fatrah), since the majority said: there is no prophet between our Prophet and 'Isa, peace be upon them both. Some people said: between them ﷺ there were four prophets, three from the Children of Israel and one from the Arabs, namely Khalid al-'Absi, and he was sent to his own people, while the Children of Israel were not sent to the Arabs. It has been answered that what occurred during the period of interruption was only the Sayl al-Arim and nothing else, and the thirteen messengers were the entirety of those who were among their people from Saba' ibn Yashjub until Allah destroyed them all. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ That is: We do not requite with such a severe, utterly destructive recompense anyone except one who is extreme in ingratitude or disbelief. Thus there is no objection on the restriction that a believer may be punished in this world, for in al-Kashf it is said: it is not meant that the believer is also punished, for that is not punishment in the true sense but purification (tamhis); and because what is meant is punishment for all the evil he does, which does not apply to the believer. There is no barrier to the recompense being general for all requitals, with punishment intended absolutely without restriction to what preceded, by the indication of ﴿We requited them for what they disbelieved﴾, which specifies punishment in it. Rather al-Zamakhshari said: this is the correct view, because of the absence of a pronoun return and because the concluding statement is thus more emphatic and better placed; and the objection does not arise according to what is in al-Kashf.

The majority read "yujaza" with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the zāy, in the passive, with "al-kafur" in the nominative as the substitute for the subject. It was also read "yujazi" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, in the active, whose subject is His pronoun alone, exalted is He, with "al-kafura" in the accusative as the object. Muslim ibn Jundub read "yujza" in the passive, with "al-kafuru" in the nominative as the substitute. The meaning of recompense (al-mujazah), according to what you have heard from al-Zamakhshari, is reward. But al-Khafaji said: it is not found in the Qur'an except with punishment, unlike al-jaza', which is general and may be restricted to good. It is reported from Abu Ishaq: you say "jazaytu al-rajul" for good and "jazaytuhu" for evil. Mujahid's statement has the same meaning: it is said of punishment "yujazi" and of reward "yajzi".

Some eminent scholars said: Abu Ishaq must have meant that when you use the two verbs without making the second object explicit, they are used in this way; but when you mention the second object, each of them is used for good and evil. This is contradicted by "We requited them for what they disbelieved", and likewise "Is he requited" in Muslim's reading, since requital in that is used for evil while the second object is not mentioned. And [consider] his statement:

"His sons requited Abu al-Ghaylan for his old age and good conduct, as Sinimmar is requited."

Al-Raghib said: it is said "jaztuhu" and "jazaytuhu", and only "jaza" has come in the Qur'an, not "jaza" with the alif, because al-mujazah is recompense, which is the exchange of a blessing for a blessing equal to it, and the blessing of Allah, mighty and majestic, is exalted above that; for this reason the word al-mukafa'ah is not used of Him, glorified and exalted is He. There is heedlessness in this regarding what is here, unless it is said that he meant that "jaza" with the alif did not come in the Qur'an for what is a blessing attributed to Him, exalted is He, for it has not occurred to me that it comes in that sense. And Allah knows best. What seems good to me is the statement of Abu Hayyan: most commonly al-jaza' is used for good and al-mujazah for evil, but in their restriction each of them may stand in the place of the other. And in His statement, glorified is He, "We requited them for what they disbelieved" rather than "We requited them with [al-mujazah]," according to the second reading, in the demonstrative there is an indication of the people enjoying what pleases them, and then falling into what harms and injures them. It is possible that the reason for expressing it with the more commonly used "jaza" for good is that each word fits its cause, and that the expression with "dhalika" first and "nujazi" second is such that each suits its own reason. This applies to both readings of the demonstrative, so reflect deeply.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 18:

﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed, towns (lying) in plain view﴾ and so on to its end. Its whole is joined to the whole of what precedes it, as the joining of one narrative to another. It is a recounting of the blessings they were given in their journeys and their trading, and of their ingratitude concerning them, and of what befell them because of that. What came before was a recounting of the blessings they were given in their dwellings and places of residence, and of what they did with them and what was done to them. By "the towns which We had blessed" is meant the towns of al-Sham (Syria), owing to the abundance of their trees and fruits and the ample provision for their people. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the towns of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem); from Mujahid that they are al-Sarawiyya; from Wahb, the towns of San'a'; and Ibn Jubayr said: the towns of Ma'rib. The reliable view is the first, to the extent that Ibn 'Atiyya said: the consensus of the exegetes is upon it.

The meaning of ﴿in plain view﴾, according to what is related from Qatada, is: continuous, with some of them close to others such that those in one of them can see what is opposite them in the other. This requires extreme nearness, but there will come shortly, if God Most High wills, what has been said regarding the distance between every two towns. Al-Mubarrad said: "in plain view" means elevated, i.e. upon the hills and the mounds, and these are the noblest of towns. It was also said: "in plain view" means well known; one says "this is an apparent matter", i.e. well known, and the town becomes known for its goodness and for the care of its people toward those who pass by it. It was also said: they were placed upon the roads so that the passage of travellers would be easy.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What appears to me is that the meaning of ﴿in plain view﴾ is outside the cities. It is an expression for the small villages which lie on the outskirts of the cities, as if by this attribute he distinguished the small villages from the full towns, which are the cities. The outskirts (zawahir) of cities are what lies outside them in the open country. From this is the saying: 'We alighted at the outskirts (zahir) of such-and-such a town', i.e. outside it. From this is the poet's verse:

"If a company of Quraysh had witnessed me, the Quraysh of al-Bitah, not the Quraysh of the outskirts (al-Zawahir)."

He means that those who come out from the valley (al-Batha') of Makkah; and those who dwell outside the town are called the people of the outlying areas (al-Dawahi), and also the people of the deserts (al-Bawadi)."
Page 130

﴿And We made the travel therein measured﴾, i.e. We made the distance of some of them from others a fixed measure of travel. It was said: whoever set out from one town in the morning reached another at the time of midday rest and siesta, and whoever set out after noon reached another at sunset. Thus there was no need to carry provision nor to spend the night in an empty land, nor fear of an enemy or the like. It was also said: between every two towns there was one mile. Al-Dahhak said: the towns were according to the measures of the stages (marahil). This is the most suitable with the meaning of ﴿in plain view﴾ as you have heard from Qatada, and likewise with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Travel in them﴾, for it indicates extreme nearness, as if they had not left the towns themselves. The apparent view is that ﴿Travel﴾ is a command from Him, mighty and majestic, upon the tongue of a prophet or the like, and it is by implicit saying, i.e. We said to them: "Travel in those towns ﴿by night and by day﴾", i.e. whenever you wish, of night or of day, ﴿secure﴾ from everything you dislike; no one differs in this except that those in them differ according to the times. The nights are mentioned first because they are the likely time of fear from an assassin, although it is said that the night is more hidden for the ambush; or because they precede the days; or the sense is: "Travel therein secure", even if the duration of your journey is prolonged and extends for many nights and days. Qatada said: they would travel a distance of four months in security, and if a man found the slayer of his father he would not harm him. Or the sense is: "Travel therein your nights and your days", i.e. for the duration of your lives, you encounter in them nothing but safety; and the nights are mentioned first for their precedence.

Whatever the case, the benefit of mentioning the nights and days is known, even though travel is not free of them. It is also permitted that there is no actual saying at all, and that the granting to them of the aforementioned travel and the facilitation of its beginnings and causes has been made equivalent to saying to them and commanding them to do so. The imperative on both interpretations is for permission (ibahah).

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 19 (part 1 of 2):]

﴿So they said, "Our Lord, lengthen the distances between our journeys."﴾ When the duration of the blessing was long upon them, they became insolent, grew bored, and preferred what is lower over what is better, as the Children of Israel did. They said: "If only our trading routes were farther apart, what we import from them would be more desirable and more costly." So they sought a change in the connection of inhabited lands and the separation by deserts and wastelands. Implicit in this was the pride and arrogance of those among them who were able to cross these distances by riding mounts and carrying provisions, toward the poor who were unable to do so. So God Most High hastened to answer them, by ruining the intermediate towns and making them barren, where no caller calls and no one answers. The apparent meaning is that they said this by way of explicit speech (lisan al-qal). Al-Imam (al-Razi) allowed that they may have said ﴿make [them] distant﴾ by way of implicit speech (lisan al-hal), meaning: since they were ungrateful, they effectively sought that the distances between their journeys be lengthened and that the populated lands of their dwellings be ruined.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read "ba'-‘id" with a shadda on the ‘ayn, as an imperative verb of request. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyya and 'Amr ibn Qa'id read "Rabbuna" with a damma (as the subject) and "ba''ada" with a shadda as a past-tense verb. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Kalbi, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Salam and Abu Haywa read "Rabbuna" with a damma and "ba'id" as an imperative of the form mufa'ala. Ibn al-Hanafiyya also, Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan (brother of al-Hasan), Sufyan ibn Husayn and Ibn al-Sumaytha read "Rabbana" with a fatha, "ba'ada" with a damma as a past-tense verb, and "bayna" with a fatha, except that Sa'id among them read the nun with a damma and made "bayna" the subject. For whoever reads with a fatha, the subject (fa'il) in his view is a pronoun referring back to "al-sayr" (the journey). For whoever reads "Rabbana" with a fatha, it is a vocative (munada). If an imperative follows it, that is a sign of insolence and arrogance. Fa'ala may be used in the sense of fa'ala (without the infix), and if it is a past-tense verb, that is a complaint about the distance between their towns, despite its shortness, because of their excess in luxury and pampering; or a complaint about what befell them from the distance of the journeys they had sought after they had occurred; or a supplication in the form of a statement. For whoever reads "Rabbuna" with a damma, the verb in his view can only be past-tense, and the sentence is declarative, containing a complaint, according to what has been said.

The accusative "bayna" after every transitive verb, in one of the readings, whether past or imperative, is according to Abu Hayyan a direct object (maf'ul bihi), and this is supported by the nominative reading. Or it is an adverb of place (zarfiyya), and the verb is treated as intransitive, or as transitive with an omitted object, namely "al-sayr" (the journey). This is easier than removing the adverb of place from its adverbial function, since it is not inflected (ghayr mutasarrif).

[Page 131]

It is also read "bu'ida" in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mur read "safarina" in the singular.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, by exposing themselves to God's wrath and punishment when they became insolent toward the blessing and denied it. ﴿So We made them into tales﴾. "Ahadith" is the plural of "uhdutha," which is what is narrated for amusement and wonder, not the plural of "hadith" contrary to analogy. Making them the very tales is either hyperbole, or there is an elided noun, meaning: We made them into a story by which people speak of them, marveling at their conditions and taking warning from their fate and final end.

It was said that the meaning is: nothing of them remained except the talk about them. Had a group of them remained, they would not have been "tales." ﴿And We scattered them completely﴾, meaning We dispersed them in every manner of dispersion. Either "mumazzaq" is a verbal noun, or it is a noun of place, meaning every place and location of dispersion. In the expression "tamzeeq," which specifically means separating what is joined and tearing it apart, there is, for the magnitude of the matter, a strong indication of the intensity of the impact and pain, which is not hidden. That is: We scattered them with a scattering beyond which there is no limit, such that it became a proverb for every separation after which there is no reunion. It is reported from Ibn Salam that the meaning is: We made them dust scattered by the winds, and this fits "tamzeeq" better. However, the majority of the great exegetes are of a different view, that the meaning of their "tamzeeq" is their dispersal by distance. You have already been told not long ago the hadith about the manner of their dispersal in the Prophet's ﷺ answer to Farwa ibn Musayk.

In the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari): Ghassan went to al-Sham, Anmar to Yathrib, Judham to Tihama, and al-Azd to 'Uman. In al-Tahrir (Ibn 'Ashur): Qudā'a settled in Makka, Asad in al-Bahrayn, and Khuza'a in Tihama. The apparent meaning of the verse is that this happened after the sending of the great flood (sayl al-'Arim). In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan): In the hadith it is said that Saba' was the father of ten tribes. When the flood came upon Ma'rib, six tribes went to the right of it and four tribes went to the left. Some claimed that their dispersal occurred shortly before the coming of the flood.

'Abd al-Malik said in his commentary on the qasida of Ibn 'Abdun: The land of Saba' in Yemen had settlement extending over more than a two-month journey for a rider traveling hard, and its people would light fire from one to another over a distance of four months. So they were scattered with complete dispersal. The first to leave Yemen at the beginning of the matter was 'Amr ibn 'Amir. The cause of his departure was that he had a wife who was a soothsayer, called Tarifa al-Khayr, who saw in her dream that a cloud had covered their land, thundered and flashed lightning, then struck with lightning, burning everything it touched. Tarifa was greatly frightened by this and came to the king 'Amr, saying: "I have never seen the like of today. It removed sleep from me. I saw a cloud that thundered, flashed, roared and struck with lightning, and it fell upon nothing without burning it." When he saw the fear within her, he calmed her. Then 'Amr entered his garden, accompanied by two of his slave girls. Tarifa learned of this, went out to him, and her servant named Sinan went out with her. When she emerged from her house, three manajid (small burrowing creatures resembling jerboas) appeared to her, standing on their legs with their forepaws over their eyes. She sat down on the ground, placing her hands over her eyes, and said to her servant: "When these manajid leave, inform me." When they left, he informed her, and she set off quickly. When she reached the canal in 'Amr's garden, a tortoise leapt out of the water and fell on the path on its back, trying to turn over but unable to, seeking help with its tail, throwing dirt over its belly from its sides, and spraying urine upon its belly. When Tarifa saw it, she sat down on the ground. When the tortoise returned to the water, Tarifa went on until she entered upon 'Amr at midday, at an hour when the heat was intense. There the trees were swaying without wind. When he saw her, he felt shy before her, ordered the two slave girls to leave for another side, then said to her: "O Tarifa!" She spoke as a soothsayer and said:

"By the light and the darkness, by the earth and the sky, the trees are indeed perishing, and the water will return as it was in the former age."

'Amr said: "Who told you this?" She said: "The manajid informed me, of years of hardship in which a child will cut off his parent."

He said: "What are you saying?" She said: "I say the words of a distressed companion: I have seen a tortoise sweeping away the dirt with a sweep and throwing urine with a throw."

[Page 132]

She entered the garden and there the trees were swaying without wind. He said: "What do you see in this?" She said: "It is a great calamity, a terrible affliction from grave matters and great disasters." He said: "And what is it, woe to you?" She said: "Indeed, and in it is woe, and you shall gain nothing from it, and woe is in what the flood will bring." 'Amr was thrown from his bed and said: "What is this, O Tarifa?" She said: "A great affair, a long sorrow, and few survivors." He said: "And what is the sign of what you mention?" She said: "Go to the dam. When you see a rat using its two paws to dig much into the dam, and turning over the rock with its two legs, then know that the flood is flood and the matter has come to pass." He said: "And what is it that you mention?" She said: "A promise from God Most High has descended, falsehood has vanished, and the punishment has befallen us.
