So by other than you, O 'Amr, will it happen. The loss." 'Amr set out, and there was the rat turning over with its two legs a rock that fifty men could not lift. He returned saying:

"I have seen a matter that caused me pain, and the severity of illness stirred in me from its terror,
From a rat like the stallion of a boar of the thicket,
Or a ram of the flock from the young of the herd,
Dragging a bulk of boulders of the Arim (dam),
Having claws and fangs that gnaw,
Nothing that it has dragged of rock has escaped its cutting."

Tarifa said: "Among the sign of what I mentioned to you is that you sit and order a glass vessel to be placed before you, for the wind will fill it with dust from the valley of Bat-ha' from the plain of the valley and its slopes. You know that the gardens are shaded and no sun or wind enters them." 'Amr ordered a glass vessel placed before him, and it had not remained long before it was filled with dust. He informed her of this, and said to her: "When will that destruction happen that occurs in the dam?" She said to him: "Between me and you is seven years." He said: "In which of them will it be?" She said: "No one knows that except God Most High. Had anyone known it, I would have known it. There is not a night that comes upon me between now and the seven years but I think its destruction will come on its morrow or its evening."

Then 'Amr saw in his dream the flood of al-'Arim, and it was said to him: "The sign of this is that you see the pebbles appear in the palm fronds." He looked at them and found pebbles had appeared among them. He knew it was certain to happen and that their land would be ruined. So he concealed this, and resolved to sell everything he had in the land of Ma'rib, and to leave it with his son. Then he feared that the people would object to this, so he ordered one of his sons, when he summoned him for what he would summon him to, to refuse him, and to do this to him in front of the people. When he slapped him, he was to raise his own hand and slap him. Then 'Amr prepared food and sent to the people of Ma'rib that 'Amr had prepared a meal on a day of glory and renown. They were summoned to his food. When the people sat for the meal, his son whom he had instructed sat beside him, and he began to order him, and he refused. 'Amr raised his hand and slapped him, and the son slapped him back. His name was Malik. 'Amr cried out: "Alas for my humiliation! On the day of 'Amr's pride and splendor, a child strikes his face!" He swore that he would surely kill him. They did not cease pleading with him until he relented. He said: "By God, I will not stay in a place where this was done to me, and I will surely sell my wealth so that no one will inherit anything from it after me." The people said to one another: "Let us seize upon 'Amr's anger and buy his wealth from him before he is pleased." So the people bought from him all his wealth in the land of Ma'rib. Part of the story spread about what had reached them concerning the matter of the flood of al-'Arim. Some people of al-Azd rose and sold their wealth. When they sold much, the people were alarmed by this and refrained from buying. When 'Amr's wealth had all been gathered, he informed the people about the matter of the flood and departed. Because of his departure a great multitude departed with him. They settled in the land of 'Akk, and 'Akk fought them, so they left their lands. Then they made peace and stayed there until 'Amr died, and they dispersed throughout the lands. Some of them went to al-Sham, and they are the descendants of Jafna ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir. Some went to Yathrib, and they are the sons of the tribes of al-Aws and al-Khazraj, whose father was Harithah ibn Tha'laba ibn 'Amr ibn 'Amir. The Azd of al-Sarat went to al-Sarat, and the Azd of 'Uman

[Page 133]

went to 'Uman. Malik ibn Fahm went to Iraq. Shortly after 'Amr, Tay' departed from the land of Yemen and settled at Ajja' and Salma. The sons of Rabi'a ibn Harithah ibn 'Amir ibn 'Amr settled in Tihama, and they were called Khuza'a because they "withdrew" (inkhaza'a) from their brothers. Then God Most High sent the flood upon the dam and it destroyed it. Concerning this, Maymun ibn Qays al-A'sha said:

"In that is an example for the one who takes warning, and Ma'rib, over which al-'Arim has passed,
Its dam Rukham's daughter for them, Himyar, when its flood came, did not stumble,
So it watered the crops and their vines, despite the abundance of their water when it was divided,
So they became hands that cannot even give a weaned child a drink from it."

Al-Maydani related from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, that Tarifa the soothsayer (kahina) had seen in her divination that the dam of Ma'rib would be ruined, and that the flood of al-'Arim (sayl al-'Arim) would come and destroy the two gardens. So 'Amr ibn 'Amir sold his property and departed with his people until they reached Mecca, where they settled in it and in its surroundings. Then fever afflicted them, and they were in a land where they did not know what fever was. So they called Tarifa and complained to her of what had befallen them. She said to them: "What you complain of has afflicted me too, and it is separating us." They said: "What then do you command?" She said:

"Whoever among you has a distant aim, a strong camel, and a new water-skin, let him join the lofty palace of Oman." So the Azd of Oman went. Then she said: "Whoever among you has vigour, strength and patience in the face of the calamities of time, let him take up residence in the arak trees of the valley of Murr." So Khuza'a went. Then she said: "Whoever among you wants the places that stand firm in mud and feed people in famine, let him join Yathrib of the palm trees." So the Aws and the Khazraj went. Then she said: "Whoever among you wants wine, leaven, kingship and rule, who wears brocade and silk, let him join Busra and Ghuwayr," and these two are in the land of Syria. So those who settled there were the family of Jafna from Ghassan. Then she said: "Whoever among you wants fine thin garments, noble horses, treasures of provision, and shed blood, let him join the land of Iraq." So those who settled there were the family of Jadhima al-Abrash, those in al-Hira, and the family of Muhriq.

The truth is that their scattering throughout the lands was after the sending of the flood. Yes, it is not far-fetched that some of them left before it, when they sensed its occurrence. In the proverb: "They went as the hands of Saba'" (dhahabu aydi Saba'), and it is said: "They were scattered as the hands of Saba'" (tafarraqu aydi Saba'), and it is related as "ayadi" (ayadi Saba'). It means the children, because they are the arms (a'dad) of a man, since he is strengthened by them.

In al-Mufassal it is stated that "al-aydi" means "the souls" (al-anfus), metaphorically or by way of metonymy. Al-Kashshaf said: "And this is good." Its accusative case is in the sense of a circumstantial (hal) with the implied "like" (mithla), because the meaning requires it while it is not made definite by an annexation. It has also been said that it means "lands" or "paths," from their saying "take the hand of the sea," meaning its way and its side; that is, they scattered along various paths. Apparently, on this view, it is in the accusative as an adverb of place without the implied "in" (fi), as the scholar al-Yamani pointed out. Perhaps it may be thought that "al-aydi" or "al-ayadi" means "blessings," but that is not so. It is said of a person whose concerns are scattered and whose thoughts are dispersed that he is "ayadi Saba'." On this is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azza:

"Ayadi Saba', O 'Azza, I was not after you, so the eyes have not since you left them seen a sight."

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story, ﴿are signs﴾, great ones, ﴿for everyone who is steadfast, grateful﴾. That is, his nature is patience over desires and the impulses of passion and over the hardships of acts of obedience. It has also been said: his nature is patience over blessings, by not becoming boastful and not becoming insolent, though this is not the intended meaning. ﴿Grateful﴾: his nature is thankfulness for blessings. The singling out of these people for this is because they are the ones who benefit from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 20:

﴿And Iblis indeed found his assumption about them to be true﴾ That is, he confirmed his assumption about them, or found his assumption to be correct. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ("about them") refers to Saba'. The basis of his assumption was seeing their immersion in desires. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the children of Adam, and the basis of his assumption was that he had witnessed their father Adam, peace be upon him, and he was the one who had listened to his whispering, so he analogised the branch to the root and the child to the parent. It was also said that he perceived the desire and anger that were implanted in them, and these two are sources of evils. It was also said that this arose from hearing the words of the angels, peace be upon them: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], on the day when He, glorified is He, said to them: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. It is possible that the basis of this was the evil that he himself possessed, as it has been said:

When a man's deeds are evil, his suspicions become evil, and what he habitually imagines comes true.

It is also permissible that each of what has been mentioned is a basis for his assumption about Saba'. The discourse, according to the first view regarding the pronoun, as al-Tibi said, is a continuation of what precedes it, either as a parenthetical clause or as a conjunction; and according to the second view it is like a concluding statement (tadhyil) emphasising it.

The Basrans read "ṣadaqa" with light stress (takhfif), so "ẓannahu" is in the accusative by dropping the preposition; the original is "ṣadaqa fī ẓannihi," meaning he found his assumption to be correct in reality, so "ṣadaqa" then means "aṣāba" (hit the mark) metaphorically. It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) of an implied verb, meaning "yaẓunnu ẓannahu," like "fa'altahu juhdaka" (you did it with your effort), that is "tajhad juhdaka" (you strive your effort); and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), and "ṣadaqa" is explained by what has passed. It is also permissible that it is accusative as a direct object, the verb being transitive to it directly, because truthfulness (ṣidq) originally pertains to statements, and speech is among the things that take a direct object without a preposition. The meaning is "he confirmed his assumption," as in the hadith: "He fulfilled His promise and aided His servant," and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23].

Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them, al-Zuhri, Abu al-Jahjah al-A'rabi, one of the eloquent Arabs, and Bilal ibn Abi Barzah read "Iblīsa" in the accusative and "ẓannuhu" in the nominative, as stated in al-Bahr. The one who holds this reading with the intensive "ṣaddaqa" means that he found his assumption to be true. However, Ibn Jinni mentioned that al-Zuhri used to read it with light "ṣadaqa," meaning he spoke the truth to him when their misguidance was imagined to him.

'Abd al-Warith, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read "Iblīsu" and "ẓannuhu" both in the nominative, making the second a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal). Al-Zamakhshari left the reader unnamed regarding this, saying: it was read with light stress and both in the nominative, meaning: the assumption of Iblis was confirmed about them. And if it were read with intensive stress with both in the nominative, it would be for intensification in "ṣaddaqa," like the saying of the poet:

My soul and what my right hand possesses are ransomed for the horsemen whose suspicions about them were true (ṣadaqat fīhim ẓunūnī).

This indicates that no one read it that way, and Allah knows best. In all the readings, "'alayhim" is connected to the preceding verb and is not connected to "ẓann" in any of them.

﴿So they followed him﴾ That is, Saba'; it was also said the children of Adam. ﴿except a party of the believers﴾ That is, except a party who are the believers, who did not follow him, with "min" being explanatory (bayaniyyah). Their fewness is either due to their small number in themselves or their fewness in comparison with the disbelievers. This is definite according to the view that the pronoun refers to the children of Adam. I think you would prefer that the fewness is in themselves according to the view that the pronoun refers to Saba', since the abundance of believers among them is not common in itself; or (it means) except a party from among the groups of believers who did not follow him, and they are the sincere ones, so "min" is partitive (tab'iyyah). The intended meaning is the general following, which is broader than disbelief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 21:

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾ i.e., no domination or control through whispering and misleading.

﴿Except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt concerning it﴾ This is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of causes, and "man" (man) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah); to make it an interrogative is far-fetched. The future knowledge that is given as a cause is not the eternal knowledge that subsists in the Essence of the Holy One, but rather its relation to the known object in the world of witnessing (alam al-shahadah), upon which reward and punishment, in the form of reward and retribution, are based. It implies the meaning of distinction (al-tamyiz) because of the position of "min" (from). That is: he had no authority over them in any matter whatsoever, except that Our knowledge relates to the one who believes in the Hereafter as distinguished from the one who is in doubt concerning it, a present relation upon which the recompense is based. To this the words of many of the imams of tafsir allude.

It has been said: the meaning is that We make the believer distinct from others externally, so that he becomes distinguished in the eyes of people. It has also been said: what is meant by the occurrence of knowledge in the future is the occurrence of the known object, since it is necessarily connected to it; it is as if it were said: he had no authority except that the believer might believe, whose faith was decreed, and the one whose misguidance was decreed might go astray. This formulation was preferred over the literal wording for the sake of emphasis, because it makes the known object identical with knowledge. It has also been said that what is meant by knowledge is the recompense, as if it were said: [distinguishing] according to faith and its opposite. It has also been said: knowledge is in its apparent sense, except that the future is in the sense of the past, and God's eternal knowledge of the people of doubt requires the domination of Satan over them.

It has been said: what is meant is that We deal with them in the manner of one who does not know this, but acts in order to know it. It has also been said: what is meant is that Our friends and party know this. The weakness of some of these opinions is not hidden from you. The apparent wording would have been "except that We might know who believes in the Hereafter from those who do not believe in it," but it was diverted from this to the present sublime wording for a reason: faith is contrasted with doubt, to indicate that even the lowest degree of disbelief is destructive. The present tense is used in the first clause to indicate that what is considered in faith is its conclusion, and because it is acquired through gradual, continually renewed reflection. The second clause is nominal to indicate that what is considered is persistence and steadfastness in doubt until death. "Shakk" (doubt) is made indefinite with tanwin to indicate paucity, and "fi" (in) is used to indicate that even a little of it surrounds its possessor. It is construed with "min" rather than "fi" and placed first, because only doubt arising from it (the Hereafter) causes harm, and because the doubt of a person concerning matters related to it suffices.

Al-Zuhri read «liyu'lama» with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the lām, in the passive voice.

﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾ i.e., a Trustee (wakil) standing over their conditions and affairs. It is either an intensive form of "hafiz" (preserver), or in the sense of "muhafiz" (one who guards), like "jalis" and "mujalis," "khalit" and "mukhalit," "radi'" and "muradi'," and so on.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 34, verse 22:**

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to the polytheists to whom the example of the people of Saba' was struck, whose story is well known among them through transmission in their reports and poetry, as a warning about the falsehood of what they hold and as a rebuke to them: ﴿Call upon those whom you claimed﴾, that is, whom you claimed to be gods. This is how the majority (al-Jumhur) of exegetes estimated it, holding that the pronoun is the first object and "gods" (ālihah) is the second object, and the first object was omitted for lightness, because the relative clause and its relative pronoun are like a single noun, so there is a length that is sought to be lightened. The second object was omitted because its qualifier, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿besides God﴾, has taken its place, so there is no excessive elision in omitting both together. It is not permissible for ﴿besides God﴾ to be the second object, since the sentence is not complete with it together with the pronoun, and the arrangement of the discourse does not fit. What meaning is intended for them by "besides God" [as a second object]? Moreover, there is a difference of opinion over whether omitting one of the two objects of this type of verb is permitted for brevity. Whoever permits it says that it is rare in their speech. Likewise, it is not permissible for the phrase ﴿they do not possess﴾ to be the estimate, because what they claimed is not that they are without possession, but rather the opposite. Nor is that a "claim" in the common sense, even if it is granted that it proceeded from them; rather it is a truth. Ibn Hisham said: The better option is to estimate "you claimed that they are gods," because the usual construction with (zaʿama, to claim) is that it does not take two explicit objects, but rather something that takes the place of both of them, from an anna clause and its complement. It has not occurred in the revelation except in this way. That is, the most fitting option is that the estimate should agree with what is stated explicitly in the revelation.

The majority's estimate has been preferred, because it is further from incurring excessive elision. The imperative is for reproach and for challenge, that is: call upon them in what concerns you, whether repelling harm or bringing benefit, perhaps they will answer you, if your claim is true. It is narrated that this was revealed at the time of the hunger that befell the Quraysh.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight﴾, is a resumed statement in the position of an answer, and He did not give them time to answer, to indicate that it is determined, for it does not admit of obstinacy. It has also been permitted to estimate "then answer on their behalf, saying: They do not possess," etc., and this includes a clarification of the state of the gods in reality
[Page 136]
and that, if they do not possess the measure of an atom, that is, of good or evil, benefit or harm, how could they be gods who are worshipped?

﴿In the heavens or on the earth﴾, that is, in any matter whatsoever. The mention of the heavens and the earth is for generality by custom, so that by them is meant all existing things. This is like saying "the Emigrants and the Helpers" and meaning all the Companions, may God be pleased with them. So it should not be imagined that they possess anything outside of them. It is also permissible to say that their mention is because some of the gods of the addressees are heavenly, like the angels and the stars, and some are earthly, like the idols. So the intended meaning is the negation of the power of the heavenly among them over a heavenly matter, and of the earthly over an earthly matter. The negation of their power over anything else is known a fortiori. Or it is because the proximate causes of good and evil are heavenly and earthly, so the intended meaning is the negation of their power over any of the proximate causes, so how much more so over other than them.

﴿And they have not﴾, that is, their gods have not, ﴿in them any partnership﴾, that is, a partnership of anything, neither in creation, nor in ownership, nor in disposal. ﴿And He has not﴾, that is, God, mighty and majestic, has not, ﴿among them any supporter﴾, that is, a helper who assists Him, glorified is He, in the management of their affairs. ﴿And intercession does not benefit with Him﴾, that is, it does not exist at all, as in the line of poetry:

*On a faded road whose landmark none can follow*

This is due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ The negation was attached to its benefit rather than to its occurrence, to explicitly deny what is their aim from its occurrence.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾ is an exception from the most general states, according to what al-Zamakhshari chose. The word "one" (man) is an expression for the intercessor, and the lam attached to it is for specification, like its use in "the generosity is for Zayd." The lam in "for whom" (lahu) is attached to "permits" (adhina). The intended meaning is the negation of the intercession of their gods on their behalf, but this is mentioned in a general form so that it may be a demonstrative path, that is: intercession does not benefit in any state, or occurring for anyone, except occurring for an intercessor whom He has permitted for it, from among the prophets, the angels and the like, from among those qualified for the station of intercession. It is clear that they are not permitted to intercede for the disbelievers, for God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is correct﴾ [al-Naba' 38]. Intercession for them is far from what is correct, and the non-permission for the idols is even clearer and clearer. Thus the deprivation of these disbelievers from it entirely is made clear. Or ("one") is an expression for the one interceded for, and the lam attached to it is for causation, and the lam in "for whom" is attached to "permits," that is: intercession does not benefit except occurring for one for whom permission was given to the intercessor, that is, for his intercessor, on the basis of an implied element, because the one interceded for has not performed any act for which he would be permitted that his intercessor intercede for him. Al-Zamakhshari chose that the lam in "for whom" is for causation, that is: except for whom permission was given to the intercessor on his account. Its rationale, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is the occurrence of an allusion to both the intercessor and the one interceded for, since the one for whom permission is given is the one interceded for, and the one permitted is the intercessor. Also, the aim is to clarify the locus of benefit, which is the one interceded for, so explicitly mentioning him is more important. It is not hidden that the previous view is clearly strained, in that it involves an implied element which the context does not require. The meaning according to this view is: intercession does not benefit from the intercessors who are qualified for it, except when it occurs for the one for whom permission was given to the intercessor, and concerning whom, of those deserving intercession. As for anyone else, who does not deserve it, it does not benefit them at all, even if it is supposed that intercession occurs from the intercessors, since they have not been permitted to intercede for them, but rather for others. From this it is established that these disbelievers are deprived of the intercession of the qualified intercessors by the literal expression, and of the intercession of the idols by its implication, since when they are deprived of it from those capable of it in general, then it is more fitting that they be deprived of it from those entirely incapable of it.

Abu Hayyan went to the view that the exception is from the most general of beings, that is: intercession does not benefit anyone except one for whom... etc. He inferred the possibility that "one" is an expression for the one interceded for, and the lam, taking the apparent sense into account, is connected to "intercession." Abu al-Baqa' permitted its connection to "benefits." This was criticized on the grounds that it is transitive only by itself. Abu Hayyan said concerning it: if the object is postponed, then the entry of the lam is rare.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿was permitted﴾ in the passive voice, so its subject is the deputy of its agent.
[Page 137]

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say﴾ — what? — ﴿"What did your Lord say?" They say, "The truth."﴾ The form of the verb with the intensive (tafʿīl) is for privation, as in "qarradat al-baʿīr" when she removed its ticks from the camel. From this comes "tamrīḍ" (nursing the sick). So "tafzīʿ" is the removal of fear. Fear is, as al-Raghib said, a contraction and aversion that afflicts a person from a frightening thing. And "until" (ḥattā) indicates a limit (ghāyah). The scholars differed over what is limited (al-mughayya), since there was nothing before it that could be the limited by apparent consideration. They therefore differed greatly over the intended meaning of the verse. It was said: it is what is understood from the hadith of intercession and points to it, since His saying, exalted is He,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾. This indicates that there are intercessors and those for whom intercession is made, and that there is a seeking of permission for intercession, because the occurrence of permission necessarily requires that it be sought beforehand, and this requires waiting and anticipating the answer. Since this is a speech issuing from the station of majesty and greatness, how much more so, given what precedes it, does this indicate that everyone at that station is behind the veil of majesty, with the garment of awe cast upon them. What follows the particle of limit (ḥatta) is also very strongly indicative of this. It is as if it were said: The intercessors and those for whom intercession is made stand at that station, in which those seeking intercession cling to the hems of hope before those from whom intercession is sought, and in which the one from whom intercession is sought stands with the posture of seeking refuge in God, exalted is His majesty, so he knocks at the door of intercession by seeking permission for it, and they all remain waiting, anxious and terrified, not knowing what the Supreme King, exalted and high, will inscribe on the paper of their request, or what will be valid for them after the presentation of their condition. Until the fear is removed from the hearts of the intercessors and those for whom intercession is made, by the appearance of the first signs of a good inscription and the radiance of the lights of acceptance and approval from the horizons of the mercy of the Exalted King, they say, that is, some of them say to others. The apparent meaning is that the speaking group are those for whom intercession is made; and if you wish, return the pronoun to them from the beginning, since they are the most in need of permission and the most concerned with its matter: "What has your Lord said?" They say, that is, the intercessors, for they are the ones directly seeking permission and the mediators for those who ask for intercession, saying before Him, mighty and majestic: "He has said the truth," that is, what occurs in accordance with what wisdom requires, which is permission for intercession for whomever He has approved.

And the apparent meaning is that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Great﴾ is part of the speech of the intercessors. They said it acknowledging the greatness of the presence of might, exalted is His majesty, and the insignificance of the rank of everyone else. That is, He, exalted is His rank, is the one uniquely characterized by height and greatness; none of His creation shares in that with Him, and none of them, whoever he may be, has the right to speak except after His permission, exalted and high is He. In this there is, after the elevation of their rank by granting them permission for intercession, a kind of humility on their part that is what it is, and in it also is a kind of praise, as is not hidden. This clause, limited by what has been mentioned, may well be an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: How will permission be granted in that station to those who seek it? And what will be the condition there for the intercessors and those for whom intercession is sought? So it is said: They stand waiting, anxious and terrified, until when, etc. The verses indicate that those for whom intercession is made are the believers, while the disbelievers are far from the station of seeking intercession and from the removal of fear from their hearts by a thousand thousand stations. Some have made, on this reading, the limit (what has been mentioned) refer to the pronoun of ﴿their hearts﴾ as referring to the angels, with the intercessors specified by it; the first pronoun of ﴿they said﴾ is also for them, and the second pronoun of "they said" is for the angels who are above them, who are the ones who convey that to them. And he said: Their terror is either due to the great matter accompanying the permission, or to a swoon that overtakes them upon hearing the speech of God, exalted is His majesty, or from observing that a shortcoming occurred in specifying those for whom intercession is made, based on the coming of the permission for intercession in general. This, as you see, is not so.

Al-Zajjaj said: The explanation of this is that when Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended to the Prophet ﷺ with the revelation, the angels, peace be upon them, thought that he had descended with something of the matter of the Hour, so they were terrified by that. When the fear was lifted from them, they said: "What has your Lord said?" They asked: What did Gabriel, peace be upon him, descend with? They said: The truth. End of quote.

This was narrated from Qatadah, Muqatil, and Ibn al-Sa'ib. However, they said: The angels were struck senseless by it, so Gabriel, peace be upon him, began to pass by every heaven, removing the fear from them and informing them that it was the revelation.

Al-Zajjaj did not clarify the connection of the verse with what precedes it, nor did he investigate the limit (ghayah) with anything. Imam al-Razi mentioned something similar to this, then said regarding it: The word "until" (ḥatta) is a limit connected to His saying, exalted is He: "Say" (qul), because it is explained by the revelation; so when He, glorified is He, said "Say," those in the heavens were terrified. By my life, this is one of the strangest things.

Al-Fadil al-Tibi, after quoting that interpretation, said: Most of the exegetes' speech is upon it, and it is supported by what we have narrated from al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When God, exalted is He, decrees the matter in heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His saying, exalted is He, as if it were a chain upon a smooth rock. When fear is removed from their hearts, they say: What has your Lord said? They say: He who said the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great."

And from Abu Dawud, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When God, exalted is He, speaks with the revelation, the people of heaven hear a sound like the dragging of a chain over stone, so they swoon and remain thus until Gabriel comes to them. When Gabriel, peace be upon him, comes to them, fear is removed from their hearts [fuzza'a]; they say: O Gabriel, what has your Lord said? He says: The truth, the truth."

Then he mentioned, regarding the matter of the limit and the connection of the verse with what precedes it, the reason for this: that the meaning of what is limited is extracted from what is implied. That is because the polytheists, when they claimed the intercession of the gods and the angels, were answered by His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Call upon those you claim besides God" — from among the idols and the angels — "and you named them by His name and sought refuge with them; for they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and intercession does not benefit from them except for the angels, but with permission and great terror; and they intercede only for those with whom He is pleased." So He expressed the angels, peace be upon them, by His saying, exalted is He: "except for one whom He has permitted, until when fear is removed from their hearts, they say: What has your Lord said?" The verse is a kinaya, as if it were said: Intercession does not benefit except for one whose condition and custom is this, and who does not remain steadfast at a shock of the shocks of this Clear Book and at hearing the speech of truth, meaning those who, when revelation descends upon them, become terrified and swoon, until when Gabriel, peace be upon him, comes to them, fear is removed from their hearts, and they say: What has your Lord said? He says: The truth. End of quote.

This is not hidden from anyone with even slight discernment, and that this is among what should not be relied upon.

As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyyah: the interpretation of the verse concerning the angels, when they hear the revelation, refers to Gabriel, or to the command given by God, exalted is He, so they hear it like the dragging of an iron chain over iron, and so they are terrified out of reverence and awe; and it has been said that the fear of the Hour's coming is the correct view, and it is what the hadiths have consistently reported — this arises from being deprived of soundness of taste and precision of examination. The interpretation we mentioned first is far better in its goodness than what has been mentioned from most exegetes. What you have heard of the narration does not contradict it, since there is no indication in it that he, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned that in the context of explaining the verse, and there is no contradiction between the two terrors. Most exegetes seem to have looked at the apparent correspondence of the wording with the hadith, so they applied the verse to that, and fell into what they fell into, however numerous and great they were. The one who holds to what preceded looked at the correspondence of the context, verified the absence of contradiction, and it became clear to him what they had said, so he turned away from it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak that he said regarding the verse: Ibn Mas'ud claimed that the angels, the successive ones who go back and forth to the people of the earth, record their deeds; when the Lord, blessed and exalted, sends them, they descend, and a loud sound is heard from them; so those below them among the angels think it is from the matter of the Hour, and they fall down in prostration. This happens each time they pass by them, and they do so out of fear of their Lord, blessed and exalted. But Ibn Mas'ud, in my view, is too great to bear the verse upon this. So the apparent meaning is that this is not sound from him.

Similar to this is what some claimed: that this is the terror of the angels of the lowest heaven at the descent of the arranged ones (al-mudabbirat) to the earth. It has also been said: "until" is a limit connected to His saying, "you claimed" — that is, you claimed disbelief until the limit of the terror; then you abandoned what you claimed and said: He has said the truth. To this points what Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said regarding the verse: "until when fear is removed from their hearts" — that is, Satan is removed from their hearts, leaving them and their wishes and what used to mislead them. They say: "What has your Lord said?" They say: "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great." Then he said: This refers to the children of Adam — that is, their disbelievers at death, who acknowledge when acknowledgment no longer benefits them. The apparent meaning is that in the speech concerning this there is a turn (iltifat) from address in "you claimed" to the third person in "their hearts." And the first pronoun of "they say" is for the angels appointed to seize their souls. The intended meaning of removing fear from the hearts is the uncovering of the veil and of the obstacles to perceiving the truth from them. As for what is reported from al-Hasan, that he said: "It is only said to the polytheists: What has your Lord said?" — that is, through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them — "so they acknowledge when it does not benefit," it may be like the statement mentioned above that this is at death, and it may be a statement that this is on the Day of Resurrection; but making "until" a limit of the claiming is not apparent in it, since that claiming does not literally accompany them to the Day of Resurrection, as is not hidden. And further removed than this statement is that it is a limit to His saying, exalted is He: "of those who are in doubt concerning it," with the pronoun of "their hearts" referring to "whom" in terms of its meaning; and the terror is the uncovering of the veil and the places of perceiving the truth. Rather, this is something that the speech of God, exalted is He, should not be interpreted as.

Some claimed that the meaning is: when Israfil, peace be upon him, calls them from their graves, they say in response: "What has your Lord said?" Al-Bahr relates this. Then he said: The terror (tafzi') is from fazaʿ, which is calling for help and seeking aid, as Zuhayr said:

When they are terrified, they fly to their helper, tall spears, neither weak nor unarmed.

You know that terrifying in the sense mentioned does not take "ʿan" as its complement, and the matter of the limit is not apparent in it; in sum, that claim is nothing.

Abu Hayyan chose that the thing limited is the following (al-ittiba') in His saying, exalted is He: "Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except for a group of the believers." The pronoun of "their hearts" refers to what the pronoun of the subject in "they followed him" refers to, namely the disbelievers; likewise the second pronoun of "they said." The first pronoun of "they said" is for the angels, and likewise the pronoun of "your Lord." The clause of His saying, exalted is He: "Say: Call upon those who..." etc. is parenthetical between the limit and the limited, and the terror is the state at the departure of life or the Day of Resurrection; and making their following of Iblis accompany them to that day is a metaphor, and its remoteness is not hidden. The view, in my opinion, is what was mentioned first. "Mā dhā" may be read as the object of "qāla" meaning: what thing has your Lord said. It may also be in the nominative position, with "mā" as an interrogative subject, "dhā" as a relative pronoun whose predicate is it, the clause "qāla" as the relative clause, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: what is it that your Lord has said.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Talhah, Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, Ibn al-Sumayqa, Ibn 'Amir, and Ya'qub read "fazza'a" with the doubled ʿayn and the active voice, the agent being the implied pronoun of God, exalted is He, meaning: God, exalted is He, removed the fear from their hearts. Abu Hayyan said: it is His pronoun, exalted is He, if the pronoun of "their hearts" refers to the angels; and if it refers to the disbelievers, then it is the pronoun of the one who incites them.

Al-Hasan read "fuzi'a" with a single ʿayn and the passive voice, so "ʿan qulūbihim" is the deputy subject, as in the reading of the majority. He and Abu al-Mutawakkil also, along with Qatadah and Mujahid, read "farragha" with the fa, the unpointed ra, and the ghayn with a dot, doubled and active, meaning: removed.

Al-Hasan also read it in the same way, except that he lightened the rā' (reading fuzzzi'a with a light rā'). Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Hasan (also), Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Qatadah (also) and Abu Mijlaz read "fuzzi'a" (فُرِّغَ) in the same manner, except that they made it passive in form (بَنَوْهُ لِلْمَفْعُولِ). Ibn Mas'ud, in one narration, and Isa read "ifranqa'a" (اِفْرَنْقَعَ). It was said that it means "tafarraqa" (scattered, dispersed). Al-Zamakhshari said: it means "inkashafa" (was uncovered, dispelled). The word is composed of the letters of separation (حُرُوفِ المُفارَقَةِ) with the addition of the ʿayn, just as "iqmatarra" (اِقْمَطَرَّ) is composed of the letters of qamt with the addition of the rā'. However, this gives the impression that the ʿayn and the rā' are among the letters of augmentation, and that is not the case.

Ibn Abi Abla read "al-ḥaqqu" (اَلْحَقُّ) with a ḍammah (raised), meaning: what is said (by Him) is the truth (أيْ مَقُولُهُ الحَقُّ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 24:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?"﴾ He (ﷺ) was commanded to say this as a rebuke to the polytheists, by compelling them to acknowledge that their gods do not own even an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, and that the Provider is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for they do not deny Him. Since they sometimes hesitated in answering, fearing being bound by the argument, he (peace be upon him) was told: ﴿Say: "Allah."﴾, since they have no other answer either. ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ That is: one of the two parties is either us, the company of monotheists, who single out Allah alone, Mighty and Majestic, for provision, for inherent power, and for worship; or you, the group of polytheists who associate others with Him, who are unable within themselves to repel the slightest harm or bring the least benefit, and among whom are those who have descended to the lowest of the possible ranks, characterized by one of two states: either steadfastness upon guidance or immersion in error. This is from the fair speech which everyone who hears it, whether friend or foe, says to the one addressed by it: "Your companion has been fair to you." Its placement after the eloquent proof presented beforehand is a clear indication of which of the two parties is upon guidance and which is in error. However, allusion is more eloquent than explicit statement, more effective in bringing the disputant to the goal, more forceful in securing victory, and it weakens the opponent's clamor and breaks his strength with ease. Similar to this is a man's saying to his companion: "Allah Most High knows the truthful one from me and from you, and indeed one of us is a liar." And from this is Hassan's saying, addressing Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who had satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before he embraced Islam:

Do you satirize him, when you are no match for him? So your evil, for your good, is the ransom.

And the saying of Abu al-Aswad:

The basest say, the Banu Qushayr, all the days long, "Do not forget Ali."

The cousins of the Prophet and his nearest kin, the most beloved of all people to me.

So if their love is good, I shall attain it, and I am not wrong if it is error.

Abu Ubayda held that "aw" (or) here has the meaning of "wa" (and), as in his saying:

Equal are the breaking of his loaf or the breaking of one of his bones.

The statement falls under the figure of al-laff wa al-nashr al-murattab (the ordered wrapping and unfolding), in that "upon guidance" returns to His saying "indeed we" (إنّا), and "in error" returns to His saying, glorified is He, "you" (إيّاكم), since reason judges thus, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nest, are ripe jujube and a decayed date-stone.

The farness of this is not hidden. In any case, this is not at all from the sphere of taqiyya (dissimulation), as some ignorant people claim. The apparent meaning is that "upon guidance" and what follows is the predicate of "indeed we" or "you", without any ellipsis, since the meaning is: indeed one of us is characterized by one of the two states, as when you say: "Zayd or 'Amr is in the market or in the house." It has been said: it is the predicate of "indeed we", and the predicate of "you" is omitted, its estimate being "upon guidance or in clear error." It has also been said: it is the predicate of "you", and the predicate of "indeed we" is omitted, indicated by what has been mentioned. "You" (إيّاكم) is in the estimate of [a predicate?] ... but when the (attached) pronoun was omitted, the independent pronoun was separated.

In al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan), it is said: there is no need to posit an ellipsis in a case like this; it is needed only in a case like "Zayd or 'Amr is standing." So reflect. The obvious reading is that "clear" (مُبِينٍ) is an attribute of "error", and it is permissible that it be an attribute of both it and "guidance." The attribute, like the pronoun, must be singular after a conjunct introduced by "or." He introduced "upon" (عَلى) with "guidance" to indicate the elevation of its possessor, his firmness, and his command over what he wants, like one standing on a high place or riding a horse he drives wherever he wishes. And he introduced "upon" with "error" to indicate the immersion of its possessor in darkness, until it is as if he were in a dark abyss, not knowing where to turn. Thus there is a metaphor in the statement, either implicit (makniyya) or subsidiary (tab'iyya).

In the reading of Ubayy: "Indeed we or you, either upon guidance or in clear error."

[Page 141]

This is the most equitable phrasing, in that it describes the lapses from which no believer is free using the language normally used for grave matters, and attributes them to the self (nafs); and it describes the grave matters of disbelief and the like using the language normally used for lapses, and attributes them to the addressees. Moreover, he mentioned the criminality attributed to the self in the past tense (sigha al-madi), which denotes certainty, while the action attributed to the opponent is in the present tense (sigha al-mudari'), which does not denote that. He also mentioned that there is an allusion (ta'rid) in the verse, and that it does no harm to what has been mentioned. Some have claimed that it belongs to the category of mutarakah (disengagement from the disbelievers), and that it has been abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 26:

﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, at the gathering (al-hashr) and the reckoning (al-hisab). ﴿Then He will judge between us with truth﴾ He, glory be to Him, will decide between us and will distinguish, after the true state of each of us and of you has become manifest, with justice, by admitting the people of truth (al-muhiqqin) to Paradise and the people of falsehood (al-mubtilin) to the Fire. ﴿And He is the Opener﴾, the Judge in matters that are closed (al-munghalIqa), so how much more in clear matters such as the abolition of polytheism and the establishment of monotheism (tawhid). Or [it means] the Judge in every matter, whether hidden or manifest, and the intensification [of the meaning] is in quality (al-kayf) according to the first [interpretation] and in quantity (al-kamm) according to the second. Perhaps the first aspect is preferable. In it there is an indication of the reason why the settling of disputes is called "fath" (opening), and that it is originally a comparison of what he judges in with a matter that is closed, just as it is likened to a matter that is knotted, in their saying: "hallal al-mushkilat" (solver of difficulties). ʿIsa [ibn ʿUmar] read ﴿al-Fatih﴾ (with the alif). ﴿And He is the All-Knowing﴾ of what He ought to judge by, or of everything.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 34, verse 27:

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners."﴾ This is an inquiry into their argument after the proof has been established against them, as an added rebuke. In his choice of meaning, Abu Hayyan preferred that *arani* (أرى) be taken in the sense of *a'lama* (أعلم, "inform"), so that it takes three objects: the first-person pronoun (ياء المتكلم, *ya' al-mutakallim*), the relative pronoun (الموصول, *al-mawsul*), and *shuraka'* (شُرَكاء, "partners"). The returning pronoun of the relative clause (عائد الموصول, *ta'id al-mawsul*) is omitted, so the sense is "you joined them." The intended meaning is: "Inform me, with proof and evidence, of how partnership is possible." It is also permitted that *ra'a* (رأى) is visual (بصرية, *basariyyah*), transitive to two objects by the transitive form (بالنقل, *bi'l-naql*): the first-person pronoun and the relative pronoun. Then *shuraka'* would be a circumstantial accusative (حال, *hal*) from the omitted relative pronoun, meaning "you joined them, supposing their partnership." Or it could be a second object of *alhaqa* (ألحق), with the verb implicitly carrying the sense of "make" or "name" (تضمين, *tadmin*, "implicit meaning"). The intended meaning is then "show them to me so that I may look at what quality you joined them to God, the Mighty and Majestic, who has nothing like unto Him in deserving worship," or "you joined them to Him, Glorified be He, by making them or naming them partners." The purpose is to show the magnitude of their error.

Some eminent scholars said: "The phrase 'show me' (أرُونِي) is not meant literally, because the Prophet (ﷺ) saw and knew them. It is therefore a metaphor (مجاز, *majaz*) and a figurative illustration (تمثيل, *tamthil*). The meaning is: 'Whatever you claim as a partner, when it is displayed to the eyes, which is wood and stone, your disgrace is complete.' This is like saying to a man of lowly origin, 'Mention to me your father, with whom you compared yourself to the noble so-and-so,' not meaning the actual mention, but intending to rebuke him, and that if he mentions his father he will be exposed."

﴿Nay﴾ is a restraint (رَدْع, *rad'*) on them from the claim of partnership, after breaking it by refutation, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Uff to you and to what you worship besides God﴾ (Al-Anbiya 21:67), after he had confronted his people. ﴿Rather, He is God, the Mighty﴾, that is, the One described by overpowering dominance, which requires necessary existence, ﴿the Wise﴾, the One described by brilliant wisdom, which requires comprehensive knowledge of things. These whom they have joined are far removed from being described by that, and a thousand thousand stations away from circling around what it requires. The pronoun (الضمير, *al-damir*) either returns to what is in the mind, and what follows it, which is "God," as a predicate (خبر, *khabar*) of it that explains it, and ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾ are two attributes of the majestic Name. Or it returns to "our Lord" in His words, Glorified be He: "«Our Lord will judge between us»," as has been said. Or it is the pronoun of the matter (ضمير الشأن, *damir al-sha'n*), with "God" as the subject (مبتدأ, *mubtada'*) and ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾ as its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter, because according to the sound opinion its predicate is only a sentence.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 28:**

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively (kaffatan) to mankind.﴾ The apparent reading is that *kaffatan* is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of *al-nās* (mankind), and it has been placed before *illā* together with what follows it for emphasis, as Ibn 'Aṭiyya said. Its origin is from *al-kaff*, meaning restraint, but it is intended to mean generality, because of the restraint it contains against departing. It became so well known in this sense that its meaning of restraint was entirely set aside. Thus *jā'a al-nās kaffatan* means "the people came all together." This reading is supported by what Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid, that he said concerning the verse: "That is, to mankind entirely." It is also supported by what Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, that he said: "That is, to mankind comprehensively." Likewise, what 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Qatada, that he said concerning the verse: "God the Exalted sent Muhammad ﷺ to the Arabs and the non-Arabs, and the most honoured of them before God the Exalted are the most obedient to Him." And what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "That is, to the Arabs and the non-Arabs and all nations." This is based on the permissibility of placing the ḥāl before its referent when that referent is governed by a particle (ḥarf al-jarr). This is the view he adopted, contrary to many grammarians: Abu 'Alī, Ibn Kaysān, Ibn Burhān, al-Radī and Ibn Mālik, who said:

*Anteposing a ḥāl over what is governed by a particle: they have refused it, but I do not forbid it, for it has come down (in usage).*

Abu Ḥayyān, after he transmitted the permissibility from those mentioned other than al-Radī, said, and this is the correct view: "Among the examples of Abu 'Alī is *zaydun khayru mā yakūnu khayrun minka* (Zayd is best when he is better than you)." The poet said:

*When manliness wearies a man in his youth, its pursuit of him in his maturity is severe.*

Another said:

*I consoled myself, all of you, after your separation, with remembrance of you, until it is as if you were with me.*

The anteposing of the ḥāl over its referent when governed by a particle, and over what is connected to it, has occurred. Among that is his saying:

*Smitten with you, I have been smitten, but the decree of separation is final, and there is no path to you.*

And another's saying:

*Heedless, death overtakes a man, and he is called, but it is too late for refusal.*

If its anteposing over the governed noun and the governing element is permissible, then its anteposing over the governed noun without the governing element is more permissible. End of quotation. They considered this the best of the aspects (of i'rāb) in the verse and said that anything else is forced. It has been objected that this leads to the governing of what precedes *illā* over what follows it, namely *arsala* (sent) governing what comes after, namely *lil-nās* (to mankind), and *lil-nās* is neither an exception, nor an excepted-from element, nor a follower of it, and they have prohibited this. It was answered that the intended sense is *wa-mā arsalnāka lil-nās illā kaffatan*, so it is prior in rank, and a similar case is valid in the correctness of governance, together with the fact that they allow more latitude with adverbial phrases than with other elements.

Al-Khafājī, may God have mercy on him, said: "The better view is that *lil-nās* be taken as the excepted element, with the exception being *mufarragh* (an exception with no stated subject), and its underlying form is: *mā arsalnāka li-shay'in min al-ashyā' illā li-tablīgh al-nās kaffatan* (We did not send you for anything among things except to convey to mankind comprehensively). As for taking it to mean *mā arsalnāka lil-khalq muṭlaqan illā lil-nās kaffatan* (We did not send you to creation in general except to mankind comprehensively) with it as the excepted element, this is extremely weak. End of quotation. It is not hidden that in the verse, according to what he preferred, there is the omission of an annexed noun, the separation between the exception particle and the excepted element, and the anteposing of the ḥāl over its referent. All of these go against the norm, and such a combination rarely occurs in eloquent speech. It was also objected to this that it would then require taking the *lām* in *lil-nās* to mean *ilā* (to). This is not a valid objection, because *arsala* is transitive with *lām* and with *ilā*, as Abu Ḥayyān and others have mentioned. So there is no need to make it mean *ilā*. Furthermore, even if it were taken to mean *ilā*, no error would arise at all, since each of *lām* and *ilā* is used with the meaning of the other. Likewise, there is no need to take it as causal (ta'līliyya), except according to what al-Khafājī preferred.

Many have said: *kaffatan* is an active participle (ism fā'il) from *kaffa*, and the *tā'* in it is for intensification, like the *tā'* in *rāwiya* and similar words. It is a ḥāl of the object of *arsalnāka* (We sent you), and *lil-nās* is related to it. Abu Ḥayyān adopted this, meaning: *mā arsalnāka illā kāffan wa-māni'an lil-nās 'anil-kufr wal-ma'āṣī* (We did not send you except as one who restrains and prevents mankind from disbelief and sins).

Abu 'Alī also took it as a ḥāl of the *kāf* (of *arsalnāka*), but he said: the meaning is *illā jāmi'an lil-nās fil-iblāgh* (except as one who gathers mankind in conveying the message). Abu Ḥayyān objected that the language does not support this, because it is not established that *kaffa* means "gathered." And there is a clear objection to it, since one says *kaffa al-qamīṣ* (he gathered the collar of the shirt) when he gathers its hem, and *kaffa al-jurḥ* (he bound the wound) when he binds it with a cloth that surrounds it. Ibn Durayd said: "Everything you gather, you have *kaffa*-ed." Yet he (Abu Ḥayyān) also allowed that it may be a metaphor from restraint, because what is gathered cannot easily be scattered or spread.

It has also been said that *kaffatan* is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like *al-kādhiba*, *al-'āqiba* and *al-'āfiya*. This too is a ḥāl of the *kāf*, either remaining in its verbal-noun status without any elided element, for emphasis, or by interpreting it as an active participle, or by supposing an annexed noun, meaning: *illā dhā kaffatin*, that is, possessing restraint, that is, a preventing of mankind from disbelief. It has been said: possessing a restraining from deviating from your conveying. Some have held that it is a verbal noun functioning as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), and that its accusative case does not require the unity of the agent, as al-Radī preferred. Al-'Allāma al-Zamakhsharī held that it is an active participle from *al-kaff*, an adjective of an elided verbal noun, and its *tā'* is for the feminine. The meaning is: *mā arsalnāka illā irsālatan kaffatan*, that is, a general sending for them, encompassing them, because when it encompasses them it restrains them from anyone of them going out from it. This was objected to on the grounds that *kaffatan* is not reported from the Arabs except in the accusative as a ḥāl, restricted to a plural of rational beings, and that the omission of the qualified noun and the setting of the adjective in its place is only permissible when the qualified noun is known to be described by it in a way that it cannot suit anything else. It was answered that *kaffatan* here is not the same as the usage in which the ḥāl is obligatory, even though both return to one meaning. What has been said, that the Arabs have not used it except in this way, is not valid. And setting an adjective in place of its qualified noun is common and regular without condition when a context indicates it. Mentioning the verb before it indicates the elision of its verbal noun, as in *qumtu ṭawīlan* and *ḥasanan* (I stood long and well), meaning *qiyāman ṭawīlan wa-ḥasanan* (a long and good standing).

In the Khafājī marginal notes: It is established that 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said in his letter to the family of Banī Kākila: "I have made for the family of Banī Kākila, from the entire treasury of the Muslims (*'alā kāffati bayt al-muslimīn*), for every year, two hundred mithqāl of pure gold." And 'Alī, may God ennoble his face, said it when he ratified it. These two imams used *kāffa* for non-rational beings, and not in the accusative as a ḥāl. It is not hidden that some of the objections raised against this aspect are also raised against some of the preceding aspects, and the answer is the same answer.

What I choose regarding the verse is what is apparent, and there is no harm in anteposing, and usage has come down with it, and no analogy prevents it. The matter of crossing over the governing element with *illā* only to what is neither an exception nor an excepted-from element is easy, due to the hadith of latitude with the adverbial phrase. The verse is clearer on this for proving the universality of his mission ﷺ, and it is in this respect like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all﴾ [al-A'rāf: 158]. If al-Qāḍī Abu Sa'īd had used it as evidence, the Jew would have been dumbfounded. It may also be used as evidence by what hardly anyone can deny of his ﷺ conduct with the Jews in his time.

His ﷺ, upon him be blessings and peace, call to them to Islam: ﴿bashīran﴾ (as a bringer of good tidings) to whoever embraces Islam, with reward, ﴿wa-nadhīran﴾ (and a warner) to whoever does not embrace it, with punishment. The two descriptions are ḥāls of the object of ﴿arsalnāka﴾. They may, under some of the preceding aspects, be made a substitute for ﴿kaffatan﴾, like the substitution of the detailed for the summary. So reflect.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ this, so their ignorance leads them to persist in what they are upon of error and misguidance.

And they say, ﴿And they say﴾, that is, out of their ignorance, either in reality or in effect. For this reason the verb is not joined with *fa'* (so as to mark a consequence). It has also been said that they say it out of extreme obstinacy, and the absence of *fa'* is for that reason.

It has also been said that what drives them is extreme ignorance, and that the absence of *fa'* is because its being a consequence of what precedes it is evident, and such matters are left to the listener's mind. It has been said that this is because extreme ignorance is not the same as ignorance, and that, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that this describes some of them, while the lack of knowledge in His words, ﴿but most of them do not know﴾, describes others. What appears to me is that those who say this are some of the polytheists contemporary with him (ﷺ), not most of mankind in general, and that the present-tense form is meant to convey continuous renewal (*al-istimrar al-tajaddudi*). It has been said that it is expressed in the present tense to bring the past scene vividly before the mind, because of its strangeness. The original would be: ﴿And they said, "When is this promise?"﴾, said mockingly, meaning by "the promise" what is announced as good news and what is warned of, or the promise stated in His words, ﴿"Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us."﴾ [p. 144] ﴿"If you are truthful."﴾ They are addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers who follow him.

﴿Say: "For you is an appointment of a Day"﴾, or "a promise of a Day", on the basis that ﴿mī'ād﴾ is a mīmī noun (a verbal noun formed with a prefixed mīm), or a noun standing in place of the verbal noun, as transmitted from Abu 'Ubayda, meaning "the promised thing". It has also been said that the speech is elliptical, with an omitted governing noun (muḍāf), meaning: "for you is the occurrence of the promise of a Day", or "the fulfilment of the promise of a Day". The nunation of ﴿yawm﴾ is for magnification, meaning a great Day. It is also permitted that ﴿mī'ād﴾ be a noun of time, and that its annexation to ﴿yawm﴾ be for specification (tabyīn), meaning to clarify the time of the promise as a particular day, like the expression "saḥq thawb" (the wearing out of a garment) and "ba'īr sāniya" (a camel that draws water). The first interpretation is supported by the fact that the speech comes as a reply to their saying ﴿When is this promise?﴾. The second interpretation is that it was read as "mī'ādun yawmun", with both in the nominative and with nunation, so that ﴿yawmun﴾ in this reading is in apposition (badal), which implies that the appointment is the Day itself. That ﴿yawmun﴾ is a badal al-ishtimāl (apposition of inclusion) is far-fetched. Likewise is what Abu Ḥayyān said, that it is on the basis of an omitted element, meaning: "say: for you is an appointment, the appointment of a Day", and when the governing noun was omitted, the word that took its place received its i'rāb (grammatical case) according to it. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "mī'ādun" with ḍamma and nunation, and "yawmān" with fatḥa and nunation. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is for magnification, by suppressing a verb whose estimate is "for you is an appointment", meaning a Day whose description is such-and-such. The ḍamma is also permitted on this basis. It is also permitted that it be in the accusative of place (ẓarfiyya) governed by ﴿mī'ād﴾, on the basis that it is a verbal noun with the meaning of the promised thing, not a noun of time. Al-Baḥr says: its accusative may be on the basis of the adverb of time (ẓarf), with the governing element being an omitted muḍāf, meaning the fulfilment of a promise of a Day whose description is such-and-such. ʿĪsā read "mī'ādun" with nunation and "yawma" with fatḥa without nunation, annexed to the clause, and the basis for the fatḥa is what has passed just now.

﴿You will not delay from it an hour﴾ when it surprises you, ﴿nor will you advance﴾, meaning, from it, by an hour. The pronoun (hāʾ), according to what Abu al-Baqāʾ said, may refer to ﴿mī'ād﴾ and may refer to ﴿yawm﴾, and whichever it refers to, the clause is a description of it. In al-Irshād it is said that it is an inseparable description of ﴿mī'ād﴾. In the answer, on the basis of restricting the negation by the surprise, there is an intensification in the threat that is not hidden. It is also permitted that the negation be unrestricted by that, so the description of the appointment with what is mentioned is for its confirmation and its determination. The discussion of a parallel of this clause has already passed, so recall it.

Since their question about the time was by way of obstinacy, they were answered with a threat. Its summary is that what was taken into account in the answer was the intended purpose of their question, not what the apparent wording gives. This is not from the wise style, for the eloquent speaker turns the attention to the meaning. Al-Ṭībī said: it is from it. They asked about the time of the establishment of the Hour, and were answered about their states in it. So it is as if it were said: leave off asking about the time of its establishment, for its occurrence is inevitable; rather ask about the states of your own selves, where you will be stunned and bewildered in it because of the terror of what you witness. This is more suitable to your condition than that you ask about it. And it is as you see. It has also been said that it includes an answer that this Day is known only to God, Mighty and Majestic, because of the indefiniteness of ﴿yawm﴾, and this is an unnecessary strain.

Regarding this Day, it has been differed: it has been said it is the Day of Resurrection, and the speech of al-Ṭībī is upon this. It has been said: it is the day when their term comes and their death arrives. It has been said: it is the Day of Badr.

[Page 145]

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, and they are the polytheists of the Arabs, ﴿"We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in that which is before it"﴾, i.e., of the earlier scriptures, as related from Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj. Their intention is the denial of belief in all the heavenly scriptures that indicate the resurrection and contain that teaching. It is also related that the disbelievers of Makkah asked the People of the Book about the Messenger (ﷺ), and they informed them that they found his description (ﷺ) in their books, and that this angered them, so they said what they said. This view is judged weak, because there is nothing in the immediate context (siyaq) or the preceding context (sibaq) that indicates it. It has also been said that "that which is before it" refers to the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Atiyyah rejected the one who said this, on the grounds that "ma bayna al-yad" (what is between the hands) in the language means "what precedes." This was answered by the claim that it may refer to what has passed and it may refer to what is yet to come.

Yes, what weakens that view is that what is "before" a thing is of its own kind, but the essential meaning of their statement on this view is that they did not believe in the Qur'an
