nor in what indicates it. As for the claim that the majority usage is for what has passed, it has also been said that this is not accepted. Al-Tabarsi related that the intended "those who disbelieved" are the Jews, and in that case "that which is before it" refers to the Gospel. It should not be overlooked that this view is one to which no attention should be paid, and there is nothing in the immediate context or the preceding context that indicates it.

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to see it. The object of "tara" (you see) is "idh" or is omitted, and "idh" is an adverbial complement of it, i.e., "in what state the wrongdoers are." "Law" (if) here expresses wish, its meaning being diverted to something other than Him, the Exalted, and it has no answer; or its answer is implied, i.e., "you would see a dreadful matter" or something similar. "Al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers) is an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun, for the purpose of recording (their wrongdoing) and explaining the cause of their deserving (punishment). The original would be "if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord," i.e., at the station of reckoning.

﴿They will cast back the word among themselves﴾, i.e., they will argue and exchange words with one another. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant﴾ is a resumptive statement to explain that interaction, or it is a substitute for "yarji'u" and so on, i.e., the followers will say ﴿to those who were arrogant﴾ in the world and who led them into error and misguidance, ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers"﴾ in what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 32:

﴿Those who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed﴾ This is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), as if it were said: "What did those who were arrogant say when the followers objected to them and rebuked them?" So it is said that they said: ﴿Did we turn you away from guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals.﴾ They denied that they were the ones who had barred them from faith, and affirmed that they themselves were the ones who had barred their own selves. That is, "We were not the ones who stood between you and faith after you had resolved to enter it; rather, you yourselves deprived your own selves of its share through your crimes and your preference of disbelief over faith."

The use of idh (إذْ, "when") as a temporal adverb governed by a preposition and in the position of a genitive object of an annexed noun is common in their speech, just as it occurs annexed (mudaf). This is part of the broad usage of adverbs of time in particular (al-ittisa' fi al-zuruf). By this, the objection is answered to those who claimed that idh is among the adverbs that necessarily function only as adverbs of time, so how could it occur here in the genitive as an object of an annexed noun?

The author of al-Fara'id said that idh here has been stripped of the meaning of temporality, completely detached from it, and turned into a pure noun, because what is meant by "the time of the coming of guidance" is guidance itself, not the time as such; therefore it is annexed to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 33:

﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant﴾, in reversal of their (the arrogant ones') reversal and nullifying it, ﴿"Nay, rather, the scheming of the night and the day"﴾, that is: "Nay, rather, your scheming against us by night and by day diverted us." The genitive complement has been deleted and the adverbial noun (zarf) put in its place, by way of extension (ittisa'), or the night and the day are made the ones scheming, by way of figurative attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). It has been said that there is no need for that, for the idafa (construction) is in the sense of fi (in). It has been objected to this that, aside from the fact that the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) did not say it, the hyperbole (al-mubalagha) is lost when it is taken this way. What we have pointed to shows that ﴿scheming﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of a deleted verb. It is also permitted that it be the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject, i.e., "The cause of our disbelief is the scheming of the night and the day," or a subject whose predicate is deleted, i.e., "The scheming of the night and the day is the cause of our disbelief."

Qatada and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read (bal makrun al-layla wa-l-nahara) with tanwin and the accusative of the two adverbs, i.e., "Nay, rather, your scheming diverted us," or "a great scheming in the night and the day."

Muhammad ibn Ja'far, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Razin and Ibn Ya'mur also read "makarru al-layli wa-l-nahari" with a fatha on the mim and kaf and a shadda on the ra', with the nominative and the idafa, i.e., "Nay, rather, the recurrence of the night and the day and their alternation diverted us." They intended, as has been said, the reference to long hope and being deceived by the days, along with these leaders in disbelief in God, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Jubayr also, and Rashid al-Qari and Talha, read likewise, except that they put makarran in the accusative as an adverb, i.e., "Nay, rather, you diverted us in the recurrence of the night and the day," that is, in their recurrence, that is, constantly. It is also permitted that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), i.e., "you incite us with a constant incitement, without slackening from it." The author of al-Lawami' permitted it to be an adverb governed by "ta'murunana" (you command us) afterwards. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is a mistake, because what comes after idh does not govern what comes before it.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿when you were commanding us﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "the night and the day," or a reason (ta'lil) for the scheming. In al-Irshad he made it an adverb governed by it, i.e., "Nay, rather, your constant scheming at the time of your commanding us ﴿to disbelieve in God and set up equals to Him﴾," on the basis that their scheming is either the very act of their commanding with what was mentioned, or other matters accompanying their command that call to compliance with it, such as encouragement, intimidation, and other things.

The clause "those who were oppressed said" etc. is a conjunction (atf) upon the clause "those who were oppressed will say" etc., even though the two differ in tense (past and future).

Since this statement is a return from them to speech, other than the statement of the arrogant, "Did we divert you?", and it is an initiation of speech that came as a response to objection against them, the conjunctive particle is used here and was not used there, according to what some of them preferred. It has been said: the point in that is that when the speech of the oppressed was related after His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will throw the blame at one another﴾, it was liable to be asked: "Then what did those who were arrogant say to those who were oppressed, and was there a mutual exchange between the two groups?" So it was said: "Those who were arrogant said such-and-such, and those who were oppressed said such-and-such," and the combined two statements were brought out in the form of an answer, and part of the answer was conjoined to part of it. So reflect.

Al-Andad is the plural of nid, which is commonly used for whoever is claimed to be a partner in general. However, al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in his exegesis, which proceeds on the path of the commentators with concise clarity in rendering the Qur'an, and in his noble luminous handwriting, I saw that it is specific to those who claim divinity, such as Pharaoh and his like, because by that he became a rival (nadda) to God, Exalted, and strayed (sharada) from His mercy, glorified is He. And al-Shaykh said: because he strayed (sharada) from servitude to Him, majestic is His glory.

﴿And they concealed﴾, that is, the wrongdoers of both groups, the arrogant and the oppressed, hid ﴿the regret﴾ over what they had been in the world of misguidance and misleading, with regard to the arrogant, and of misguidance alone with regard to the oppressed. The view that their regret over misleading others also occurred, on account of its being accepted, is forced. They did not display anything that indicates it, from dialogue or otherwise. ﴿when they saw the punishment﴾, for they were stunned when they beheld it, so they were unable to speak and were occupied away from displaying it by a preoccupying distraction. It has been said: each one concealed it from his companion, out of fear of reproach. This was objected to: how can this be, given the statement of the oppressed to their leaders, "Had it not been for you, we would have been believers"? And what regret could be greater than this? Also, fear of reproach in that situation is far-fetched. It has been said: "they concealed the regret" means "they displayed it," for asarra (to conceal) is among the words with opposite meanings (al-addad), since the hamza can signify affirmation or negation. So the meaning of asarahu is "he made it a secret," or "he removed its secrecy." Its parallel is ashkaytu (I complained). Al-Zamakhshari recited for himself:

I complained to the days of their evil dealing, and of wonder, a weeper complained to the one who makes weep.

The days did nothing but increase complaint, and the days never ceased to complain, nor were they complained against.

Ibn 'Atiyya objected to this view, saying that it has never been established in any language that asarra is among the words with opposite meanings. You know that an affirming statement takes precedence over a negating one, so do not be heedless.

﴿And We placed the shackles﴾, that is, the fetters, ﴿on the necks of those who disbelieved﴾, and they are the arrogant and the oppressed. The original would be "on their necks," but the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun in order to draw attention to their blame and to alert to the cause of their being shackled. Abu Hayyan judged the relative pronoun to be general, so that the two aforementioned groups and others enter into it, for among the disbelievers is one who has no followers who would return speech to him in the Hereafter, and who is not himself a follower of a leader, like the boy whom al-Khidr, peace be upon him, killed.

﴿Are they being recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾, that is, they are not recompensed except with the like of what they used to do of evil, and the essence of it is: they are not recompensed except with evil. The verb jaza may take two objects directly, as Al-Raghib's statement indicates: "one says jaziytuhu kadha and bikadha." It is also permitted that ma be in the place of the accusative by removing the preposition, which is either ba' or 'an or 'ala, for it is reported that jaza is transitive with all of them. It has been said that this transitivity is due to its being implicitly construed with the meaning of "judging" (al-qada'). And if what you heard from al-Raghib is established, there is no need for this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 34:

﴿And We did not send into any town﴾ from among the towns ﴿any warner﴾, that is, a warner from among the warners, ﴿but its affluent ones said﴾ (mutrafuha), that is, those who were expansive in the blessings therein. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿Indeed we, in what you have been sent with﴾, by your claim, of monotheism and other things. The second prepositional phrase is connected to what is with him (ʿindahu), and the first is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿disbelievers﴾, which is the predicate of inna. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the affluent ones of every town said that to their messenger. Accordingly, the plural in ("you have been sent") is for mockery (tahakkum). It was also said: it is for giving precedence (taghlib) to the addressee over the category of messengers, or over those who followed him among the believers. Some eminent scholars said: the statement is of the type of contrasting plural with plural. It was said that the first plural refers to the messengers, indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿you have been sent﴾, and the second, ﴿disbelievers﴾, means that each one disbelieved in his messenger and addressed him with the like of that. So there is no precedence (taghlib) in the address in "you have been sent." It was also said: the first plural is ﴿warner﴾, because it conveys generality in the report, not in what is reported, since it occurs in the context of negation, and not every people denied all the messengers; so it is taken as a contrast. The statement is directed toward consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he was tested with, namely the opposition and enmity of the affluent ones of his people toward him, peace be upon him. The singling out of the affluent for denial is because they are, for the most part, the first to deny the messengers, peace be upon them, since they are occupied with the glitter of this world and what has taken hold of their hearts from it. They are immersed in desires and look down on those who have not obtained a share of it. This is unlike the poor, for their hearts, being free of that, are more receptive to good. For this reason you find them to be the majority of the followers of the prophets, peace be upon them, as came in the hadith of Heraclius.

ï»؟﴿وقالُوا﴾ The pronoun refers to the affluent (al-mutrafun) mentioned earlier. It is also said to refer to the Quraysh. The apparent and immediately understood meaning is the first, and the purpose is to relate what encouraged them to disbelieve in what the warners were sent with. That is, the affluent said: ﴿نَحْنُ أكْثَرُ أمْوالا وأوْلادًا﴾ ("We have more wealth and children"), meaning that our wealth and our children are very numerous. Here the form "afal" (aktar) is for absolute increase. It is also permitted to keep it in its more common usage, with the object of comparison omitted, meaning: "We have more wealth and children than you." ﴿وما نَحْنُ بِمُعَذَّبِينَ﴾ ("And we will not be punished") with any kind of punishment that would spoil for us the pleasure of abundant wealth and children, such as fear of kings, subjugation by enemies, the non-execution of one's word, toil in attaining one's aims, and the like. The placing of the pronoun before the negative particle indicates that the addressees, or the believers, are not like that. The essence of their statement, "We are in a blessing unmixed with any calamity," is the proof of our honour before Allah, mighty and majestic, and His good pleasure with us. So if what we are upon of shirk and other things you call us to abandon were contrary to His good pleasure, we would not be in the blessing we are in. It is also possible that they measured the matters of the Hereafter, which were imagined or supposed in their view, against the matters of this world, and claimed that one who is blessed in this world is blessed in the Hereafter. A group of scholars followed this view, and they said: the negation of their being punished is either based on the absence of otherworldly punishment altogether, or based on the belief that Allah, exalted is He, has honoured them in this world, so He will not humiliate them in the Hereafter, assuming it occurs. Al-Khafaji, regarding the reason for placing the pronoun before the negative particle, said: it indicates that the believers are punished, mocking them because of their assumption that wealth and children repel punishment from them, as some of the polytheists said. And you know that the more apparent thing upon it is the sequencing (tafri'). Abu Hayyan went to the view that the punishment negated is more general than the otherworldly punishment and the worldly punishment with which the prophets, upon them be peace, may warn and threaten their people if they do not believe in them. Perhaps what we mentioned first is more fitting to the context, so reflect deeply.

[Page 148]

﴿Say﴾, in rejection of what they claimed, that this is a sign of honor and approval: ﴿Indeed my Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾ (to extend it for him) ﴿and restricts it﴾ for whom He wills to restrict it for. Thus He, glorified is He, may extend provision to the disobedient and restrict it for the obedient. He may also reverse the matter, extend it for both of them, or restrict it for both of them. He may extend it for one person, obedient or disobedient, at one time and restrict it for him at another. He does each of these according to what His will, mighty and majestic is He, requires, a will built upon profound wisdoms. So if extension were a sign of honor and approval, it would be exclusive to the obedient. Likewise, if restriction were a sign of humiliation and wrath, it would be exclusive to the disobedient. But it is not so. The summary, as has been said, is a denial that this is a proof of what they claimed, since the enemy and the friend are equal in it.

A group said: what is meant is that He, exalted is He, does this according to His will, which is built upon wisdoms. Therefore the matter of reward and punishment, whose basis is obedience and its absence, is not to be measured by it.

Nasir al-Din said: if that were due to honor or humiliation that necessitates it, it would not be by His will, exalted is He. This is based on the premise that necessity contradicts choice and will. Al-Khafaji held this view, taking it from the words of our master Jalal al-Din, and he refuted with it those who rejected it. It is not hidden that the claim of the affluent (al-mutrafin) that God, exalted is He, is under obligation regarding what they have of extended provision, and likewise regarding what their enemies have of restricted provision, is not evident, so that it would need to be refuted by affirming a will that does not coexist with obligation.

Al-A'mash read ﴿ويُقَدَّرُ﴾ (wa-yuqaddaru) with a doubled letter here and in what follows. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this. Among them are those who claim that the basis of extension is nobility and honor, and the basis of restriction is humiliation and baseness. Among them are those who were bewildered and objected against God, exalted is He, regarding extension for some people and restriction for others, until one of them said:

*How many a learned one, whose doctrines have wearied (the minds),*
*and an ignorant one, whom you find provided with sustenance!*

*This is the one who has left minds bewildered,*
*and made the eminent scholar a heretic.*

This speaker meant by "the eminent scholar" himself. By my life, he is more deserving of the description of the dull ignorant one than of this description. The eminent scholar is the one who says:

*Among the proofs of destiny and its decree*
*is the misery of the intelligent and the good living of the fool.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 34, verse 37:

﴿Nor is it your wealth or your children that will bring you near to Us in closeness.﴾ This is a new sentence from the Mighty and Majestic One, addressed to people by way of *talwin* (shifting of the form of address) and *iltifat* (turning from one mode of address to another), for the sake of emphasizing the truth and confirming what preceded it. So says *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*. It is also permitted that what came before is meant to deny that nearness to God and honour are the basis and cause of abundant provision. This denial means that abundance of provision is not a cause of nearness and honour, and the address is to the disbelievers. *Allati* refers to wealth and children. Since the broken plural (*jam' taksir*), whether it denotes rational or non-rational beings, is equal in the rule of feminine agreement, and since the plural (*al-majmu'*) carries the meaning of a group (*jama'a*), the singular and feminine forms are valid. That is: "Nor is the group of your wealth and your children the group that brings you near to Us as a nearness." There is no need to posit an elided noun (*mudaf*) in the noble text. What is mentioned is an estimation of meaning, not a grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). From al-Zajjaj: there is an omission at the beginning of the sentence, indicated by what is at its end, and the estimate is: "Nor is your wealth by that which brings you near to Us as a nearness, nor your children by that which..." etc. You know that there is no need for this either. It is also permitted that *allati* be an adjective for a singular feminine noun estimated as *bil-taqwa* (by piety) or *bil-khasla allati* (by the quality which). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *allati* be a metonymy for piety, because what brings one near to God is nothing but that. That is: "Nor is your wealth or your children by that which is placed for bringing near."

Al-Hasan read *bil-lati* in the plural, and it refers to wealth and children, like *allati*, as you heard earlier. It was also read *bil-ladhi*, meaning "by the thing which brings you near."

*Zulfa* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) like *qurba*. Its accusative case is by way of the verbal noun from the meaning. Al-Dahhak read *zulafan*, with a fatha on the *lam* and tanwin on the *fa*, the plural of *zulfa*, which means nearness.

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ This is an exception from the object of ﴿brings you near﴾, according to the view of a group. It is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) if the address is general to believers and disbelievers, and a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) if the address is specific to the disbelievers. The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) is then in the accusative or nominative position, as its subject, with what follows it as its predicate, or its predicate is implied: that is, "but whoever believes and does righteous deeds, their belief and their deed bring them near."

Abu Hayyan preferred disconnection. In *al-Bahr* he said: al-Zajjaj held that it is a substitute (*badal*) for the mentioned object, but al-Nahhas considered this an error, because the pronoun of the second person cannot be substituted, so one does not say "I saw you Zayd." The positions of al-Akhfash and the Kufans are that it is permissible to substitute from the pronouns of the second and first person, but substitution in the verse is not valid. Do you not see that it is not valid to empty the verb that is the relative clause of what comes after *illa* (except)? So if you said *ma Zayd bil-ladhi yadribu illa Khalidan* (Zayd is not the one who strikes except Khalid), it would not be valid. End of quote.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that making it an exception from the object is not valid if *allati* is a metonymy for piety, because it would follow that wealth and children are piety for someone other than the one who believes and does righteous deeds, but they are not bringing him near. It was said there is no harm in this, for it is valid to say: "Neither your wealth nor your children are piety, except for the believers." The sum of this is that wealth and children are not piety and do not bring anyone near except the believers. When the exception is disconnected, this is valid and becomes clear. It is also permitted that it be an exception from (*amwalukum wa awladukum*, your wealth and your children), by omitting a noun (*mudaf*), that is: "except the wealth of those who believe and do righteous deeds and their children." In this, when *allati* is taken as a metonymy for piety, there is emphasis, since the wealth and children of the righteous believer are made the very essence of piety. Then, the bringing near of wealth for the righteous believer is by spending it on what pleases God, and the bringing near of children is by teaching them good, giving them understanding of the religion, and preparing them for righteousness and obedience.

﴿Those, for them is the reward of double﴾ *Ula'ika* refers to *man* (whoever), and the plural is used in view of its meaning, just as the singular was used earlier in view of its form. The distance implied in *dhalika* is to indicate the high rank of these people and the remoteness of their station in virtue. That is: "Those who are described with belief and righteous deeds, for them is the reward of double," meaning God rewards them with the doubled reward, that is, multiplied reward, so He rewards them for one good deed with ten times its like, or more, up to seven hundred. The construction of *jaza'* (reward) with *al-di'f* (double) is an annexation of a verbal noun to its object.

Qatada read *jaza'un al-di'fu* with both words in the nominative. Then *al-di'f* is an apposition (*badal*). Al-Zajjaj permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is the double." Ya'qub, in one narration, read *jaza'an* in the accusative and *al-di'fa* in the accusative as well. Then *jaza'* is a specification (*tamyiz*), or an accusative of circumstance (*hal*) from the subject of *lahum* if *al-di'f* is the subject, or from it if it is the subject, or an accusative as a verbal noun for an implied verb indicated by *lahum*, that is, "they will be rewarded with a reward." It was also read *jaza'un* with the nominative and tanwin, and *al-di'fa* with the accusative, by making the verbal noun operate.

﴿For what they did﴾ of righteous deeds, ﴿and they will be in the chambers﴾, that is, in the chambers of Paradise and its lofty dwellings, ﴿secure﴾ from all the hardships of this world and the Hereafter. Al-Hasan, 'Asim in one of his transmissions, al-A'mash, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b read *fi al-ghuurafat* with the *ra'* sukun. Some reciters read it with a fatha. Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, Talha, Hamza, and Khalaf read *fi al-ghurfa* in the singular with the *ra'* sukun. Ibn Thabit also read it in the singular with a damma on the *ra'*, and the singular is used to indicate the genus, because they are not all in one chamber, and the singular is more concise where there is no ambiguity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 38:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by rejecting and discrediting them, ﴿seeking to frustrate [them]﴾ — that is, according to their false assumption, [seeking to frustrate] Allah, mighty and majestic, or the prophets, peace be upon them. Its meaning is: they suppose that they have the upper hand and that Allah the Exalted, or His prophets, peace be upon them, have no power [over them]. The sense of mutual contest (al-mufa'alah, the form of the verb indicating reciprocity) is not intended here.

﴿Those﴾ whose rank in evil is far removed, ﴿will be brought forth into punishment﴾, [and] what they have relied upon will not benefit them in any way. In mentioning punishment instead of its proper place [i.e., the Fire] there is an emphasis that is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 39:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it for him.﴾ That is, He, glory be to Him, expands it for him at times and constricts it for him at other times. So do not fear poverty; spend in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and draw near to Him, Mighty and Majestic, with your wealth,
[Page 150]
and expose yourselves to His breezes (nafahat), exalted and high is He. The thrust (masaq) of the verse is therefore admonition and encouraging detachment from this world, and urging drawing near to Him, exalted is He, through spending. This differs from the thrust of its earlier parallel, for that one was a refutation of the disbelievers, as you have heard. Also, what came before is general, whereas what is here is specific: the extending and restricting pertain to one single person considered across two times, as indicated by His saying here "for him" (lahu), and by the absence of that phrase there. Although the pronoun may be somewhat ambiguous, the earlier parallel, being free of that, and this mention coming after it containing it, serve as an indication that what was mentioned is intended. So do not be heedless.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾: it is possible that "ma" is conditional, in a position of accusative governed by "anfaqtum" (you spend), and His saying, ﴿then He will replace it﴾, is the answer of the condition. It is also possible that "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), in a position of nominative as the subject, with the clause after it being its predicate, and the "fa" entered because the subject includes the meaning of a condition. "Min shay'" (of anything) is a specification under both possibilities. The meaning of "yukhlifuhu" (He replaces it) is: He gives in its place a substitute and something that stands in its stead as compensation for it. This occurs either in this world, through wealth, as is the apparent meaning, or through contentment, which is a treasure that does not perish, as has been said; or in the Hereafter, through reward, than which every replacement is lesser. Some scholars restricted it to the Hereafter. Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that he said: "If one of you has something, let him be moderate, and let him not misinterpret this verse, [And whatever you spend of anything, then He will replace it], for provision is apportioned, and perhaps what has been apportioned to him is little, while he spends as one who is given abundance." Others, other than al-Firyabi, among those mentioned, related from him that he said regarding the verse: "Whatever replacement there is, it is from Him, exalted is He. And it may be that a person spends all his wealth in good and is not replaced until he dies." A similar verse is: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ [Hud: 6]; he says: whatever provision He gave it is from Him, exalted is He, and perhaps He does not provide for it until it dies. The first is more apparent, because the verse is an exhortation to spend, and that expansion and restriction, when both are from Him, Mighty and Majestic, it is not fitting for one who has been granted abundance to fear loss through spending, nor for one for whom He has decreed a lesser amount to seek to increase it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾, is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) that confirms this, as if it were said: so He provides for him from where he does not reckon.

Al-Shaykhan related from Abu Hurayrah who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: There is no day on which the servants rise in the morning but two angels descend. One of them says, 'O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement,' and the other says, 'O Allah, give the one who withholds a loss.'"

Al-Bayhaqi related in (Shu'ab al-Iman) from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Every expenditure the servant makes, its replacement is upon Allah, the Exalted, as a guarantor, except expenditure on construction or in disobedience."

Al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: Spend, O son of Adam, and I shall spend upon you."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in (Nawadir al-Usul) from him, who said: "The Prophet, upon him blessings and peace, said: Indeed, aid descends from the heaven in proportion to the burden."

In a lengthy hadith from al-Zubayr, Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Spend, and I shall spend upon you; expand, and I shall expand upon you; do not constrict, lest I constrict upon you; do not hoard, lest I hoard upon you. Indeed, the gate of provision is open from above the seven heavens, extending to the Throne; it is never closed, night or day. Allah, exalted is He, sends down provision from it upon every person according to the measure of his intention, his giving, his charity and his expenditure. Whoever gives much, more is given to him; whoever gives little, less is given to him; and whoever withholds, it is withheld from him. O Zubayr, eat and feed, do not tie up (the wealth) lest it be tied up upon you, do not count lest it be counted against you, do not be stingy lest stinginess be decreed upon you, do not make things difficult lest they be made difficult for you." The hadith continues.

The meaning of "al-raziqin" (the providers) is those who convey provision and bestow it. "Al-Raziq" is applied literally to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to others, as indicated by His saying, ﴿then provide for them from it﴾ [An-Nisa: 8]. Yes, it is not said of anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, "Raziq" (the Provider) in the absolute sense, so there is no difficulty in His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾; the aspect of His superiority is most evident. It has been said that applying "raziq" to other than Him, exalted is He, is metaphorical, on the basis that he is an intermediary in conveying His provision, so he is a provider in form, and thus the matter of comparative superiority was questioned, since the one preferred must share with the one preferred over in the essence of the act literally, not merely in form.

Al-Amidi answered that the meaning is: the best of those who are named by this name and are called by it, literally or metaphorically, and this is a kind of general metaphor.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 40:

﴿And the day He gathers them all together﴾, that is, the arrogant and the oppressed, or the two groups, "and what they used to worship besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic." ﴿And the day﴾ is an adverb governed by a verb either placed before it, meaning "and remember the day," or placed after it, meaning "and the day We gather them all together." ﴿Then He will say to the angels﴾ and so on: there will occur, on that day, of states and terrors what the scope of speech cannot encompass. The apparent sense of the conjunction with "then" (thumma) requires that the saying to the angels be delayed relative to the gathering, and there is in the reports something that bears witness to this. It has been narrated that after the creatures are gathered they will remain standing in the place of standing for seven thousand years, not speaking, until our Prophet (ﷺ) intercedes for the judgment to be decided. So perhaps at that point the One, glorified be He, will say to the angels, peace be upon them, ﴿Did these used to worship you?﴾ as a rebuke to the polytheists, a reproach to them, and a dashing of their hopes, which were vainly attached to the intercession of the angels, peace be upon them, since He, glorified be He, knows what they will answer, along the lines of His, exalted be He, saying to Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Their being singled out for mention is because they are the most honourable of the partners of the polytheists, those who have no scripture, and the righteous are customarily addressed. Their worship is the origin of polytheism, based on what Ibn al-Wardi reported in his history concerning the cause of the emergence of idol worship among the Arabs: that 'Amr ibn Luhayy passed by a people in al-Sham and saw them worshipping idols. He asked them, and they said to him, "These are lords we take, in the form of the celestial bodies, so that we seek victory through them and ask them for rain." So he followed them and brought an idol with him to the Hijaz, and it was an envoy to the Arabs. They worshipped it, and the worship of idols continued among them until Islam came. The worship of Jesus, peace be upon him, occurred long after that. Thus, by the manifestation of their deficiency from the rank of being worshipped and their exemption from being worshipped, the state of the rest of the partners becomes evident by way of a fortiori reasoning.

﴿And these﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿used to worship﴾ (kanu ya'budun) is its predicate, and ﴿you﴾ (iyyakum) is the object of ﴿worship﴾ (ya'budun), placed first for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah), although it is more important given the matter of rebuke. The fronting of its object was used as evidence for the permissibility of fronting the predicate of kana when that predicate is a clause over it, as Ibn al-Sarraj held, since fronting a complement indicates the permissibility of fronting the governing verb. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that this rule is not consistent, and then said: "The better view is to prohibit that, unless there is a sound report from the Arabs indicating its permissibility." The majority of the readers recited "nahshuruhum" and "thumma naqulu" with the nun in both verbs.

They say: this is an explanatory resumptive clause (*istinaf bayani*), as if it were asked: "What will the angels say then?" So it is answered: they will say, glorifying Him above that, ﴿Glory be to You; You are our Protector, not them﴾. The shift to the past tense form (*sigha al-madi*) indicates certainty, meaning: You are the One whom we take as our ally, not them. There is no alliance between us and them. By this, they declared their innocence of approving of their worship. Then they turned away from that and denied that they had actually worshipped them, saying: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, meaning the devils, as narrated from Mujahid, since they used to obey them in what the devils embellished for them of worshipping other than God, the Exalted. It was also said that the devils took the forms of a group of jinn for them and said: "This is the form of the angels, so worship it," and they worshipped it. It was also said that they used to enter the bellies of the idols when these were worshipped, and so they were worshipped through the worship of the idols. It was also said that they meant they had worshipped something they imagined to be the jinn, not us, so they actually worshipped the jinn, not us. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that among the disbelieving nations there were some who worshipped the jinn, and in the Qur'an there are verses from which it appears that the jinn were worshipped, as in Surat al-An'am and elsewhere.

﴿Most of them believed in them﴾. The second pronoun refers to the jinn and the first to the polytheists. "Most" is taken in its literal sense, because among the polytheists there were some who did not believe in them and worshipped them only following their people, like Abu Talib. Or "most" means "all." Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr*, preferred the first view, because "most" meaning "all" is not literal. He said: They did not claim comprehensive knowledge, since among the disbelievers there may be someone whom God, the Exalted, did not inform the angels, peace be upon them, about. Or they judged most of them by their belief in the jinn, because belief is an act of the heart, so they did not claim knowledge of the actions of all their hearts, since that belongs to God, Mighty and Majestic. It is also permissible that the first pronoun refers to humankind, so "most" is literal, meaning most of them affirm that they are gods. It was also said they affirm that they are daughters of God, ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. And it was said they affirm that they are angels.

**﴿So today none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another﴾**. This is among what will be said to the angels, peace be upon them, when they answer by disowning what the polytheists attributed to them. They are addressed with this before all the witnesses, to make manifest their own powerlessness and their inability to benefit those who claimed to worship them, and to state explicitly what will utterly dash the hopes of those polytheists. It is also said that this was said to the disbelievers, but that is not the correct view. The *fa'* (the particle *fa*, "so") indicates that what follows is a consequence drawn from the angels' answer. The attribution of the absence of benefit and harm to an unspecified "some of you" serves to emphasise the point that is intended, namely that the angels cannot benefit their worshippers. This is placed in the same series as the absence of benefit from the worshippers to the polytheists, as though the angels' benefit to their worshippers were as impossible and as absent as the worshippers' benefit to them. The mention of the absence of harm, although there is no question of it, is either to generalise the powerlessness, or to apply the absence of benefit to the supposition of worship and the absence of harm to the supposition of abandoning it. It is also said that what is meant is the averting of harm, with the omission of a *mudaf* (the first term of a possessive construction, here "averting"), but this is far-fetched. The "day" here is the Day of Resurrection. The restriction of the ruling to that day, although it holds in general, is because the polytheists' hope of benefit was pinned on that day.

**﴿And We will say to those who did wrong: Taste the Fire which you used to deny﴾**. This is coordinated with ﴿He says to the angels﴾. It is also said that it is coordinated with ﴿لا يَمْلِكُ﴾ (*lā yamlik*, "will not have power").

It has been objected that this is among what is said on the Day of Resurrection, addressed to the angels and following upon their reported answer, and that this report is a narration by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of what will be said to the worshippers on that day, immediately after the narration of what will be said to the angels, peace be upon them. It has been answered that this does not prevent it. So reflect.

The relative pronoun (*al-mawṣūl*, "which") occurs here as a description of the second term of the possessive construction (*al-muḍāf ilayhi*), whereas in the Sajdah, in His saying ﴿the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾, it is a description of the first term (*al-muḍāf*). Abu Hayyan said: "This is because they were then already engaged with the punishment, as His saying indicates: ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [As-Sajdah: 20]. So what they were engaged with is described there. Here they were not yet engaged with it, rather this is the first time they saw the Fire after the Gathering, so what they witnessed is described." To make the relative pronoun here a qualifier of the first term, on the grounds that its feminine gender is borrowed so that the two verses are alike, is a forced and unsightly construction.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 43:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ is an explanation of another aspect of their disbelief. That is, when Our verses, which declare the truth of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) and the falsehood of shirk (associating partners with God), are recited to them through the tongue of the Messenger ﷺ, ﴿they say, "This is not"﴾, meaning the Messenger of God ﷺ who recites the verses. The use of "this" (hadha) is contemptuous. May God destroy them. ﴿"but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship"﴾, so that he may make you his followers without having any divine religion. The attribution of "fathers" to the addressees, rather than to themselves, is meant to stir up their tribal zeal ('asabiyya), as an exaggeration in confirming them in shirk and repelling them from tawhid.

And they say, "This is not", meaning the recited Qur'an. The reference of "this" is like the earlier reference. ﴿"but a fabricated lie"﴾, that is, speech diverted from its proper meaning, having no reality corresponding to it, ﴿"invented"﴾ by attributing it to God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth﴾, that is, of the matter of prophethood, which is accompanied by such extraordinary events (khawariq al-'ada, departures from normal custom) as it is; or of Islam, which separates a person from his spouse and his child; or of the Qur'an, by which souls are moved. The conjunction (of the two descriptions) is due to a difference in aspect, in that the first is intended in its meaning and the second in its inimitable composition. ﴿"when it came to them"﴾ without any reflection or consideration of it, ﴿"this is nothing but evident magic"﴾, whose magical nature is manifest.

In the mention of "said" (qala) a second time, and in the explicit mention of the disbelievers, and in what the two lams (in "lilhaqqi" and "lamma") contain of an indication to the speakers and to what was said about them, and in what the word "lamma" contains of hastening to pronounce this false statement, there is a great denunciation of it and an eloquent expression of astonishment at it. It is also permissible that each sentence was uttered by a different group of the disbelievers.

Page 153

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 44:

﴿And We did not give them﴾ — i.e., the people of Makkah — ﴿any books that they study﴾ which would establish the validity of polytheism, so that they might have an excuse for it. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾ [al-Rum: 35], and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21]. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. Al-Suddi said: the meaning is, "We did not give them books that they study, so that by studying them they would know the falsehood of what you have brought." This returns to the first meaning. The intended point is the negation that they have any proof for the validity of the polytheism they hold. "Min" (from) is extra (silah). The plural "books" is, as has been said, an indication that its falsehood is so severe, and its establishment by any transmitted or rational proof so impossible, that it would require repeated proofs of great strength; so how could one claim what clear proofs have consistently contradicted?

Abu Haywah read "yadarrisunaha" with a fatha on the dal, a shadda on it, and a kasra on the ra', the present tense of "iddarasa" (the form ifta'ala from "al-dars," study), meaning "they study it together." Also from him, "yudarrisunaha," from "al-tadris," which is the repetition of study; or from "darasa al-kitab" without shadda, and "darrasa al-kitab" with shadda, where the doubling is taken to indicate plurality of the action.

﴿Nor did We send to them before you any warner﴾ — i.e., We did not send to them before you any warner who called them to polytheism and warned them of punishment for abandoning it. It has already become clear that this has no basis in any respect, so from where did they derive this deviant position? There is in it an unmistakable degree of mockery and ascribing ignorance to them.

It is also permissible that what is meant is that they were unlettered people in a period of interruption (fatrah), having no excuse for polytheism nor for not responding to you, unlike the People of the Book, who have books and a religion that they refuse to abandon, and who argue against following the Prophet by saying that their prophet warned them against abandoning his religion, even though he made the falsehood clear, since there is established a matter from before him concerning following him and the announcement of him in the books. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that the earth has never been without a caller to the Oneness of God, exalted is He. Thus the meaning is the negation of sending a warner specifically to these people who would address them directly. Among the Arabs there was much of the warning of Isma'il, peace be upon him, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 54]. But none devoted himself to warning and fought for it except Muhammad (ﷺ). End of quote.

Then He threatened them with His saying, glorified is He:

﴿And those before them denied﴾ from the earlier nations and the bygone generations, with what they denied.

﴿And they have not reached﴾ i.e., the people of Makkah, ﴿one-tenth [mi'shar]﴾ i.e., a tenth of what ﴿We gave them﴾. Some said that al-mi'shar is a tenth of a tenth, but Ibn 'Atiyyah did not approve of this. Al-Mawardi said: the intent is hyperbole in minimization, meaning they did not reach the least little of what We gave those earlier deniers of long lifespans, bodily strength and abundant wealth.

﴿So they denied﴾ i.e., those deniers ﴿My messengers﴾ whom I sent to them, ﴿so how was My rejection﴾ i.e., My rejection of them through destruction. So let these people beware of the like of that.

The first fa' (ﻑ) is causal (sababiyyah, indicating cause). The first ﴿and denied﴾ (kadhdhaba) is treated as intransitive (lazim), i.e., those before them committed denial and undertook it, and the parallel is for someone to say: "So-and-so embarked on disbelief, so he disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ)." From here they said that ﴿they denied My messengers﴾ is conjoined to (﴿and those before them denied﴾) as the restricted (muqayyad) conjoined to the absolute (mutlaq), and it is the explanation of the meaning of ﴿and they have not reached﴾, and it is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). The second fa' is explanatory (fasihah), so the meaning is: when they denied My messengers, My rejection came upon them through destruction, so how was My rejection of them. The destruction was made a rejection by treating the deed as if it were speech, as in his saying: "We insult with deeds, not with speech," or as in the line:

Their greeting among them is a painful striking.

Some allowed that the form of taf'il in (﴿kadhdhaba﴾ of ﴿those before them denied﴾) is for intensification (takthir), and in (﴿they denied﴾) for transitivity (ta'diyah), while the denier in both is one and the same, i.e., they multiplied lying and became accustomed to it, until it became a disposition for them, so that they became bold enough to deny the messengers. On both views there is no repetition. It is also permissible that ﴿they denied My messengers﴾ be conjoined to what is ﴿they have not reached﴾, being part of the parenthetical clause, and the pronoun refers to the people of Makkah, meaning: these did not reach a tenth of what We gave those earlier deniers, and they surpassed them in denial, because their denial of the Seal of the Prophets (ﷺ) is a denial of all the messengers (peace be upon them) in two respects. On this view no repetition is imagined, as is not hidden. That the clause of ﴿they have not reached﴾ is parenthetical is the apparent view, and making ﴿and those before them denied﴾ a preparation so that this clause would not be so is refuted by ﴿so how was My rejection﴾, because its meaning is definitively for the earlier deniers. Thus there is no harmony except by saying it is parenthetical. Returning the pronoun of ﴿they have not reached﴾ to the people of Makkah, and the object pronoun in ﴿We gave them﴾ to ﴿those before them﴾, and explaining the relative pronoun as stated above, is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. It was also said that the first pronoun refers to those before them and the second pronoun to the people of Makkah, meaning: those did not reach a tenth of what We gave these of clear signs and guidance. It was also said that both pronouns refer to those before them, meaning: they denied, and they did not reach, in thankfulness for the blessing and in repaying the favour, a tenth of the blessings and kindness We gave them. Abu Hayyan preferred this view, giving as his reason the coherence of the pronouns, since he made the pronoun of ﴿so they denied﴾ refer to those before them. So do not be heedless.

[p. 154]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 46:

﴿Say: I admonish you with one thing﴾ That is, I only guide you and advise you with one single quality. It is, as Qatadah said, what is indicated by His words, ﴿that you stand up for Allah﴾, taking it as being in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar) which is either a substitute (badal) for it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is your standing up," or an object of an omitted verb, that is, "I mean your standing up." Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) to "one thing."

It has been objected that ﴿an taqumu﴾ is definite, since it is taken to mean "by your standing up," and that ʿatf al-bayan, according to the Basrans, must be definite following definite, whereas according to the Kufans it follows what precedes it in definiteness and indefiniteness, and the difference is something no one has held.

The apparent position is that al-Zamakhshari holds the permissibility of a difference (between the two), and Ibn Malik, one of the qualified scholars of Arabic, explicitly attributed this to him in al-Tashil. It is also permissible that he expressed it as ʿatf al-bayan while intending badal, because the two are closely related. Here is the imam of the discipline, Sibawayh, who calls emphasis (tawkid) a description (sifa) and ʿatf al-bayan a description as well. Furthermore, the claim that the masdar formed with "anna" is always definite or always treated as definite is not accepted. Standing (al-qiyam) is a metaphor for earnestness and striving. It has also been said that it is literal, and that what is meant is standing up away from the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but this is not the case. It has been transmitted that Ibn Jurayj denied that this was intended. That is: if you strive and exert yourselves in the matter, sincerely for the sake of Allah the Exalted.

﴿in pairs and singly﴾ That is, dispersed, two by two and one by one, for crowding, for the most part, causes distraction of the mind, obstruction of thought, confusion of speech, and lack of fairness, as is witnessed in those lessons in which a group gathers, where hardly any verification can be reached.

In placing "in pairs" first is an indication that it is more reliable and closer to tranquility. In al-Bahr it is said that it is placed first because seeking the realities with two who support each other in reflection is more fruitful than a single thought; when the truth flashes between two, each of them then reflects afterwards and gains more insight, and the opening spreads between the two.

﴿Then you reflect﴾ upon his matter (ﷺ) and what he has brought, so that you may know its truth. The pause (waqf) here is according to Abu Hatim.

His words, the Exalted, ﴿There is no madness in your companion﴾ are a resumptive statement (istinaf) directed from Him, the Exalted, to alert to the method of consideration and reflection: that such a great matter, under which lies the dominion of this world and the next, is not undertaken to be claimed except by a madman who does not care about being exposed when challenged for proof and his incapacity appears, or by one who is supported by Allah the Exalted, designated for prophethood, confident in his argument and proof. Since you know that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is the most rational of people, the most truthful in speech, the most intelligent in soul, the most excellent in knowledge, the best in conduct, and the one who most combines human perfections, it is necessary that you believe him in his claim. How much more so, when there have been added to that miracles before which the solid mountains would crumble.

The expression of him, upon him be blessings and peace, as "your companion" is to indicate that his condition (ﷺ) is well known among them, because he grew up among them, known for what we have mentioned. It has also been permitted that it be connected to what precedes it, and the pause on "madness" is taken as the object of an omitted verb of knowing, indicated by the reflection, since reflection is the path to knowledge. That is: then you reflect so that you know what your companion has of madness; or it is an object of "you reflect" with reflection taken as a metaphor for knowledge; or it is an object for the purpose without any metaphorical usage, according to what Ibn Malik held in al-Tashil, that "tafakkara" is construed like verbs of the heart. It has also been permitted that there is an implicit meaning, that is: then you reflect knowing what your companion has of madness. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: according to Sibawayh it is the answer to what is treated as an oath, because "tafakkara" is among the verbs that give distinction, like "tabayyana," and the reflection in this case would be on the signs of Allah the Exalted and belief in Him. And that, as you see, is not right. The negation here is absolute, the "ba" means "in," and "min" is an extra particle. It has also been said that "ma" is interrogative of denial, and "min" is explicative, and it has been permitted that it too be an extra particle, but that prolongs the distance, and omitting it is preferable.

﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾ This is the punishment of the Hereafter, for he, upon him be blessings and peace, was sent close to the Hour, and it has come in a hadith: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and the Prophet (ﷺ) joined the middle finger and the index finger, according to the well-known report.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say: "Whatever reward I have asked of you"﴾ i.e., whatever benefit I have asked of you in return for conveying the message, ﴿it is yours.﴾ The intended meaning is the outright negation of asking, like your saying to your companion: "If you give me something, then take it," while you know that he has not given you anything. So "mā" is a conditional particle, and its object is ﴿sa'altukum﴾ (I have asked you). This is what is related from Qatadah. It has also been said that "mā" is a relative pronoun, the returning pronoun is omitted, and "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and the "fa" (then) entered the predicate because it implies the meaning of a condition: i.e., "that which I have asked you of reward, it is yours, and its fruit returns to you." And this, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is an allusion to the love for the kinsfolk in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. That this belongs to them is clear according to the view that by "the near of kin" is meant their (the Quraysh's) kinship; but according to the view that by it is meant the kinship of the Prophet, peace be upon him, then because the Prophet's kinship is also their kinship; or it is an allusion to that and to what is implied by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it, except from whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 57]. It is evident that taking a way to Him, Exalted is He, is their greatest benefit. It has also been permitted that "mā" be negative and "min" be extra, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿then it is yours﴾ is the answer to an implied condition, i.e., "so if I have not asked you, then it is yours," but this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾ supports the intended meaning of the outright negation of asking. It has been read "in aji" with the yā' sukūn.

﴿And He is over all things Witness﴾ i.e., Observer, so He, glorified is He, knows my truthfulness and the sincerity of my intention.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 48:

﴿Say: Indeed my Lord hurls the truth.﴾ Al-Suddi and Qatada said: "With the revelation (wahy)." In another report from Qatada: "With the Qur'an." The outcome is one, and the root meaning of qadhf (hurling) is throwing with great force. Here it is used metaphorically for casting (al-ilqa'), and the bi (with) is extra (za'ida), meaning: indeed my Lord casts down the revelation and sends it down upon the heart of whomever He chooses from among His servants, glory be to Him. It was also said that qadhf is implicitly (mudamman) carrying the sense of ramy (throwing), so the bi is not extra. It was also permitted that al-haqq (the truth) means the opposite of al-batil (falsehood), and the bi is for accompaniment (mulabasa), with the object of hurling omitted. The meaning would then be: indeed my Lord casts what He casts to His prophets, peace be upon them, of revelation, in truth and not in falsehood.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: He hurls falsehood with truth, that is, He brings it against falsehood until He annihilates and removes it, mighty and majestic is He. Al-haqq is the opposite of al-batil, and the bi is like it in your saying "I killed him with the blow" (qatal-tuhu bi al-darb). In the statement there is a explicit metaphor (isti'ara musarraha) of the follow-up type (taba'iyya): the borrowed-from term is sensory (hissi) and the borrowed-for term is intellectual ('aqli). It was also permitted that the metaphor be implicit (makniyya). It was said: the meaning is that He throws the truth to the far reaches of the horizons, and that this is a metaphor for spreading it abroad. Then the statement becomes a promise of the manifestation and spread of Islam, and in it is as much metaphor as there is.
[p. 156]

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ is a second predicate (khabar thani), or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning: He, glory be to Him, is the Knower of the unseen. Or it is an adjective (sifa) carried to the position (mahall) of inna with its noun, as many grammarians permitted, though Sibawayh forbade it. Or it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿hurls﴾. It is not required that the predicate clause be free of a returning pronoun (ai'd), because the substituted element is not, in every respect, intended to be dropped. Al-Kisa'i said it is an attribute (na't) of that pronoun, and his school permits describing an implied third-person pronoun with an adjective.

ʿĪsā, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Abū Ḥaywa, and Ḥarb from Ṭalḥa recited (عَلّامَ) in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said it is an attribute of "my Lord." Abu al-Fadl al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya said it is a substitute (badal). Al-Huwfi said it is a substitute or an attribute. It was also said it is in the accusative by way of praise (al-madh). Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Bakr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited (الغِيُوبِ) with kasra, like (البِيُوتِ), while the rest recited it with damma, like (الشُّعُورِ). In both cases it is a plural (jam'). It was also recited with fatha, like (صَبُورٍ), on the basis that it is a singular used for emphasis (mubalagha).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 49:

﴿Say: The truth has come﴾, i.e., Islam and tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), or the Qur'an. It was also said: the sword, because the truth becomes manifest through it. But this is, as you see, far-fetched. ﴿And falsehood can neither originate nor restore anything﴾, i.e., disbelief (kufr) and polytheism (shirk). ﴿Nor restore﴾, i.e., it has gone and vanished such that no trace of it remains. The expression is taken from the death of a living being: when it dies, it no longer has the capacity to begin any act (ibda') or to repeat it (i'adah), i.e., to do something a second time, as one says "he neither eats nor drinks," meaning he is dead. The statement is therefore a kinaya (metonymy) for what has been mentioned, or a majaz (figurative usage) based upon the kinaya. They recited, in support, the verse of ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras:

"ʿUbayd has been left desolate of his people; today he neither originates nor restores."

A group said: the "falsehood" is Iblis, and it is so called because he is its source and origin. In that case there is no kinaya in the statement. The meaning is: he does not create a creation, nor does he restore; or, he does not originate any good for his people, nor restore it, i.e., he does not benefit them in this world or the Hereafter. It was also said that it refers to the idol, and the meaning is: "what you have heard." It is reported from Abu Sulayman that the meaning is that the idol does not initiate speech so as to be answered, nor does it refute the truth that has come with any argument.

As for "wa ma" in all of these interpretations, it is a negating particle (nafiyah). It was also said that, on every view other than the first, it is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari) governing what follows it, i.e., "what is it that falsehood originates, and what is it that restores?" and its ultimate sense is negation. The statement has been permitted to be a completion of what preceded it, or to be of the type of reversal and reciprocal application (al-'aks wa al-tard), or to be a concluding summary (tadhyil) confirming that. So reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 50:**

﴿Say, "If I go astray"﴾ from the truth, ﴿then I only go astray to my own detriment﴾, meaning that the harm and burden of that will return upon me, for the self is the one that earns evil and commands to evil. ﴿And if I am guided﴾ to the truth, ﴿then it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾. The guidance is by His guidance and His enabling success, exalted and majestic is He. The word *mā* (what) is either a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*) or a verbal-source particle (*maṣdariyya*). The apparent form would have been "and if I am guided, then it is for it (*fa-lahā*)," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self, and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 46]. Or it would be "if I go astray, then I only go astray to the detriment of myself," so that the antithesis would be apparent. But he (ﷺ) departed from that, being satisfied with the antithesis in meaning, because the whole discourse is built upon it, since every harm comes from the self, through it, and its burden falls upon it. The particle *ʿalā* (upon) in the first clause indicates the meaning of *lām* (for) in the second, and the *bāʾ* (by) in the second indicates the meaning of causation (*sababiyya*) in the first. It is as if it were said: "Say: If I go astray, then I only go astray by means of my self, to the detriment of my self; and if I am guided, then I am only guided for my own self, by the guidance and enabling success of God, glorified is He." He expressed this with ﴿what my Lord reveals to me﴾ because it is necessarily connected with it. Taking *ʿalā* to mean causation, although the antithesis appears in it, is a deviation from the apparent sense without a subtle reason.

It is also permitted that the meaning of the first clause be: "Say: If I go astray, then I only go astray to my own detriment, not to the detriment of others," and in this case the antithesis is not apparent at all. The ruling, according to what al-Zamakhshari said, is general. He (ﷺ) was only commanded to attribute it to himself because, when the Messenger enters within it, despite the greatness of his station and the soundness of his path, others are more appropriate for it. The Imam said: That is, the going astray of my self is like your going astray, because it proceeds from my self and its burden falls upon it. As for my guidance, it is not like your guidance by reflection and inference (*naẓar wa-istidlāl*), but it is by the luminous revelation (*waḥy*). Thus the combined ruling is specific to him, upon him be blessings and peace. In what he mentioned there is an indication of what al-Tibi said, that the proof from transmission (*naql*) is higher and more majestic than the proof from reason (*ʿaql*), but in this there is a discussion.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Thabit and ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Muqri' read *ḍalilt* with a kasra on the *lām*, and *aḍillu* with a fatḥa on the *ḍād*; this is the dialect of Tamim. ʿAbd al-Rahman read the hamza of *aḍillu* with a kasra. It is also read *rabbī* with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ*.

﴿Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near﴾, so nothing is hidden from Him, glorified is He, of the speech of each one, whether guided or astray, nor of his action, even if he strives to conceal them. He will therefore recompense each according to what befits him.
