Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 51:

﴿And if you could see when they are seized with terror﴾: that is, a constriction and recoil from a dreadful, fearsome matter has overtaken them. The address in "you could see" (tara) is either to the Prophet ﷺ or to everyone who is capable of seeing. The object of "tara" is omitted, meaning "the disbelievers" or "their terror." Or it is "idh" (when) used figuratively, since what is meant by seeing a time is seeing what occurs in it. Or the object is left unstated, the verb being treated as intransitive, meaning: if seeing should occur from you. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: you would see a tremendous matter. This terror, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, is on the Day of Resurrection, and the apparent meaning of it is the terror of resurrection, and this is related from al-Hasan. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Qatadah that it is in this world at the time of death, when they witness the angels, peace be upon them. Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Dahhak that it is the Day of Badr, so it is said to be the terror of war. And from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, it is the terror of having their necks struck and of witnessing the punishment. It has also been said that it is at the end of time, when the Mahdi appears and sends an army against the Sufyani, and he defeats them; then the Sufyani marches against him until, when he is in a desert of the earth, he and those with him are swallowed up by the earth, so none of them escapes except the one who reports about them. So the terror is the terror of what will befall them on that day.

﴿So there is no escape﴾: they cannot escape God, Mighty and Majestic, by flight or otherwise from what He wills for them, may He be glorified. ﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾: from the place of standing to the Fire, or from the surface of the earth to its depths, or from the plain of Badr to the well, or from beneath their feet when they are swallowed up. The mention of the nearness of the place is intended to convey the swiftness of the descent of punishment upon them and their being held in contempt and destroyed; otherwise, there is no nearness or distance with respect to God, Mighty and Majestic.

The clause is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "they were seized with terror," according to the view taken by a group. In al-Kashshaf it says: "It seems that the benefit of the delay is that one should supply 'so there is no escape' a second time, either for emphasis, or because each of the two is different from the other, drawing attention to the fact that the non-escape is a cause of the seizing, and that the seizing is a cause of its certain realization in existence; and in this there is good emphasis." It has also been said that "there is no escape" is a sentence meaning: they did not escape and they were seized. Ibn Jinni chose this view, objecting to the earlier explanation that it is not meant that "if you could see" at the time of their terror and seizing, but rather that "if you could see when they were seized with terror" and they did not escape and were seized. What was transmitted from al-Kashshaf resolves this objection.

It is also permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "they were seized with terror," or from the predicate of the implied "la" (there is no), which is "for them," with or without "qad" supplied. Regarding the "fa" in "so there is no escape," it has been said: if it is causal (sababiyyah), it enters upon the caused, because their not escaping results from their terror and bewilderment; and if it is explanatory (ta'liliyyah), it enters upon the cause, because the mention of the cause follows the mention of the effect. And when "they were seized" is conjoined to it, or made a circumstantial clause from the predicate, it is what is intended by the subsequent elaboration.

ʿAbd al-Rahman, the mawla of Banu Hashim, related from his father, and Talhah, read "fa-la fawtun wa-akhdhun" as two verbal nouns (masdar) with tanwin. Ubayy read "fa-la fawta" as indeclinable (mabni) and "wa-akhdhun" as a verbal noun with tanwin. When "akhdhun" is in the nominative, it is either the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and their state is seizing," or a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "and there is seizing there." Abu Hayyan went to this view. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has been read 'wa-akhdhun' in the nominative, on the basis that it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of 'la fawta,' and its meaning is: there is no escape there, and there is seizing there."

﴿And they say, "We believe in Him"﴾: i.e., in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, according to what a group has transmitted from Mujahid. A (different) group said: i.e., in Muhammad (ﷺ), whose mention has already occurred in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Your companion is not possessed﴾. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the punishment, and it was said that it refers to the Resurrection. Its reference to Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, was preferred, because belief in him (ﷺ) encompasses belief in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in what was mentioned of the punishment and the Resurrection.

﴿And how can they reach [such] attainment?﴾ Al-tanawush means al-tanawwul (taking hold of, reaching), as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, and it is narrated from Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an easy taking hold of a nearby thing. One says nasha yanushu-hu and tanawashahu al-qawm, and tanawashu fi al-harb, meaning some of them struck others with weapons. The rajiz (rajaz poet) said:

"She reaches for the basin with a reaching from on high,
a reaching by which she cuts across the wide deserts."

Keeping it on its general sense is preferable, i.e., "From where can they attain faith ﴿from a distant place﴾?" For it lies within the domain of obligation (taklif, religious responsibility), and they are far removed from it. Al-Bahr (the exegesis Al-Bahr al-Muhit) transmits from Ibn 'Abbas the explanation of ﴿al-tanawush﴾ as "return," i.e., "From where can they return to the world?" Ibn al-Anbari recited:

"He wished to return to Mayy,
but there is no way to reach her."

It is not hidden that this is not a clear text on that point. The intended meaning is an image of their state in seeking salvation through faith after it has passed them by and become distant, by the state of one who wants to reach a thing after it has moved far from him and escaped him, making it impossible.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read ﴿al-tanā'ush﴾ with a hamza. This is explained as the conversion of the waw into a hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: "Every waw that carries a necessary damma, you have the choice: if you wish, you keep it, and if you wish, you convert it into a hamza. So you say thalath adwur without hamza and thalath adu'ur with hamza." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying: "It is not absolute. It is not permitted in the medial position when it is an assimilated (idghām) form, as in ta'awwud and ta'awwudh as verbal nouns, and this has been stated explicitly in al-Tas-hil. Nor is it permitted when it is sound in the verb, as in tarahwak tarahwuk and ta'awana ta'awunan. On this basis, the stated explanation is not valid, because al-tanawush is like al-ta'awun in that its waw is sound in the verb, since you say tanawush and it is not hamzated."

Al-Farra' said: it is from na'asht, i.e., "you delayed," and he recited the verse of Nahshal:

"He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me,
though after affairs there have arisen [new] affairs."

I.e., "he wished, at last." The pronoun refers to the client (mawla) in his saying:

"A client who disobeyed me and was self-willed in his opinion,
just as one lacking [power] is not obeyed in what I wish."

Thus the hamza in it is original, and the word has come from two roots. Some of them said: it is from na'asht al-shay' when you sought it. Ru'ba said:

"The neighbor of Abu al-Khabush thrust me
toward you, in pursuit of the sought-after fate."

So the hamza is also original. It has been said that, according to these two views, al-tanawush carries the meaning of reaching from a distance, because the latter requires that, and seeking does not apply to a thing that is near you and present with you; thus ﴿from a distant place﴾ serves as emphasis. Or al-tanawush may be taken in the general sense of reaching. Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) discussed the interpretation of the distance in its qualifier as temporal distance, saying it is not correct, because the borrowed term (al-musta'ar minhu) is spatial, and what is mentioned of the states of the borrowed term (al-musta'ar lahu) is not.

﴿وقَدْ كَفَرُوا بِهِ﴾ [while they had disbelieved in it] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a conjoined clause (maʿṭūf), or a resumptive new sentence (mustaʾnaf). The first is closest. The pronoun in ﴿بِهِ﴾ refers back to the pronoun in ﴿آمَنّا بِهِ﴾ [we believed in it], ﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [before] meaning before that, at the time of obligation.

﴿ويَقْذِفُونَ بِالغَيْبِ﴾ [and they hurl at the unseen] means they used to pelt with conjecture and speak about what had not become clear to them, and what did not arise from verification concerning the matter of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus they attributed a partner to Him, glorified is He, and said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," exalted is Allah far above that in great exaltation. Or it concerns the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, and they said of him, far be it from him: "a poet, a sorcerer, and a soothsayer." Or it concerns the punishment or the resurrection, and they made definite statements denying it. ﴿مِن مَكانٍ بَعِيدٍ﴾ [from a far-off place] means from a distant position relative to the affair of those about whom they spoke. The clause is conjoined to ﴿وقَدْ كَفَرُوا﴾. The apparent form would have been "وقَذَفُوا" [they hurled], but the verb was shifted to the present form (muḍāriʿ) to narrate a past state as if present. It has been said that the statement is perhaps an analogy for their condition in speaking about what appears to them without verification, to the case of one who throws something he cannot see from a far-off place, where there is no room for conjecture about its reaching the target. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it is conjoined to ﴿قالُوا آمَنّا بِهِ﴾ [they said, "We believed in it"], on the basis that in their seeking they set forth an analogy of obtaining what they had neglected of faith in the world by saying "we believed" in the Hereafter. That is a remote aim, like one who hurls something from a far-off place where there is no room for conjecture about its reaching, while he wishes that it land in its place, because he is absent from it and distant.

[p. 159]

Mujahid, Abu Haywa and Mahbub on the authority of Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يُقْذَفُونَ﴾ [they are hurled at] in the passive voice. Mujahid said: that is, the revelation pelts them with what they dislike of what was hidden from them of the heaven. The clause seems to stand in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾, as if it were said: "and they had disbelieved in it before, while they are being pelted with the truth that was hidden from them and concealed from them." The purpose is to magnify the gravity of their disbelief. It is also permissible that by ﴿الغَيْب﴾ [the unseen] is meant what was concealed of their faults, that is: "and they had disbelieved, while revelation from heaven pelts them and strikes them with what was concealed of their faults." Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: that is, "and they are pelted with the unseen from where they do not know," and its meaning is that they are recompensed for the evil of their deeds, and they have no knowledge of its source, either in the state when repentance is no longer possible at the sight of death, or in the Hereafter. End. Yet the circumstantial reading of the clause on this basis carries some obscurity. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, "and the devils hurl them with the unseen and instruct them in it." It seems the clause is conjoined to (قَدْ كَفَرُوا) [they had disbelieved]. It has also been said: that is, they are cast into the Fire, and that, as you see, is weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 34, verse 54:

﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the return to the world. Al-Hasan said: it is accepted faith. Qatadah said: obedience to God, exalted is He. Al-Suddi said: repentance. Mujahid said: family, wealth and children. It has also been said that the meaning is: a barrier is placed between the army and the believers by the sinking of the army into the earth, or between them and the destruction of the Ka'bah, or between them and deliverance from the punishment, or between them and the bounty and pleasures of the world. This is also related from Mujahid. The verb ﴿ḥīla﴾ is in the passive voice, and its deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il), as Abu Hayyan said, is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun, i.e., "it was barred," meaning the barring (al-ḥawl) itself, and its sense is that the barring occurred. Because it is a pronoun, it is not a emphatic verbal noun, so it stands in the place of the subject. On this basis the line of poetry is explained:

"She said: whenever you are denied and made to make excuses, you will be grieved; and if your passion is uncovered, you will be humbled."

That is, "it is made to make excuses," meaning the making of excuses itself. Al-Hawfi said: the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) stood in the place of the subject. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr objected to this, saying that if it were so, it would be in the nominative case, and attaching a pronoun does not justify building it (on a vowel, i.e., making it mabni). Otherwise, one could say "jā'a ghulāmuka" with a fatḥah, and no one says that. Yes, there are places where building occurs due to attachment to a mabni word, which you have mastered in grammar. What does al-Hawfi say about the line:

"Indeed a barrier has been placed between the caravan and the bounty"?

Here he put ﴿bayna﴾ in the accusative together with its attachment to a case-inflected noun. Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿ḥīla﴾ with ishmam of the ḍamma on the ḥā' (a faint rounding of the vowel).

﴿As was done to their likes before﴾: that is, to their similar ones among the disbelieving nations of the past. The phrase ﴿min qablu﴾ ("before") is connected to ﴿ash-yā'ihim﴾ ("their likes"), on the basis that the intended meaning is those who share their attributes from earlier times, i.e., in the first age. This is supported by the fact that what is done to all of them in the Hereafter occurs at one time. Alternatively, it is connected to a verb, if the barring is in this world. It is related from al-Dahhak that the intended meaning of ﴿ash-yā'ihim﴾ is the People of the Elephant. Apparently he applied the verse to al-Sufyani and those with him.

Page 160

﴿Indeed they were in disquieting doubt﴾: that is, in a state that caused suspicion. This is on the reading that it derives from ﴿arābahu﴾, meaning he caused him to fall into suspicion and accusation, or it means one who has suspicion, from ﴿arāba al-rajul﴾, meaning he became one who has suspicion. Either the doubt has been likened to a person who can be disquieting, by way of implicit metaphor (al-isti'āra al-makniyya al-takhyīliyya), or the ascription is figurative, in that what belongs to the doubter is ascribed to the doubt for emphasis, as one says "the poetry of a poet." It is perhaps from here that Ibn 'Atiyya said: disquieting doubt is the strongest form of doubt. The plural pronoun refers to the likes (ash-yā'), and it is said to refer to those earlier people mentioned.

And God knows best.

Among the allusive (ishara) interpretations of some verses of the surah is what has been said regarding ﴿And We gave David grace from Us: "O mountains, echo with him, and the birds"﴾. The mountains are taken as an allusion to the realm of dominion (ʿālam al-mulk), and the birds to the realm of the unseen (ʿālam al-malakūt). They have mentioned that when remembrance (dhikr) takes firm hold, it spreads through all parts of the body, so the one who remembers hears every part of himself remembering. When his state ascends, he hears everything in the realm of dominion in the same way. When it ascends further, he hears everything in existence in the same way, and ﴿there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾: the heart. ﴿That you make complete coats of mail﴾: these are the profound wisdoms that appear from the heart upon the tongue. ﴿And measure well in the links﴾: that is, in the stringing of speech, by speaking wisdom according to what the mind of your listener can bear. It has been transmitted: "Speak to people in what they recognize. Do you wish that God and His Messenger (ﷺ) be denied?"

From here it becomes difficult to answer those among the Sufis who speak of things that most scholars who hear them deny, and by which many people have gone astray. ﴿And to Solomon the wind﴾: the wind of divine care. ﴿Its morning course was a month and its evening course was a month﴾: he would exercise influence by spiritual resolve and by casting lights into the hearts of his followers from a distance of a month. ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord﴾: an allusion to the strength of his inner being, since the one who rebelled and committed evil was subdued to him. ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾: that is, one who gives thanks through states, meaning taking on the character of God, exalted is He.

﴿Then when We decreed death for him, nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth eating away at his staff﴾: in this there is an allusion that the weak may give knowledge to the strong. ﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾: these are the stations of the people of the inner reality among the knowers, ﴿clearly visible towns﴾: these are the stations of the people of outward observance among the ascetics. ﴿Travel through them by night﴾: in the nights of human nature, ﴿and by day﴾: in the days of spiritual nature, ﴿safely﴾: under the protection of the Sharia.

Some of the new sect of the unveilers (al-Kashfiyya) said: the blessed towns are the Imams, may God be pleased with them, and the visible towns are their callers and their envoys between them and their followers. ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾: by inclining to the world and abandoning the journey, due to the badness of their preparedness. ﴿Until, when terror is removed from their hearts, they say: "What has your Lord said?"﴾: in this there is an allusion that awe prevents understanding. ﴿And We have not sent you﴾: that is, We have not brought you out from non-existence into existence, ﴿except comprehensively to mankind﴾: the first and the last, ﴿as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾: and this is his state, upon him be blessings and peace, in the world of spirits and in the world of bodies. ﴿But most people do not know﴾: since they have no light by which to be guided. ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say﴾: "This is nothing ﴿but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship﴾." These are the highway robbers upon God's servants, and like them are those who denounce God's friends and drive people away from believing in them and following them.

﴿Say: "If I go astray, I go astray only to my own detriment; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me"﴾: "Indeed the soul commands to evil." ﴿By what my Lord reveals to me﴾: from the Qur'an. In this there is an allusion that it is a light with which no darkness remains, or that the degrees of guidance by it vary according to the variation in understanding that arises from the variation in the purity and cleanness of the inner being. It has been transmitted that the Qur'an has an outer and an inner meaning, and a person can hardly reach its inner meaning except by purifying his inner being, as His saying, exalted is He, points to: ﴿None touch it except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 79]. We ask God, exalted is He, to enable us to understand its outer and inner meanings, and whatever depths He wills, for He, glorified and exalted, is the Capable who says to a thing, "Be," and it is.
